Four non-negotiable principles

One route from idea to lasting public value

  • Humans remain accountable. AI never grants authority a person does not already hold.
  • AI outputs are verified, not trusted by default. Every claim traces to a citable source.
  • Public value, equality and accessibility are built in — screened before delivery, not audited after.
  • Evidence, metadata and provenance are mandatory for anything material or public-facing.

Spotlight · new in 3.4.0

Human oversight that is measured, not assumed

Nine new chapters: oversight principles and controls, how to measure oversight without monitoring people, skill atrophy and automation drift, a twelve-step runbook with governance templates, neuroinclusive AI at work, and a register of 164 obligations across the four nations.

Common tasks

2 minutesBeginner

Decide how much human review my output needs

Answer six questions and get an H0–H5 level, the reviewers required and the evidence to keep.

 3 minutesBeginner

Write an AI-use declaration and evidence pack

Generate a copy-ready record of sources consulted, checks made and who approved what.

 5 minutesIntermediate

Screen a change for equality and accessibility impact

Flag protected characteristics, access needs, assisted digital and exclusion risks early.

 10 minutesIntermediate

Draft a public transparency record

Produce an ATRS-shaped record describing the tool, its purpose, data, oversight and risks.

 5 minutesAdvanced

Check quantum and cryptographic exposure

Score harvest-now-decrypt-later risk against NCSC migration milestones.

 ReferenceIntermediate

Find the authoritative source for a rule

Search 69 tiered laws, standards, guidance documents and tools.

Not sure whether to use AI at all? Ask three questions first: is there a simpler non-AI way to meet the user need; can you explain the decision to the person it affects; and could you defend this use at a public inquiry? If any answer is no, stop and seek advice.

AI Capability Governance and Implementation

The guidance for deploying AI agents in the public sector, sequenced into one route — and the operating capability that turns experimentation into governed services. Crown-copyright sources are the government's own; every illustrative figure is labelled.

Start here

Eight stages from mandate to governed operation. The last stage feeds the third: every review either re-authorises the agent, changes it, or ends it.

Stage 8 returns to stage 3 — the loop does not close

Usage and cost Who uses it, how often, what it spends

Accuracy and drift Evaluation results against the baseline

Risk and incidents New risks, near misses, escalations

Value realised Benefits claimed against benefits evidenced

Review or retire Re-authorise, improve, restrict or decommission

Monitoring and human oversight are continuous duties held by the named owner, not a phase that ends at go-live.

Where this guide sits

The hierarchy of AI-related guidance a public-sector team works inside. This guide is a proposal: it interprets and sequences the guidance above it, and it does not replace or override any of it.

International frameworks

OECD AI Principles, EU AI Act risk tiers, ISO/IEC 42001 management standards.

UK statute and cross-government policy

Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR, Equality Act 2010, Procurement Act 2023, the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

Central guidance in force

AI Playbook for the UK Government, Service Standard, Technology Code of Practice, ATRS, Data Ethics Framework, NCSC secure-AI guidelines.

Departmental policy and standards

Organisational AI policy, data classification, security standards, delegated authority and spend controls.

This implementation guide

AI Capability Governance and Implementation — 69 chapters, assessment tools and register schemas that turn the guidance above into delivery.

Proposal

Team-level artefacts

Agent register entries, ATRS records, assurance evidence, instruction blocks and cost models.

Multidisciplinary from the outset

Every source in this app lands on the same point. The AI Playbook makes skills and expertise a principle in its own right. The Service Manual builds the multidisciplinary team into the Service Standard. NCSC wrote its secure-AI guidelines for data scientists, developers, managers, decision-makers and risk owners together. The roster is in Teams; the readiness barometer is in the Observatory.

Part 1 · Start hereChapter 1.2 · 2 of 85

Responsible AI · start here

What do you want to do?

Start from your task. This part of the playbook routes you to the proportionate tool, template, assessment or support. Governance follows what the AI can see, create and do, not which company made it.

Quick route selector · five questions

Can I use AI for this?

1. Would the output decide, or directly change, someone’s rights, entitlements, safety or access to a service?
2. Will you use personal data or information marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or above?
3. Can the AI take actions, run on a schedule or work through several steps without you?
4. Is there an approved tool in your organisation's catalogue that already does this?
5. Could a conventional rule, form or automation do the job reliably?

Your route

Answer the five questions

The route appears when every question has an answer. “Not sure” is a valid answer.

A first sort, not an approval. Any route other than an approved tool leads to a registered use case.

Six things to know first

AI concepts and limitations

Generative AI predicts plausible output. It can be fluent and wrong at once, so outputs need checking in proportion to what depends on them.

Models and providers

A product can use several models from several providers, sometimes chosen automatically. The model can change without the product name changing.

Enterprise grounding

Grounding feeds organisational content to the model. Whatever the index can reach, the AI can surface, including titles, filenames and metadata.

Agents, tools and actions

An agent plans steps and uses tools to act: send, update, create or call other agents. Acting changes the risk boundary.

Human oversight

Oversight works only if the reviewer has the competence, the evidence and the authority to challenge, override or stop.

Deployment route

The same model reached directly, through a cloud platform or inside another supplier’s product is a different governance object each time.

How to use this guide

87 chapters in 12 parts. Nobody needs all of it. Pick a reading mode, then a route.

Front to back

12 parts in delivery order: decide, build, assure, operate, fund, the people and pilot material, then the deployment part and the reference. Roughly a day's read.

By role route

10 routes below, each an ordered set of chapters for one job. Twenty to forty minutes.

By task

Use the launchpad or search: rate readiness, tier an agent, price a job, build an instruction block, check exit readiness.

Routes by role

Each route is an ordered set of chapters. Click any step to jump there.

Data and information

Get data ready, keep metadata and indexing honest, govern connectors and treat AI outputs as records.

All colleagues

Find an approved tool, get a route for your task, and know where to get help.

Accountable leader or SRO

Decide where AI is worth the risk and the spend, and be able to answer for it.

Service owner

Adopt agents without destabilising a service people depend on.

Product or delivery manager

Frame the problem, prove the value, keep the team moving.

AI engineer or technical owner

Build well-grounded agents and prove they work.

Assurance, ethics or audit

Apply proportionate control and see the evidence behind it.

Commercial, finance or FinOps

Fund adoption honestly and keep exit possible.

People, learning and adoption

Build capability that outlasts the pilot.

Pilot participant

Use the guide during a real deployment and record what happens.

What each part is for

1 · Start here

What the guidance says, what this guide adds, and the ten capability domains it all rests on.

2 · Decide and prioritise

Whether to do it at all: evidence quality, use-case selection, criticality and the assurance tier that follows.

3 · Design and build

Capability class — generative, agentic or declarative — then instructions, architecture, grounding and the autonomy boundary.

4 · Assure and govern

The trust cycle, the operating model, risks and mitigations, registers, transparency records and recovery.

5 · Operate and oversee

Life after approval: the portfolio view, the agent lifecycle, public-service impact and readiness tracking.

6 · Fund and buy

The full investment line, unit economics, supplier requirements and exit.

7 · People and adoption

Teams, roles, pathways, inclusion and the organisational adoption programme.

8 · Live pilot

How this guide is being tested in a real deployment, and what would justify a permanent toolkit.

9 · Product documentation

Requirements, architecture, design, theory of change and the research base for the guide itself.

10 · Knowledge and navigation

Glossary, thesaurus, generated knowledge graph, taxonomies, ontology, site map, guided tours and platform links.

11 · Deploy for real

The part that turns the guide into a deployment: fifty-four real services placed on volume and criticality, a generator that derives the whole governance set for any case, four agents carried end to end — one in each quadrant — and an explicit list of what this guide still does not cover.

12 · Reference

Devolved and international comparators, and every source behind the content.

How to read the labels

Verified Present in a surfaced source.

Interpretation A conclusion drawn across sources.

Proposal Recommended future state, not adopted policy.

Illustrative Looks like data, carries no measured source.

What this guide is not

It does not override departmental policy, professional advice or formal approvals.

It is not the register of record for any live deployment.

It holds no personal, case or OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data; assessments stay on your device.

It cannot issue an approval — the accountable owner does that.

Part 1 · Start hereChapter 1.4 · 4 of 85

The playbook

Ten principles, one life cycle

The AI Playbook for the UK Government (opens an external website) (GDS, 10 February 2025) supersedes the Generative AI Framework and covers all AI: machine learning, NLP, computer vision, generative and agentic systems. The ten principles are paraphrased below; open each for its first moves.

The deployment life cycle

Playbook principle 5: manage the whole life cycle, including the unglamorous parts. Each stage has a gate; nothing moves right without passing it.

Stage 1

Discover
  • Frame the problem and the user need: is AI the right tool at all?
  • Triage risk: personal data, decisions about people, public-facing?

Assemble the multidisciplinary team; screen for DPIA and equality impacts

Gate · A named SRO and a written problem statement

Stage 2

Design
  • Decide buy vs build; source and assess the data
  • Threat-model with security; place the human-oversight points

Legal, ethics and commercial shape the approach, not the finished thing

Gate · DPIA drafted; risks owned; oversight designed in

Stage 3

Build & evaluate
  • Develop securely; verify the model and data supply chain
  • Evaluate accuracy, bias and robustness against agreed baselines
  • Red-team it: prompt injection, misuse, edge cases

Gate · Evaluation results reviewed by the whole team

Stage 4

Deploy
  • Pass assurance gates; publish the ATRS record
  • Switch on human review and incident response
  • Tell users they are interacting with AI

Gate · Assurance sign-off; transparency record live

Stage 5

Operate & retire
  • Monitor drift, bias and hallucination in production
  • Re-evaluate on every model or data update
  • Plan decommissioning and knowledge handover

Gate · Monitoring dashboards live; exit plan on file

Part 1 · Start hereChapter 1.5 · 5 of 85

The domains

Five lenses on every deployment

Cyber, data, digital, technology, and the legal-ethical frame around them. Each domain has its own authoritative guidance; a deployment is ready only when all five say so. That is why the team is multidisciplinary.

Cyber

Cyber security

NCSC secure AI guidelines
NCSC machine learning principles
Secure by Design (UK Government)

NCSC Guidelines for secure AI system development cover secure design, development, deployment and operation. Agreed with CISA and 21 international agencies; aimed at any system that uses AI, built or bought.

Secure by Design and the Government Cyber Security Standard apply to AI services like any other, plus AI-specific threat modelling: prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, over-permissioned agents.

NCSC's principles for the security of machine learning translate the threats into controls. Walk before you run with agentic AI.

Data

Data & information

Data Ethics Framework
ICO: AI and data protection
ATRS hub

The Data Ethics Framework guides appropriate, responsible data use across the public sector: transparency, accountability, fairness.

UK GDPR and the DPA 2018 require a DPIA before high-risk processing. The ICO's AI guidance, with a statutory AI code of practice in development, is the regulator's view of what good looks like. Cross-border processing (for example a US-processed model behind a UK product) needs a Transfer Risk Assessment as well as SCCs.

The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard is mandatory for central departments and arms-length bodies: a published record for every in-scope algorithmic tool.

Model quality is data quality: govern provenance, representativeness and retention for training and grounding data alike — retrieval systems inherit the permissions, quality and currency of the estate.

Digital

Digital & service

Service Standard
AI Playbook for the UK Government
AI Knowledge Hub

The Service Standard and Service Manual set the operating model: start with user needs, work in multidisciplinary teams, iterate in the open. AI services are still services.

The AI Playbook and the AI Knowledge Hub supply the patterns, case studies and communities; the PM's AI Exemplars programme is the test-and-learn engine for scaling what works.

Accessibility is law, not polish: WCAG 2.2 AA under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. AI interfaces (chat, voice, summaries) need their own accessibility evidence.

Technology

Technology & architecture

Technology Code of Practice
AI Opportunities Action Plan
Action Plan delivery progress

The Technology Code of Practice governs the technology choices: cloud first, interoperability, open standards, sustainability, exit.

Compute and infrastructure are national policy: AI Growth Zones and a compute roadmap from 21 ExaFLOPs (2025) towards 420 by 2030 under the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

Buy well: use Crown Commercial Service AI routes, insist on evaluation access and model-change notice in contracts, and design the exit before signing the entry.

Legal & ethics

Legal, ethics & society

Explaining decisions made with AI
Data Ethics Framework
Equality Act 2010 guidance

The Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty apply to automated and AI-assisted decisions. Public-law duties (fairness, rationality, giving reasons) still bind when a model is in the loop.

Explainability has a manual: 'Explaining decisions made with AI', by the ICO and The Alan Turing Institute — and explanations shown to people should reference functional needs, never a diagnosis or label.

Public trust is earned in the open: engage affected people early, say clearly where AI is used, and give a route to challenge and redress.

The evidence

Same product. Four UK evaluations. Four answers.

What varies is method, not the tool. Uncontrolled self-report gives the highest figures; comparison-group econometrics gives mid-range; counterfactual-free evaluation of a short pilot gives the lowest. Role mix is the second driver.

minutes / day

Cross-government, GDS

20,000 staff, self-reported

60

minutes / week

HMRC, randomised cohort

3,000 licences

19

minutes / day

DWP, comparison group

3,549 staff, econometric

0

robust evidence

DBT, no counterfactual

1,000 licences

Never average these numbers. The spread is evidence about evaluation design. Sources: GDS findings report (Jun 2025); HMRC phase 3; DWP evaluation (Jan 2026); DBT evaluation (Aug 2025).

Four things block the move to governed scale

Unremediated permissions

AI surfaces what a user may already reach. Permission drift becomes an incident on day one.

Makes scaling UNSAFE

No agent inventory

The transparency standard records algorithmic tools. It is not an operational register of agents.

Makes scaling UNGOVERNABLE

Unpredictable consumption cost

Credits are billed per feature, not per conversation. A builder's design choice sets a budget holder's cost.

Makes scaling UNBUDGETABLE

Unfunded human effort

Workflow redesign, local support and output verification happen but rarely appear as funded lines.

Makes scaling UNSUSTAINABLE

Activity is running ahead of visibility

Between deployment and disclosure sits a gap no current UK instrument closes. The ATRS is a transparency mechanism, not an inventory: it does not capture team-shared agents, orphaned agents, data-source approval, consumption cost or retirement.

Coding agents: two findings, both real

A finding about where to deploy, not whether.

72% said good value; 58% would not return to working without it

19%

Benefit is largest on well-scoped, greenfield and boilerplate work; smallest or negative on mature, complex codebases. Developer self-assessment is unreliable in both directions. Join the AI Engineering Lab (OCTO, GDS) before procuring independently — the evidence you generate is reusable.

What the enthusiastic version leaves out

Contrary evidence, recorded deliberately.

17%

of cross-government trial users noticed no clear time savings (GDS, Jun 2025)

7%

of Australian participants reported the tool added time (DTA, Oct 2024)

61%

of Australian managers could not confidently identify AI outputs (DTA, Oct 2024)

72%

of councils were not ready on workforce skills and expertise (LGA, Jun 2025)

Canada names a further risk no UK instrument addresses: skill atrophy and automation drift. Skill maintenance is a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight, not an optional extra (TBS Canada, May 2026).

A caution on AI-produced research

Twenty sources in one AI research draft. What checking found:

7

verified precisely

6

verified in substance

4

not verified as cited

1

could not be located

None of the unverifiable entries was obvious: each was correctly formatted, plausibly dated, attributed to a real institution. Treat AI-produced research as a hypothesis-generating artefact, never an evidence base — and keep the verification log with the output.

Evidence labels used across this app

Verified fact — supported by official, regulatory, audit or primary sources

Organisation-reported — reported by the organisation itself, not independently measured

Supplier claim — authoritative for product terms; interested-party evidence for value

Interpretation — analytical judgement drawn from cited evidence

Recommendation — action proposed, not established practice

Unresolved — evidence incomplete, conflicting or arrangement-specific

Use cases & evidence

Where AI creates value across government and public services

Eighteen categories, from productivity tools to enterprise agents — supporting people, processes and public outcomes. Use AI and agents responsibly to enhance the work of public servants and improve outcomes for citizens.

1. Knowledge retrieval & insight Find, summarise and synthesise information from trusted sources

2. Content & correspondence Draft, edit and refine high-quality content and communications

3. Contact centres & helpdesks Support staff and citizens with accurate, consistent responses

4. Casework & service operations Streamline case handling, triage and workflow automation

5. Citizen services & engagement Deliver simpler, faster and more accessible services

6. Meetings & collaboration Capture, summarise and turn meetings into actions and outcomes

7. Data analysis & reporting Analyse data, create summaries and produce management information

8. Software engineering & IT operations Accelerate development, testing and secure operations

9. HR & people management Improve people processes and the employee experience

10. Finance & procurement Enhance financial planning, analysis and supplier management

11. Education, training & skills Personalise learning and improve knowledge retention

12. Programme & project management Plan, track and report with intelligent support

13. Health & care Support clinical and administrative workflows safely and securely

14. Policing, justice & public safety Improve investigations, evidence handling and public protection

15. Regulatory & compliance Monitor compliance and produce regulatory outputs

16. Policy & strategy development Scenario analysis, option generation and evidence synthesis

17. Communications & media Create campaigns, content and prepare responses

18. Research & horizon scanning Scan trends, research and emerging opportunities

Cross-cutting capabilities — enablers for all use cases

Secure access to trusted data & knowledge AI agents & orchestration (autonomy with oversight) Human oversight & accountability Privacy, security & data protection Quality assurance & model evaluation Observability, monitoring & auditability Integration with systems & workflows Change management & adoption FinOps & cost management

Foundational enablers

Data quality & governance Information management Access management Standards & interoperability Skills & culture Ethics & responsible AI

The use-case evidence card

A consistent way to describe, evaluate and share AI use-case evidence: what the capability does, who it helps, how it works, the value it delivers, and the evidence that supports it. Evidence first. Value always. Capture consistently, share openly, decide confidently.

1. Basic information Use case name · Short description · Unique ID · Date created · Last updated · Author / owner

2. Problem & purpose Problem / opportunity · Purpose & objectives · Success criteria

3. Users & context Primary user groups · Who benefits · Operating context / environment · Geography / organisation

4. Solution & capability AI capability / agent type · Key features / functions · How it works (high level) · Human oversight points

5. Data & information Key data sources · Type of data · Data sensitivity · Information governance

6. Implementation & integration Platform / technology · Systems / tools integrated · Deployment model · Date went live / expected · Resource requirements

7. Outcomes & value Quantitative outcomes (measured) · Qualitative outcomes (observed) · Value delivered (how & for whom)

8. Costs & financials Cost model (licence, usage, etc.) · Estimated / actual cost · Cost per user / transaction · Ongoing cost considerations · Funding source / owner

9. Risks & assurance Key risks · Mitigations in place · Assurance / evaluation approach

10. Evidence & validation Evidence summary · Evidence sources · What evidence is available (performance results, user feedback, evaluation report, audit / review, other)

11. Limitations & lessons Known limitations / constraints · Lessons learned / recommendations

12. Transferability & reuse Potential for reuse (high / medium / low) · Reusable artefacts available · Transferability notes

13. Lifecycle & review Lifecycle stage (ideation, pilot, live, scaled, retired) · Review frequency · Next review date · Sunset / retirement plan

Evidence strength
  • Strong — Independently validated
  • Medium — Reported results with some validation
  • Emerging — Pilot / early indications
  • Weak — Unverified claims
  • Unknown — Insufficient evidence
Evidence status

Live / in use Pilot / trial Planned Retired / stopped Unknown

Worked, failed and unproven

Sharing the full picture — successes, failures and emerging ideas — so we learn faster and build smarter. Transparent evidence helps the public sector avoid repeating mistakes and scale what works. The cases below are illustrative.

Worked — repeatable success

Evidence shows value, quality and user benefit.

Case: ACAS 'Haste' helpline knowledge assistant

Helps advisers quickly find accurate, impartial information during calls.

What worked
  • Grounded in authoritative, approved and consistent formats
  • Tested with 1,000 differently worded questions
  • High accuracy and consistency across impartiality and bias checks
  • Clear roles, assistant, not decision maker
  • Positive adviser feedback and time savings
Outcomes
  • Faster information retrieval
  • Improved accuracy and consistency
  • Better adviser experience
  • Scalable to wider teams

Failed — learned & corrected

Initial attempt did not deliver — lessons captured and applied.

Case: AI-assisted NHS document processing

Automated extraction from clinical documents produced high initial error rate.

What went wrong
  • Poor data quality and inconsistent document formats
  • Incomplete metadata and missing context
  • Model hallucinations and incorrect extractions
  • Insufficient validation and no independent review loop
  • Rushed from prototype to wider use
What we did next
  • Reduced manual re-keying and error tracking
  • Good accuracy in structured readings
  • Went back with clear agendas and permissions
  • User trust and change impact still being assessed
  • Scalability and cost model not yet validated

Unproven — promising, not yet validated

Early potential identified — evidence still limited.

Case: Agent automatically summarises meeting action agent

Summarises meeting decisions, actions and sends updates to owners.

What we know so far
  • Long-term testing across teams and meeting types
  • Long-term accuracy and retention unknown
  • Cost at scale and return on investment not established
  • Governance and data sensitivity assessments in progress
Next steps

Extended pilot, independent evaluation, costing and governance review before scaling

  • Data quality and validation are critical
  • Human review and iterative testing prevent scale of error
How we succeed together

Share openly, including failures Ground in authoritative sources Test with real users Measure impact and value Capture lessons and publish patterns Reuse and continuously improve

Four proven delivery patterns

Each pattern is a pipeline with human oversight built in — not a single tool. Use them as the starting shape for a new use case.

Meeting intelligence pipeline

Transforming conversations into decisions, actions and organisational memory

1. Meeting planning 2. Consent & capture 3. Transcript creation 4. AI processing & summarisation 5. Decisions & actions 6. Risks & insights 7. Distribution & integration 8. Organisational memory

Authoritative knowledge assistant

Delivering trusted, accurate answers grounded in authoritative sources, with human expertise in the loop

1. Define need 2. Retrieve 3. Evaluate & ground 4. Generate response 5. Human review 6. Deliver answer 7. Feedback & learn 8. Maintain sources

AI-assisted engineering lifecycle

Secure. Quality. Production-ready. Human in control.

1. Discover & plan 2. Architect & design 3. Build & code 4. Test & validate 5. Review & assure 6. Deploy & release 7. Operate & monitor

AI-assisted programme & portfolio management

Smarter oversight. Better decisions. Greater impact.

1. Capture & ingest 2. Analyse & understand 3. Plan & optimise 4. Monitor & track 5. Decide & recommend 6. Collaborate & execute 7. Learn & improve

Responsible AI · assess a use case

Classify first, then answer only what your tier needs

As AI can see more, do more and act more independently, the assurance required rises. Criticality & gates scores the service impact; this chapter sets the route from what the AI itself can do.

Class

1. Ask

  • Answer and assist
  • Provides information, answers or summaries based on a prompt.
  • Example: Ask about a policy or summarise a document.
2. Create
  • Generate content
  • Creates new content, analysis, images or code.
  • Example: Draft a briefing, a presentation or code.
3. Connect

Use organisational information

Retrieves and works with data from organisational sources and external systems.

Example: Search SharePoint or analyse internal data.

4. Act
  • Take actions
  • Makes changes in systems, files or records, or triggers workflows.
  • Example: Create a record, send an email or start a process.
5. Delegate
  • Complete multi-step work
  • Plans and performs several steps with tools and limited supervision.
  • Example: Research, analyse, write a report and share it.
6. Persist
  • Operate proactively
  • Runs autonomously or on a schedule, monitoring and acting over time.
  • Example: Monitor changes, raise tickets or act on triggers.

Generative, declarative and agentic: the three capability types

The capability classes say what the AI can do; the capability type says how it is built. Both set the assurance.

goes deeper on choosing between them.

Generative

Creates content in response to a prompt: text, summaries, images or code. A person decides what happens next.

Declarative

Configured, not coded. Purpose, instructions, knowledge and permitted actions are declared; the platform supplies the model and orchestration.

Agentic

Plans and takes actions across tools under delegated authority, choosing its own path to a goal, sometimes on a schedule.

ClassUsual capability typeMinimum assurance
AskGenerativeReview the output.
CreateGenerativeReview the output; label AI involvement.
ConnectGenerative, grounded · or Declarative with knowledge sourcesTest what the index and connectors expose; review sources.
ActDeclarative with actions · or AgenticApproval before action; log every action; least-privilege connectors.
DelegateAgenticFull agent route: identity, tool permissions, approval points, behavioural tests.
PersistAgentic, scheduled or proactiveSpecialist assurance: defined oversight, monitoring and a kill switch.
What to assure: Generative

Output quality, grounding sources, data entered, transparency labels.

T3 · T4 · T6
What to assure: Declarative

The declared configuration: instructions, knowledge sources, actions, owner, version and publishing scope. Reviewed like code.

T7 · A2 prompt and skills record
What to assure: Agentic

The whole human-agent system: identity, tools, approval points, escalation, logs, cost caps and the kill switch.

Decision record outcomes

Approve

Proceed within the documented scope and controls.

Approve with conditions

Proceed once named conditions are met; conditions are tracked.

Pilot

Controlled authority for a limited population, time and data set.

Restrict

Narrow the users, data or actions permitted.

Extend

Extend a pilot to gather the missing evidence.

Stop

Do not proceed. Record the reason and lessons.

Part 2 · Decide and prioritiseChapter 2.5 · 10 of 85

Criticality & assurance gates

Usage is not the same as criticality

Evaluate across ten dimensions to identify the agents that need stronger governance, assurance and operational support. Score each 1 (very low) to 5 (very high); the total sets the criticality tier and the action.

1. Usage & adoption

How many people use it and how often?

2. Audience & reach

Who relies on it? Internal teams, partners, other organisations, or the public?

3. Business impact

How important is it to achieving business outcomes or service delivery?

4. Decision impact

Does it influence, recommend or make decisions that have significant consequences?

5. Data & information

What is the sensitivity, value and regulatory significance of the data it uses or produces?

6. Autonomy level

How independently can the agent act? Human-in-the-loop versus autonomous.

7. Irreversibility

How easy is it to reverse an error or unintended action?

8. Integration & dependencies

How integrated is it with other systems, processes or agents?

9. Risk & compliance

What are the legal, regulatory, security and reputational risks?

10. Public consequence

Could failure cause harm, loss of trust or impact citizens?

CRITICALITY SCORE

— —

0 of 10 dimensions scored

Score every dimension for a criticality tier.
From score to action

12–20 LowMonitor, light governance, owner accountable

21–30

ModerateStandard governance, regular review and quality checks

31–40

HighEnhanced assurance, monitoring, human oversight required

41–50

Very highEnterprise governance, formal support, continuity and audit

Scoring guide
  • 1 Very low — Minimal impact or exposure
  • 2 Low — Limited impact or exposure
  • 3 Moderate — Noticeable impact or exposure
  • 4 High — Significant impact or exposure
  • 5 Very high — Critical impact or exposure
Example agents across tiers

LowPersonal research assistant used by creator only

ModerateTeam policy search agent used by a department

HighCase triage agent influencing case allocation and actions

Very highCitizen service agent that makes determinations or commitments

Key questions to ask
  • Who owns it and is responsible for its use?
  • What happens if it gives the wrong answer?
  • Where does it get its information from?
  • How is it tested, monitored and reviewed?
  • Does it support a critical business process?
  • Is it shared outside its original team or creator?
  • Could it become business or citizen critical?
Important reminders
High usage does not equal high criticality
Low usage can still be business critical
Reassess regularly as agents, usage and context change
When in doubt, apply the higher level of control

Assurance increases with audience, autonomy, information sensitivity, criticality and consequence. Pick a tier to see the gate required before use.

Assurance by design, proportionate by risk, continuous by evidence

A holistic, cross-disciplinary approach ensuring AI systems and agents are safe, secure, reliable, fair — and deliver public value.

Assurance domains

Security Privacy & data protection Data & information governance Ethics & fairness Transparency & explainability Human oversight & accountability Reliability & safety Evaluation & testing Auditability & evidence Risk management Legal & compliance Accessibility & inclusion

Applied across the lifecycle

1. Plan & designDefine purpose, risks, requirements and success measures

2. Build & deployDevelop, test, assure and prepare for secure deployment

3. Operate & monitorMonitor performance, risks, usage and emerging issues

4. Review & improveLearn from evidence, update controls and improve continuously

Key assurance questions
  • What are we trying to achieve and for whom?
  • What could go wrong and who could be harmed?
  • Is the data appropriate, accurate and lawful?
  • How will decisions be explained and challenged?
  • Can we evidence compliance and responsible use?
  • How will we monitor, learn and improve?
Evidence & assurance artefacts
  • Risk assessments
  • Data & DPIA records
  • Model cards & evaluations
  • Test results & red-team reports
  • Decision logs & audit trails
  • Policies, standards & guidance
  • Change logs & reviews

The human oversight and accountability chain

Agents must operate within clearly defined accountability and oversight boundaries, with named owners and transparent decision trails. Clear accountability at every step; human judgement at the right points.

1
Source owner
  • Owns the authoritative information and data made available.
  • Ensure accuracy and currency
  • Define permitted use
  • Manage access and permissions
2
Agent owner
  • Owns the agent's purpose, behaviour and operation.
  • Define purpose and scope
  • Configure behaviour and guardrails
  • Monitor performance and usage
3
Reviewer
  • Reviews AI outputs, recommendations and actions.
  • Validate accuracy and relevance
  • Check for bias, risk and compliance
  • Decide to approve, edit or escalate
4
Decision-maker
  • Accountable for the decision and its consequences.
  • Make or authorise the decision
  • Consider impact on people and services
  • Record the rationale
5
Service owner
  • Accountable for the service, outcomes and performance.
  • Ensure outcomes are achieved
  • Manage risks, incidents and issues
  • Provide assurance and improvements
6
Audit & redress
  • Provides independent assurance and holds the organisation to account.
  • Audit and review activity and controls
  • Ensure records, transparency and compliance
  • Enable challenge and redress
Human oversight points

1. Source approvalInformation is approved for use by the agent.

2. Configuration reviewAgent design and guardrails are reviewed and authorised.

3. Output reviewOutputs are checked for quality, risk and compliance.

4. Decision authorisationFinal decision is made or authorised by a person.

5. Outcome monitoringOutcomes and performance are monitored and reviewed.

6. Independent assuranceIndependent review, audit and redress are available.

Benefits

Clear accountability Better decisions Reduced risk Greater trust Stronger public value

Part 2 · Decide and prioritiseChapter 2.6 · 11 of 85

Maturity & assurance · illustrative frameworks

Where you are, and how much control that needs

Two illustrative frameworks from the capability report: a seven-stage maturity model for organisations, and six assurance tiers for agents. Neither scores named organisations; both are diagnostic tools to calibrate against evidence. Over-control halts adoption; under-control creates unmanaged exposure.

The seven-stage maturity model

Observable evidence at stage 2

Bounded pilots; named sponsors; temporary funding; largely self-reported benefit evidence.

Evidence to collect before claiming progression

Named owners, repeatable gates, measured outcomes — not licensed tools.

Leadership & service ownership

Named accountable owners, clear outcomes, risk appetite and decision records.

People & workforce

Role-based training, protected learning time, inclusive adoption measures, staff consultation.

Technology & agents

Register, architecture, approved platforms, integrations, autonomy level, observability.

Data & information

Authoritative sources, metadata, permissions remediation, retention, provenance.

Security & assurance

Threat model, DPIA where required, evaluation evidence, incident route, audit logs.

Commercial & supplier

Licensing clarity, usage data, audit rights, exit, substitution, support terms.

Finance & FinOps

Forecasts, showback, anomaly alerts, unit economics, value attribution.

Community learning

Reusable artefacts, supersession, contribution workflow, evidence of reuse.

Six agent assurance tiers — controls scale with autonomy

Bounded autonomy and recoverability adopted from Government of Canada agentic-AI guidance (May 2026).

1

Personal assistantDrafting, summarisation and retrieval for one accountable user

Acceptable-use policy, permissions hygiene, human verification, retention and transparency guidance.

2

Personal or team agentBounded knowledge and repeatable team tasks

Registered owner, approved sources, test prompts, sharing gate, usage telemetry.

3

Departmental reusable agentMultiple teams or a repeatable departmental process

Business, technical, information, risk and support owners; service level; change control; retirement plan.

4

Operational agentActs on records, workflows or line-of-business systems

Distinct identity, least privilege, action logging, rollback, incident response, continuous monitoring.

5

Citizen-impacting agentInfluences access, rights, safety, services or public communication

Impact assessment, legal basis, accessibility and equality assessment, transparency, redress, independent assurance.

6

Part 3 · Design and buildChapter 3.2 · 13 of 85

Design and build · capability classes

Generative, agentic and declarative

Three ways of using the same underlying models, with different failure modes and therefore different controls. Most real deployments combine all three, which is exactly why the class needs naming before the controls are chosen.

Generative

Produces content, analysis or options on request. Nothing changes until a person acts on the output.

You specify: A prompt, grounding sources and an output format.

Drafting, summarising, translating Analysis and option generation Search and question answering Code and test generation

Primary failure Plausible but wrong output accepted without review. Tier tendency Usually low to moderate: consequence sits with the person who acts on the output.

Controls that carry the weight

  • Accuracy and grounding evaluation
  • Citation and provenance
  • Disclosure that AI was used
  • Human review before use

Agentic

Takes actions across tools and systems under delegated authority, deciding its own path to a goal.

You specify: A goal, tools, permissions, guardrails and approval thresholds.

Triage and routing Multi-step workflow execution System updates within limits Orchestration across services

Primary failure Correct-looking action taken outside intended scope, or an irreversible action taken without approval. Tier tendency Moderate to high: the agent itself changes the world, so authority and reversibility dominate.

Controls that carry the weight

  • Capability separated from authority
  • Least-privilege permissions and recertification
  • Approval gates for consequential actions
  • Full action logging and rollback

Declarative

You state the outcome, rules and boundaries; the platform resolves how they are met and keeps behaviour inside the declaration.

You specify: Instructions, knowledge sources, permitted actions and constraints — as configuration, not code.

Configured assistants defined by a manifest Policy and rules expressed as configuration Low-code flows with declared triggers Templated agents published to a team

Primary failure The declaration drifts from intent, or nobody owns the specification that is now running in production. Tier tendency Varies with what is declared: the specification is the control surface, so review it as you would code.

Controls that carry the weight

  • Version control over the declaration
  • Named owner for the specification
  • Change assessment on every edit
  • Regression tests against the declared outcome

Side by side

Generative Agentic Declarative

What you supply Prompt and sources Goal, tools and authority Instructions, sources and constraints

Who chooses the path The person The agent, within guardrails The platform, within the declaration

What changes Nothing until a person acts Systems and records directly Whatever the declaration permits

Primary failure Wrong content believed Wrong action taken Wrong specification running

Assurance emphasis Output quality and provenance Permissions, approval and rollback Change control over the declaration

Register fields that matter most Sources, evaluation, review point Permitted actions, authority level, escalation Version, owner, constraints, publication scope

Which class is this?

Three questions. The answer sets the controls that matter most — not whether the work is allowed.

Does it change anything outside the conversation?
Who decides the steps?
Can its effects be undone without a person?

Most deployments are all three at once

Declarative shell

The declaration sets purpose, sources, permitted actions and limits — and is the artefact under change control.

Generative core

Inside those limits, the model drafts, summarises and reasons; evaluation and provenance apply here.

Agentic actions

Only declared actions run, each with its permission, approval threshold and audit trail.

Record the class in the register alongside purpose and authority. It tells a reviewer which controls to look for before they open the evidence — and it makes the difference between an agent that drafts and an agent that acts visible without reading the configuration.

Responsible AI · agents and skills

Assure the whole human-agent system, not only the output

What starts an agent, how it plans, what it can reach, where people stay in control, and what it leaves behind. Skill studio builds the instruction block; Autonomy boundaries sets the limits.

1. Trigger

What starts the agent?

  • User request
  • Scheduled task
  • Event: new email, meeting or file
  • System trigger: ticket or alert
  • API or webhook

2. Agent core

  • Model: chosen models and settings

  • Reasoning and orchestration: plans tasks, selects tools, handles errors

What it can reach and do

  • Call APIs and applications

Where people stay in control

5. Outcome

What it delivers

  • Completed task or output
  • System update or action taken
  • Notification or communication
  • Log and evidence: what happened, when and why

Cross-cutting control rails

Information and data controls

Classification and retention

Risks the agent route must test

Prompt and skill supply chain

A shared skill or instruction changed without review changes every agent that loads it.

Proposed

External input and prompt injection

Documents, web pages and emails can carry instructions that redirect the agent.

Proposed

Identity, delegation and shared accounts

Agents acting through shared or delegated contexts can reach more than the requester could.

Reported

Unexpected discovery

Permissions alone may not stop titles, filenames and metadata surfacing through the index.

Reported

Multi-agent orchestration

Agents calling agents need identity, approval points and automated records at each hop.

Reported

Telemetry gaps

Agent activity logs may not show enough to reconstruct what happened.

Reported

Continuous assurance

  1. 1. Test before deployment

    Behaviour, safety and access

  2. 2. Monitor in operation

    Usage, outcomes and incidents

  3. 3. Learn and improve

    Feedback and evaluation

  4. 4. Reassess on change

    Model, tools, data and permissions

  5. 5. Retire when no longer needed

    Revoke access, close data, capture lessons

Prompts and skills as organisational products

A personal prompt stays personal. Once a prompt, skill or agent instruction is shared, it needs an owner, a version, a test set, security checks, a cost profile and a retirement date, and it goes in the prompt and skills register.

  • Is the prompt or skill personal or organisational?
  • Does it need version control and approval?
  • Has it been tested for safety, consistency and cost?
  • Could deterministic automation do the job better?
  • Can it be shared or changed without review?
  • How will it be withdrawn?

Deterministic alternative test

Before building a generative skill or agent, check whether conventional automation is safer, cheaper and more consistent.

If a rule, form, flow or script can do the job reliably, use it. Generative AI earns its place where judgement over unstructured material is the actual task.

Part 3 · Design and buildChapter 3.5 · 16 of 85

Design and build · connectors, MCP and integrations

Every connector is a new data path and, often, a new action

MCP servers, connectors, plugins, add-ins and APIs turn a generative tool into one that can reach, and change, other systems. Each needs an owner, a scope and a log.

MCP serverAn open-protocol endpoint that exposes tools and resources to any MCP-capable client. Tools can be discovered at runtime, so capability can change without the agent being republished.

ConnectorBrings an external system’s content into an AI tool’s index or grounding, such as Copilot connectors.

Plugin or actionA packaged custom action, such as an MCP or API plugin in a declarative agent, that lets an agent read or change data.

Add-in or appAn extension that runs inside a host application, such as an Office add-in or a chat app.

API and webhookDirect integration through REST APIs, OpenAPI descriptions or event webhooks.

Integrator or gatewayA platform that brokers many connections, applies policy and logs traffic, such as an MCP gateway or integration platform.

Platform directory

Graded claims from supplier documentation. Where a route is unresolved, confirm it with the supplier before connecting.

Microsoft 365, Copilot and Copilot Studio Verified

Declarative agents call MCP servers and REST APIs through MCP and API plugins. Copilot Studio adds MCP servers through an onboarding wizard, and servers can be registered in Agent 365.

Routes: MCP plugin · API plugin · Copilot connectors · Power Platform connectors

Controls: Tools are discovered at runtime unless pinned in the manifest. Register MCP servers in Agent 365 and review each tool’s read and write scope.

MCP and API plugins for declarative agents ↗
Connect Copilot Studio to an MCP server ↗
Declarative agents for Microsoft 365 Copilot ↗

GitHub Verified

GitHub maintains a remote MCP server for repositories, issues and pull requests. Microsoft’s walkthrough wraps it as a plugin in a declarative agent.

Routes: Remote MCP server · GitHub Apps · Actions

Controls: One OAuth app per organisation, repositories scoped, no write tools without approval, and no secrets in prompts.

Build a declarative agent plugin from the GitHub MCP server ↗
Atlassian: Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, Loom

Corroborated

The official Rovo MCP server reached general availability on 4 February 2026. It is cloud-hosted and authenticates with OAuth 2.1 or API tokens.

Routes: Remote MCP server, v2 endpoint · Rovo agents

Controls: Admins choose which AI tools and domains may connect, destructive tool groups stay off until enabled, and every tool call is written to the audit log. Atlassian Cloud only, not Data Center.

Anthropic Claude Reported

Claude connects to Microsoft 365 and other systems through connectors built on MCP. Its Microsoft 365 connector reads Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive and writes to the last two.

Routes: Connectors · remote MCP servers · Skills

Controls: Set connector write scope per user, keep an admin allow-list, and record each connector in the data-source register.

No verified documentation linked yet.

Google Workspace and Gemini Unresolved

Gemini works with Workspace content and connected data. Confirm the current MCP and extension routes with Google before use.

Routes: Workspace grounding · extensions · APIs

Controls: Confirm data location, admin controls and audit logging for each extension.

No verified documentation linked yet.

Slack Unresolved

Slack can be a source or a destination for agent work. Confirm the official MCP or app route and its data residency before connecting.

Routes: App · MCP server · webhooks

Controls: Scope channels, keep private channels out without approval, and align retention.

No verified documentation linked yet.

Service and line-of-business systems Proposed

ServiceNow, Salesforce, Dynamics 365 and case-management systems publish connectors, APIs or MCP servers. Each is a new data path and a new action surface.

Routes: Connector · API plugin · MCP server · integration platform

Controls: Treat any write tool as Act class, require approval before change, and log to the incident trail.

No verified documentation linked yet.

Model Context Protocol, the standard Corroborated

An open standard that lets an AI client call tools and read resources on an outside system through one interface.

Routes: Specification · registry · gateways

Controls: Prefer official servers, pin tools where possible, review tool descriptions for injected instructions and route calls through a gateway that logs them.

modelcontextprotocol.io ↗

Nine controls for every connector, plugin and MCP server

  1. Register every connector, plugin and MCP server in the tool and data-source registers, with a named owner.
  2. Record read and write scope separately. Any write tool makes the use case at least Act class.
  3. Prefer official, supplier-maintained servers over community ones, and record which is in use.
  4. Pin tools or versions where the platform allows. Dynamic discovery means capability can change without republishing.
  5. Authenticate with OAuth and least privilege. No shared service accounts for user-level data.
  6. Log every tool call to an audit trail the service owner can read.
  7. Review tool descriptions and returned content for prompt injection.
  8. Check where each connected system stores and processes data, and whether it sits inside your data boundary.
  9. Keep a revoke route: users can withdraw authorisations and admins can disable a connector at once.

A connector can change the capability class

A generative chat tool with a read connector is Connect class. Add a write tool and it is Act class; let it run on a schedule and it is Persist. Reclassify whenever a connector or tool is added, and record it in the change register.

Part 3 · Design and buildChapter 3.6 · 17 of 85

Architecture & quality

Principles with tests, gates with teeth

A three-tier canon governs everything that influences how something is built — prototypes explicitly included, because most principle breaches enter the estate through prototypes that were never intended to survive, and then did.

Tier 1 — mandated, cited not restated

T1-01 Secure by Design T1-02 CAF & GovAssure T1-03 Technology Code of Practice T1-04 GDS Service Standard T1-05 AI Playbook T1-06 Data protection & public records T1-07 WCAG 2.2 AA

Tier 1 conformance is binary: the principle applies and is met, or a recorded exception exists. No informal partial conformance.

Tier 2 — the core seven, each with a test

AP-01
Federated, not centralised

Test: Can each element be traced to a named authoritative owner outside the central platform?Looks compliant, is not: "We will federate later, once everything is in one place."

AP-02
Discovery separated from access

Test: Can a user discover an asset exists without thereby gaining access to it?Looks compliant, is not: Endpoint or credential details published as discovery metadata for convenience.

AP-03
Human-in-the-loop by design

Test: Can any automated component write to the record without recorded human approval?Looks compliant, is not: "The user can always review it" — optional review presented as a control.

AP-04
Traceability & provenance mandatory

Test: Take any output at random: can you reconstruct inputs, owner, decision and evidence without asking a person?Looks compliant, is not: Evidence linked at closure rather than at capture.

AP-05
Reuse before build

Test: Is there a recorded reuse assessment that predates the build decision?Looks compliant, is not: Reuse assessment performed after the build decision, to justify it.

AP-06
Accessible & inclusive by design

Test: Is accessibility evidence produced before release? Does every status carry a non-colour cue?Looks compliant, is not: "We will run an accessibility audit before go-live" as the only accessibility activity.

AP-07
Guardrails enforced, not documented

Test: Attempt to breach the control through the normal interface. Does it succeed?Looks compliant, is not: A mandatory gate with no exception path — guaranteeing informal workarounds.

Prototype promotion gate. A prototype may not be promoted toward live use until Tier 1 and Tier 2 conformance is assessed and recorded. Record intended lifespan and disposal point at creation; record deferred principles; re-assess them at the gate. Human-in-the-loop applies in full even at prototype stage — autonomy introduced early is rarely removed later. Promotion is a decision, not a drift.

The assurance-gated agentic pattern

From the AI Engineering Lab's reference implementation: the transferable innovation is not any one use case — it is the operating model around it. Specialist agents routed by an orchestrator; a challenger agent that reviews outputs; a compliance agent; assurance gates executed in the workflow; immutable audit trails; human approval before anything writes to the record. The same pattern serves capability management, catalogue operations, workforce planning and architecture governance.

Specialist agents Orchestrator routing Challenger agent Compliance agent Assurance gates in-workflow Immutable audit trail Human approval to write Escalation paths

The quality gate — score prototypes like you mean it

A gate, not a form: run at the end of every iteration. Tier 0 is the brake — the only tier that can argue for less; a veto is the instrument doing its job. Scores are capped by evidence strength, unscoreable items go on an open register published with the score, and demo drift — a level-3 prototype someone useful quietly relies on — is the most common governance failure in this class of work.

Usability

Score the dimensions for a reading

The ladder: Tier 0 proportionality gate → Tiers 1–6 architecture compass → Tier 7 self-* autonomic → Tier 8 human & institutional sustainability. Evidence-rung caps; accessibility floors at human testing, not automated checks; an empty removal ledger three iterations running is itself a Tier 0 veto. The session evidence pack

Twelve components that turn a conversation into a reusable organisational asset. Session record · community owned · governed and secure · discoverable and reusable · continuously improved.

How it flows
  • 1. Capture — Capture during or after the session
  • 2. Structure — Organise using the standard evidence pack template
  • 3. Classify — Apply classification, tags and sensitivity controls
  • 4. Publish — Store in governed repositories and make discoverable
  • 5. Link — Connect to related assets, agents, use cases, and more
  • 6. Reuse — Teams find, reuse and build on the knowledge

Evidence status on every claim

VerifiedIndependently confirmed

Reported / emergingReported by a source, not yet validated

In progress / unvalidatedBeing worked through

Contradictory / needs reviewSources disagree

Outdated / supersededReplaced by newer content

The knowledge lifecycle

Good knowledge is captured once, curated well, reused often and improved continuously — and its status is always visible.

Create & capture 1. Capture Capture knowledge, evidence and experiences from sessions, projects or operations.

Create & capture 2. Classify & tag Add metadata, taxonomy, topics, sensitivity and links to related assets.

Curate & govern 3. Curate & quality Check accuracy, completeness, relevance and quality. Remove duplicates.

Curate & govern 4. Validate & approve Subject matter and governance review. Approve for use and assign lifecycle status.

Share & use 5. Publish & discover Publish to trusted repositories and make discoverable through search, portals and APIs.

Share & use 6. Use & reuse Apply knowledge in work, decisions and services. Share feedback and outcomes.

Share & use 7. Review & update Review on a regular cycle or when triggered by change. Update content, links, owners and status.

Share & use 8. Sunset, supersede or archive Retire outdated content, mark as superseded or archive with retention and audit trail.

Evidence status through the lifecycle

Draft Newly captured. Not yet reviewed.

Reviewed Peer or owner reviewed. Accuracy and relevance checked.

Validated Approved by subject matter and governance for use.

Published Officially published and visible to intended audience.

Superseded Outdated or replaced by newer content. Retained for reference.

High-quality information in, trusted retrieval and reasoning, accurate answers or actions, human review, better sources. Every link has a quality gate.

Key metrics for the chain

Answer accuracy rate Citation coverage User satisfaction score Time to answer Re-use rate of content Feedback captured Source improvements

Where should the information live?

Work down the questions in order. The first "yes" is your answer — the goal is the right information, to the right people, at the right time, securely and efficiently.

1. Is the information already in an authoritative source (for example an existing SharePoint site, policy library, DMS)?

Yes → Use existing authoritative location — keep content in place, ensure agent uses existing permissions, maintain single source of truth, lower duplication and maintenance risk.

2. Can the agent be granted access via existing permissions?

Yes → Grant access via existing permissions — respect least privilege, use groups and roles already in place, review access periodically.

3. Can permissions be adjusted for a new site (or team) without creating excessive oversharing or security risk?

Yes → Adjust permissions or create a secure location — create dedicated site or library if needed, configure granular permissions, review with the information owner.

4. Is copying or moving content necessary for the agent to function effectively?

Yes → Copy or move content with strong controls — risk of duplication and divergence, increased maintenance and update process, maintain links back to source of truth, confirm retention and records handling.

If every answer is no — reconsider the approach
  • Use metadata, views, filters or connectors
  • Use automated search over authoritative sources
  • Build a knowledge layer or index
  • Avoid unnecessary duplication
Key considerations
  • Audience — Who will use the agent and what access do they need?
  • Permissions — Does the agent respect existing SharePoint permissions?

Information governance — Is the content authoritative, current and controlled?

Duplication risk — Will copying create multiple versions or conflicting answers?

Maintenance — Can the team keep copies current and in sync with the source?

Licensing & cost — Do users have the right licences? Any connector or storage costs?

Records & retention — Where is the record of business? How long must it be kept?

Security & risk — Does the agent minimise risk of overexposure or data leakage?

Exceptions and the shadow AI route

Unmanaged external use falls when asking for an approved alternative is quicker than working around the rules.

  1. Search your organisation's catalogue for an approved alternative.
  2. If none fits, request one through a use case with the reason it is needed.
  3. Get an interim decision within an agreed time, with conditions.
  4. Record the exception in the decision register with an expiry date.
  5. Review at expiry: approve, restrict or close.

Communication authenticity

Keep clear labels on AI-sent messages and disclose material AI involvement. Removing a label is prohibited where transparency is required.

Evidence and transparency records

AI involvement statements

What AI did in producing a document, decision or message.

Source records

The sources an output drew on, so a reader can check them.

Human verification

Who checked the output, against what, and when.

Decision-support records

How AI informed a decision and who made it.

Code records

Provenance and review of AI-generated code.

Agent action logs

What an agent did, when and why.

Audit evidence

Configuration, approvals and test results for assurance.

Evidence grades for product and supplier claims

These sit alongside the guide's own conventions (verified, interpretation, proposal, illustrative). They grade claims about products and suppliers, many of which come from community calls.

Verified

Confirmed against authoritative supplier documentation or a live configuration.

Corroborated

Reported by more than one independent source or session.

Reported

Raised in a community call or channel. Not yet confirmed.

Proposed

A design recommendation in this portal, not a finding.

Unresolved

An open question. Do not rely on it until answered.

Assure and govern · data and information governance

AI governance is data governance with actions attached

Whatever an AI tool can reach, it can surface, summarise and act on. Data and information governance sets what it should reach, and treats what it produces as records.

Ownership and accountabilityEvery source has an information asset owner; the senior information risk owner accepts residual risk.

Classification and handlingClassification travels with content into prompts, indexes and outputs.

Data protectionUK GDPR lawful basis, DPIA, transfers, rights and service-level privacy notices.

Quality and authorityGrounding sources are authoritative, current and fit for the decision they inform.

Metadata and discoverabilityTitles, filenames and metadata can surface through AI. Discovery is not access.

Records and retentionPrompts, outputs, transcripts and agent logs are records with retention rules.

Access and permissionsLeast privilege, oversharing clean-up, delegated and shared contexts tested.

Sharing and reuseData-sharing agreements, data boundaries and trusted reuse such as data matchmaking.

Data controls at each lifecycle stage

StageData and information controlWhere it is recorded
1 DiscoverIdentify the information assets involved and their ownersT1 Opportunity Brief
2 CheckReuse existing datasets, catalogues and indexes before creating new onesT2 Duplication Check
3 ClassifyClassification, personal data and special category dataT3 Classification
4 AssessDPIA, lawful basis, transfers and subprocessors, data quality and authorityT4 Data Readiness · T5 Supplier
5 DesignMetadata, index scope, permissions, connectors and retention rulesT7 Agent Design Record · data-source register
6 PilotMinimisation, test data, consent and privacy noticesT8 Pilot Plan
10 OperateAccess reviews, DLP, records of AI outputs and agent logsMonitoring and assurance record
11 ReassessNew sources, connectors or locations trigger reviewT11 Change-Impact Assessment
12 RetireDisposal, records transfer and revoked accessT12 Retirement Record

What AI creates is information too

Prompts and instructions

Retain where they shaped a decision or a published output; organisational prompts are versioned products.

AI outputs

Treat as drafts until a person verifies them; keep the verified version with an AI involvement statement.

Transcripts and recordings

Consent notice, retention period and deletion route set before recording starts.

Agent action logs

Keep for audit and incident review; owner can read them.

Indexes and embeddings

Derived copies of source data; inherit the source classification and retention.

Evaluation data

Test sets and results are evidence for the decision record.

Frameworks this aligns with

Government Data Quality Framework ↗ (opens an external website)Principles and practices for assessing and improving data quality.

Seen in practice

Kingston Council ran a DPIA on data flows, storage and access before going live with AI note-taking, and updated its privacy notice. Hartlepool publishes a service-level privacy notice for the same kind of tool. Belfast City Council put data and AI governance under one Data & Analytics Board.

Key risks & mitigations matrix

Identify early. Control appropriately. Monitor continuously. Improve relentlessly.

Proactive risk management so AI agents operate safely, lawfully and effectively as digital workers. Human accountability remains non-delegable. Residual ratings assume the controls listed are in place and effective.

1. Inaccurate outputs (hallucination)

Residual: Low

Description & impact
  • Agent generates incorrect, fabricated or misleading information.
  • Poor decisions, loss of trust, reputational and service impact.
Examples
  • Factual errors
  • Fabricated citations
  • Incorrect summaries
  • Outdated information
Key mitigations / controls
  • Grounding with trusted sources
  • Retrieval + citation requirements
  • Confidence thresholds
  • Human review for high-risk outputs
Assurance & monitoring
  • Output evaluation
  • Spot checks & sampling
  • User feedback loops
  • Red-teaming
Well controlled with evidence of accuracy and oversight.

2. Data privacy & leakage

Residual: Low

Description & impact

Sensitive or personal data is exposed, misused or shared inappropriately.

Breach of privacy law, fines, individual harm, loss of trust.

Examples
  • Prompt injection
  • Unintended data exposure
  • Insecure data handling
  • Over-broad access
Key mitigations / controls
  • Data classification & handling rules
  • Least privilege access
  • Data masking & filtering
  • Secure environments & logging
Assurance & monitoring
  • Access monitoring
  • Data loss prevention (DLP)
  • Privacy impact reviews
  • Audit trails
Strong controls and continuous monitoring in place.

3. Automation bias & over-reliance

Residual: Medium

Description & impact

Users over-trust agent outputs and fail to challenge or validate them.

Poor decisions, unintended harm, reduced critical thinking.

Examples
  • Acceptance without review
  • Over-trust in suggestions
  • Deskilling of staff
  • Suppressed escalation
Key mitigations / controls
  • Human-in-the-loop for key decisions
  • Clear UI prompts & explanations
  • Challenge culture & training
  • Escalation pathways
Assurance & monitoring
  • User behaviour analytics
  • Review rates
  • Escalation metrics
  • User training effectiveness
Managed through oversight and user behaviour.

4. Over-authorisation & scope creep

Residual: Medium

Description & impact
  • Agent given more authority or access than necessary or approved.
  • Unauthorised actions, data misuse, policy breach, financial loss.
Examples
  • Excessive permissions
  • Unapproved action types
  • Gradual expansion
  • Weak change control
Key mitigations / controls
  • Least privilege & role-based access
  • Capability versus authority separation
  • Change management process
  • Approval for new actions
Assurance & monitoring
  • Permission reviews
  • Access recertification
  • Change audit logs
  • Control effectiveness testing
Requires ongoing review and re-authorisation.

5. Bias & fairness issues

Residual: Medium

Description & impact

Agent outputs unfair, discriminatory or disproportionate results.

Inequitable outcomes, legal challenge, reputational harm, loss of legitimacy.

Examples
  • Biased training data
  • Proxy discrimination
  • Unequal performance
  • Lack of representation
Key mitigations / controls
  • Fairness assessments
  • Diverse data & testing
  • Bias detection tools
  • Human oversight & appeal
Assurance & monitoring
  • Fairness metrics
  • Outcome monitoring
  • Equality impact reviews
  • Independent assurance
Continuing evaluation reduces but does not eliminate risk.

6. Security threats & misuse

Residual: Medium

Description & impact

Agent exploited, manipulated or used maliciously by attackers.

System compromise, data theft, service disruption, fraudulent actions.

Examples
  • Prompt injection
  • Model exploitation
  • Adversarial attacks
  • Tool misuse
Key mitigations / controls
  • Secure by design
  • Input validation & guardrails
  • Threat modelling
  • Anomaly detection
Assurance & monitoring
  • Security monitoring
  • Pen testing & red teaming
  • Vulnerability scans
  • Incident response testing
Risk managed with robust security controls.

7. Model drift & performance degradation

Residual: Low

Description & impact

Agent performance declines over time as data, context or patterns change.

Reduced accuracy, poor outcomes, inefficiency, user dissatisfaction.

Examples
  • Changing data patterns
  • Outdated knowledge
  • Domain shifts
  • Feedback ignored
Key mitigations / controls
  • Continuous evaluation
  • Monitoring & alerting
  • Retraining & updates
  • Feedback integration
Assurance & monitoring
  • Performance dashboards
  • Drift detection
  • KPI tracking
  • Periodic revalidation
Active monitoring keeps risk low.

8. Accountability & governance gaps

Residual: Low

Description & impact

Unclear ownership, missing controls or weak governance arrangements.

Unclear responsibility, compliance breach, regulatory scrutiny, loss of trust.

Examples
  • No named owner
  • Weak oversight
  • Missing documentation
  • Poor auditability
Key mitigations / controls
  • Named owners & RACI
  • Governance framework
  • Mandatory documentation (ATRS)
  • Clear policies & escalation
Assurance & monitoring
  • Governance reviews
  • Audit & compliance checks
  • ATRS records reviewed
  • Board reporting
Strong governance minimises risk.

How they work together

1. Create / ingest — New information, data or agents are identified and registered

2. Link & relate — Relationships are captured between assets, data and agents

3. Use & leverage — People and agents find and use trusted sources and capabilities

4. Monitor & assure — Activity, quality, risk and compliance are monitored across the landscape

5. Improve & evolve — Feedback drives better sources, smarter agents and stronger controls

The observability control tower

Real-time visibility of agents, usage, performance, risk and value — insight into every agent, control where it matters, confidence in outcomes. These are the panels the register needs to earn its keep.

Part 4 · Assure and governChapter 4.9 · 28 of 85

Human oversight · principles

The human directs; AI is in the loop

Ten principles for keeping people in charge of AI-assisted work: oversight is a competence to build and measure, not a box to tick. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

P1 The human directs; AI is in the loop

Accountability

The person is always in the director position. AI works inside a scope the person sets, and is given agency only if, when and where it is warranted. Oversight competence means setting good bounds, reading the evidence that they are wrong, and withdrawing agency without the service collapsing.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P2 Control intensity follows consequence

Proportionality

Classify every deployment as assist, recommend or determine before choosing controls. The productivity evidence comes from drafting, summarising and analysis; none of it comes from determining anything about a person. Drafting-grade controls on determination is the real risk; determination-grade controls on drafting forfeits real value.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P3 Attention is a budget, not a tax

Proportionality

Most interactions should carry no friction. High-consequence, high-uncertainty and novel cases get the full set. The first control is to reduce what reaches a person at all: triage, confidence-gating and risk-proportionate friction. You cannot train your way out of a capacity problem.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P4 Measure oversight; never assume it

Assurance

Every UK instrument makes human oversight the primary safeguard and none checks whether it still works. Behavioural signals lead; self-report, attestation and training completion do not count as evidence.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P5 Measure the system, never the person

Privacy and trust

Oversight measurement is aggregate and non-attributable, enforced in code with minimum cohort sizes. Individual-level oversight measurement is ruled out in any form. Unions are design partners before build, on a just-culture basis.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P6 Assured oversight unlocks autonomy

Delivery

Evidence of maintained oversight is what lets a team take the human out of more loops safely. Positioned as a brake it will be routed around; positioned as the route to more autonomy, delivery teams will ask for it.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P7 Verify, never fabricate

Integrity

No figure, citation, claim or capability is asserted unless it can be reproduced from a source or the data. What cannot be reproduced is labelled modelled, estimated or unconfirmed on the face of the artefact. Treat any AI-produced draft as hypotheses.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P8 Compensating is not substituting

Inclusion

Using AI to get past a stable barrier (structuring a draft, checking tone, holding many things in mind) is assistive technology. Using it to replace a judgement you could form yourself is where skill atrophy lives. A blanket rule to keep using skills unaided would be an accessibility regression.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P9 Disclose AI assistance at the right level

Transparency

Classify AI-assisted work by audience (internal, peer co-design, external) and apply the matching disclosure. The human keeps the framework, structure, final selection and original contributions; AI output is raw material that is reviewed, accepted, rejected and shaped.

Evidence grade: Proposed

P10 Evidence-led, with a stated exit

Integrity

If longitudinal research finds no material oversight decay in administrative settings, the currency regime scales back to sampling only. Stating in advance what would change our mind is what keeps the programme evidence-led.

Evidence grade: Proposed

Controls that keep oversight real

30 controls, each placed by who applies it (layer), what it does (prevent, detect, recover) and the lowest class of deployment it applies to: assist, recommend or determine. Confidence-gated disclosureEnd userPreventrecommendWithhold the recommendation where model uncertainty is highest, concentrating independent reasoning exactly where the machine is least reliable.Proposed
Disconfirmation panelEnd userPreventrecommendSurface what contradicts the recommendation, not what justifies it. Explanations alone do not reduce overreliance and may increase it.Proposed

Anti-streak interventionEnd userDetectrecommendAfter a run of unmodified approvals the interface changes state. Rubber-stamping has a behavioural signature and can be interrupted where it appears.Proposed

Part 4 · Assure and governChapter 4.11 · 30 of 85

Human oversight · telemetry

Measure the system, never the person

Signals that show whether human oversight is working, read across the service rather than used to rate individuals. Rubber-stamping, drift and lost skill show up in the shape of the data before they show up in incidents. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

Conformance tiers

Minimum viable oversight telemetry

How fast are decisions being made, by class of deployment, and what proportion are accepted unchanged? Enough to detect a fast-approval mode appearing. Fields: event_id, emitted_at, service_id, deployment_class, cohort_id, interaction.disposition, interaction.time_to_decision_ms.

Engagement measurable

Is engagement declining? Are streaks lengthening? Did behaviour change when the model changed? Fields: interaction.edit_distance_normalised, interaction.reason_text_present, interaction.consecutive_unmodified_count, case_risk_class, model.model_version.

Effectiveness measurable

Are known-bad outputs actually being caught, and what is unaided judgement doing over time? This is the only tier that measures oversight effectiveness rather than proxies for it. Fields: canary.*, human_prior.*, governance.*.

The risks sit on the human side of AI use: skills fading through disuse, trust drifting into rubber-stamping, and oversight schemes failing because they are built as staff surveillance or as a brake on delivery.
