Part 4 · Assure and governChapter 4.13 · 32 of 85

Human oversight · verification

Treat AI output as a draft to check, not a source

Practices for checking AI-assisted research, analysis and artefacts before they are relied on, and failure patterns seen in public sector work. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

Evidence handling

  • Treat an AI-produced research draft as hypotheses only. An AI-produced research draft was treated as a source of hypotheses only. None of its assertions was carried forward unchecked. Each source in that draft was located independently, and the result of every check was recorded, including failures.
  • Keep unverifiable claims, marked. Claims that could not be substantiated were kept and marked. Deleting them would remove the evidence of the checking.
  • Provenance travels with each claim. The unit here is the claim, not the document. In a portal people land on one assertion without meeting the caveats that make it safe to use, so the provenance travels with each claim.
  • Label researcher interpretation. Interpretations are labelled, never presented as findings (enforced by CHK-004).
  • Prefer counterfactual evaluations. The comparison against which a benefit is measured, typically a group not using the tool. An evaluation without one cannot separate the tool's effect from everything else. The two evaluations with a comparison or randomised design, DWP and HMRC, report lower figures than those without. Expect that pattern to hold elsewhere.
  • Treat supplier evidence as interested-party. Supplier — treated as interested-party evidence; verified independently wherever possible.
  • Grounding quality. Supplying an AI system with specific approved source material so its output is based on that material. Grounding quality is a function of source quality and currency.
  • Read live rate cards at point of use. Supplier terms. Read the live rate card at the point of building any business case; do not quote these figures from the portal.
  • Ask for realised-outcome evidence rather than inferring it. The NHS England rollout date has arrived, so ask NHS England for realised-outcome evidence rather than inferring it.

Security and privacy

  • Use the DPIA as a design tool from day one. Embed DPIA as a design tool at the start of every build; non-digital fallback routes; test with affected groups; document Equality Act/PSED compliance by default.

Delivery

  • Due diligence on AI-assisted development. Due diligence on AI-assisted development methodology should cover GDS delivery alignment, AI assistance scope, IPR and Crown copyright, spend assurance (GDS spend controls were withdrawn on 1 April 2026 and replaced by the Digital Assurance Playbook), data handling and ethical AI use.

Self-check pattern

  • Every case cites at least one source, and every source exists. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every figure carries a status label and a resolvable source. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every case has a known mechanism and every mapped control resolves. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Dates are valid year-month values. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Case and source identifiers are unique. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • No attributed death count appears on the face of any case. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Anchor case states the causation limit before any consequence claim. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Figures add up: the fines total is computed, not typed. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Anything not re-verified this release is listed as carried, not shown as fact. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Sources are fresh (checked within 90 days of viewing). A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Coverage spans sectors and all four UK nations. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every challenge states what the objection gets right and the limit of the claim. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Displayed money totals stay within 0.5% of the computed figure. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Vendor documentation is labelled supplier evidence, and only vendor sources carry that label. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every connection states the tie and the action, and every link is a full https address. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Counts written into the text match the data. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Citations of the standard do not depend on the retiring co-cddo organisation. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every post referenced in the seam, triad and resolution register exists in the join-up map. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • The resolution register covers every mechanism and every case, and cites only real cases. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every computed placeholder in the text has a value. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Every case has a DAM Policy assessment, and each case's rules agree with each rule's cases. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • Proposed return rules use the workspace's own grammar and every in-scope case is answered by one. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.
  • verified / reported / estimate / supplier evidence / author's account; sums of estimates are not audited totals; vendor docs labelled supplier evidence only (K14).. A check that runs on the artefact itself. It exists because of the defect shown.

Failure patterns to recognise

The Hidden Tab Pattern

Responsible data use

Files and messages leave organisations carrying more personal data than the sender can see or intended to send; the sensitivity/handling label sits in a register or catalogue entry that stays behind and does not travel with the file to the point of release, so nothing at the boundary can read it.

Case: MOD (UK Special Forces HQ), February 2022: a spreadsheet believed to hold about 150 Afghan relocation applicants carried, invisibly, details of about 18,700. Twin case: PSNI, August 2023, a second tab on an FOI answer exposed every officer (ICO fine £750,000).

Synthetic data presented as real

Verifying AI-assisted work

An AI assistant described synthetic events as real output, and an early build of the oversight instrument repeated it. Anything generated must be labelled on its face.

Case: Found and corrected during review, 2026.

Hand-typed figures drift from the data

Verifying AI-assisted work

A figure typed rather than computed drifts from the data it claims to summarise. Compute totals; never type them.

Case: A figure typed into an appraisal differed materially from the figure computed from its data; caught by a check that recomputes totals.

Governance as a continuous learning system

  1. 1. Pilot

    • Define scope and success measures
    • Test with real users
    • Put controls in place
    • Set stop criteria

  2. 2. Evidence

    • Gather quantitative and qualitative data
    • Assess outcomes, quality and value
    • Capture accessibility, cost and risk
    • Record unintended effects

  3. 3. Decision

    • Approve, approve with conditions, extend, restrict or stop
    • Record the rationale
    • Update registers
    • Tell users

  4. 4. Operation

    • Deploy and support users
    • Monitor controls and compliance
    • Provide guidance and training
    • Maintain human oversight

  5. 5. Monitoring

    • Track usage and adoption
    • Monitor cost and consumption
    • Identify risks and anomalies
    • Measure outcomes and value

  6. 6. Incident, change or learning

    • Respond to incidents and near misses
    • Investigate and resolve
    • Capture lessons
    • Watch product, model and policy changes

  7. 7. Reassessment

    • Assess the impact of change
    • Update the risk and control position
    • Refresh approvals if needed
    • Decide: continue, restrict or suspend

  8. 8. Retire

    • Disable access and actions
    • Remove data and integrations
    • Inform users
    • Close records and capture lessons

Turning experience into impact

Better decisionsBased on real outcomes Stronger controlsInformed by actual risks Greater valueFor users and public services More inclusiveIdentifying and removing barriers Smarter spendingUnderstanding cost and benefit Shared learningReusable patterns and guidance

Report an AI concern, incident or near miss

Report anything that went wrong or nearly did: a wrong output that was acted on, an exposed file, an unexpected action, a cost spike, an accessibility barrier. Record:

  • Tool, model and deployment route
  • Use case and what happened
  • Who was affected, and whether it was acted on
  • The control that should have prevented it
  • Corrective action and owner

Suspension and retirement

  1. Record the reason and the replacement.
  2. Tell users, with an accessible alternative.
  3. Disable agents and actions, and revoke access.
  4. Disconnect integrations and dispose of data.
  5. Update registers and remove supplier access.
  6. Record residual risks and lessons; approve closure.

Agent journey

From idea to retirement, with a gate at every stage

An agent that helps one person and an agent that decides a citizen's case are not the same thing, and should not carry the same controls. Eight stages, each with a gate question, the control that applies, the role accountable and the outcome expected.

Stage 1 of 8 Personal / low risk

Idea & discovery

What happens
  • Identify a need or opportunity
  • Explore feasibility
  • Check existing solutions and policies
Gate 1 — decision point
Is there a clear need and no existing solution?

Security & identity — least privilege, access control and monitoring

Key accountability

Creator — builds and tests the agent; owns initial purpose

Outcome at this stage
Better understanding of needs and opportunities
Success factors across the journey

Clear purpose and value Right controls at the right time User engagement and feedback Sustainable cost model Continuous learning and improvement Strong community and reuse Better public value outcomes

Personal experiment to enterprise service

A managed progression that balances innovation, control, risk and value. Agents evolve from personal productivity tools to trusted, supported services — and ownership moves with them.

1 Idea & personal experiment Individual creator Low risk · personal

2 Share & team pilot Team data owners Low to moderate risk

3 Managed team agent Named team owner Moderate risk

4 Departmental capability Departmental owner Moderate to high risk

5 Operational service Service owner High risk

6 Enterprise service Business / enterprise owner High risk · high impact

7 Cross-government capability Cross-government sponsor & owners High impact · strategic

The Copilot-to-agent capability spectrum

A continuum of assistance and autonomy — from individual productivity to enterprise agentic services. Purpose: enable people to work better today, orchestrate intelligent workflows, and deliver trusted, efficient, inclusive public services.

Avoiding the “access database moment”

How a small, helpful agent becomes business critical without visibility or control. Small agents can create big value — and big risk. Visibility, ownership and governance early in the journey prevent unmanaged tools from becoming unmanageable dependencies.

1 Personal experiment Low visibility An individual creates an agent to solve a personal problem or save time.

2 Shared with team Low to moderate visibility Shared with colleagues or a small team to help with common tasks.

3 Wider adoption Rising visibility More teams discover it and start using it organically.

4 Dependence builds Rising to high visibility Critical work starts to rely on the agent and its outputs.

5 Business critical High visibility Used across the department or service. Business processes become dependent on it.

6 Invisible criticality Gap in visibility No formal ownership, limited documentation, unknown controls, unknown costs.

7 High risk exposure Critical · unmanaged Risk of failure, data breach, inaccurate decisions or service disruption.

8 Event of failure Loss of trust and value Agent breaks, data changes or owner leaves — causing a real operational impact.

How to prevent it — early detection, ownership and routes to enterprise management

1. Discover early Agent inventory · Usage monitoring · Sharing visibility · Community reports

2. Require description Purpose & use case · Data sources · Support owner · Review dates

3. Assign ownership Business owner · Technical owner · Information owner · Risk owner

4. Assess & classify Risk & impact · Data sensitivity · Criticality score · Assurance needs

5. Control & assure Approved sources · Guardrails · Human oversight · Testing & validation

6. Monitor & review Usage & performance · Cost & consumption · Accuracy & quality · Incident tracking

7. Promote or remediate Move to managed platform (e.g. Copilot Studio) · Or retire / remediate

What goes wrong when it is left unmanaged

Shadow IT Inconsistent quality Lack of documentation Knowledge silos Unknown cost Compliance breach Loss of public trust

Accountable, transparent and auditable

Applied throughout every stage

Continuous monitoring Human oversight Audit logging Policy compliance Security Privacy Safety

Capability is not authority

An agent may be able to do many things, but can only do what it is authorised to do. Capability is about potential; authority is about permission. Capability + authority + context = action — only when all controls are satisfied can the agent act.

What the agent can do — capability

Technical potential and skills: the full range of capabilities, knowledge, tools and actions the agent is built or enabled to perform.

Natural language understanding Tool use & API integrations Reasoning & problem solving Workflow orchestration & scheduling Data retrieval (RAG) Analysis & visualisation Code generation & automation Communication (drafting, email, chat) Content creation & summarisation Learning from feedback

Governance controls

Bridging capability to appropriate action.

Policies & rulesOrganisational policies, legal requirements and ethical guardrails define boundaries.

Delegated authorityExplicit permissions granted for specific tasks, data and systems.

Conditions & controlsContext, thresholds, approvals and risk checks must be satisfied.

Human oversightPeople remain in control of decisions and can intervene or override.

Monitoring & auditActions are logged, monitored and reviewed for assurance and compliance.

What the agent is allowed to do — authority

Permitted actions in the right context, within defined boundaries, for specific purposes and users.

Draft policy briefingApproved for Policy Team (sensitivity: OFFICIAL)

Send standard email responseApproved with template and review

Summarise documents up to OFFICIALApproved with data classification filter

Update internal tracker or systemApproved with role-based permissions

Escalate issue to human reviewerRequired when confidence below threshold

Why separate capability from authority

Reduces risk Limits exposure by ensuring agents cannot act beyond intent or policy.

Improves accountability Clear ownership and delegated authority for all actions.

Supports compliance Meets legal, regulatory and ethical obligations.

Enables agility Adjust permissions without rebuilding capabilities.

Builds trust Transparent controls and oversight build confidence.

Adapts to context Decisions and permissions can vary by role, risk and situation.

How agents influence decisions and deliver public value

Seven links from capability to legitimacy — each with the elements that must hold and the risks that arise if they do not. Better governed AI agents lead to better decisions, better services, and better outcomes for everyone.

AI capability (agent)

The agent has defined capabilities, knowledge, tools and guardrails within its delegated authority.

  • Bias in training

Transparent, accountable and responsible use of AI strengthens public trust and democratic legitimacy.

  • Accountability gaps

Strong governance & ownership Policies & ethical use Security & privacy by design Quality data & provenance Monitoring & auditability Human oversight at every step Transparency (ATRS) Performance measurement Continuous improvement

Part 5 · Operate and overseeChapter 5.7 · 39 of 85

Human oversight · runbook

Twelve steps to stand up proportionate oversight

A runbook for a service or department starting human oversight of AI, with starting positions for the governance documents it will need. The templates are skeletons, not legal advice: take them to your data protection officer, equality lead and legal adviser. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

  1. Before anything: is this for you? (Adopt)

    • Run the classifier against your two or three largest AI deployments.
    • All assist-class? Tier-1 telemetry and resourced oversight declaration; stop there.
    • Anything determine-class? Work through the whole runbook.
    • Mostly recommend-class? Tiers 1 and 2; read reversibility question carefully.

  2. Who is needed (Adopt)

  3. Weeks 1–2 — decide and disclose (Adopt)

    • Classify every AI deployment in the service. Add each to the register. Export it.
    • Brief the SRO on the register summary, particularly anything determine-class that cannot evidence its safeguard works.
    • Open the DPIA and the union conversation in the same week. Both get harder the longer you leave them, and the union one cannot be recovered if it starts late.
    • Write the resourced oversight declaration for the largest deployment.

  4. Weeks 3–6 — emit tier 1 (Adopt)

    • Map your existing approval telemetry onto the seven tier-1 fields. Most case management systems already hold all seven; the work is naming, not capture.
    • Emit to the standard vocabulary codes. Resist local variants — the point is comparability.
    • Run run_baseline.py or drop the CSV into the instrument. Expect the tier-1 warning that you cannot yet assess decay. That warning is the finding.

  5. Weeks 7–10 — reach tier 2 (Adopt)

    • Add edit distance, reason capture, streak count and model version.
    • Streak must be derived from the real sequence. A field that disagrees with its own sequence is worse than an absent one.
    • First real reading. Report it to the SRO whatever it says.

  6. Weeks 11–12 — decide about tier 3 (Adopt)

    • If the service is determine-class, start the ethics and union route for canaries now. It is the long pole.
    • If not, stay at tier 2 and revisit in six months.
    • Publish the baseline internally. Including if it shows nothing — a null result honestly reported is what makes this evidence-led rather than advocacy.

  7. Integration (Adopt)

  8. What to expect to go wrong (Adopt)

    • The union conversation started too late. Recoverable only by stopping and restarting. Start it in week 1.
    • Someone asks for individual-level breakdowns. Refuse. It is technically unavailable in the aggregator by design; keep it that way. Once it exists it will be requested by someone senior enough to get it.
    • The first reading looks bad and there is pressure to withhold it. A withheld baseline is worse than no baseline, because you now know and cannot say you did not.
    • Tier-1 data reported as reassurance. It cannot detect decay. The instrument says so explicitly for this reason.
    • Local vocabulary variants. Every unprefixed local code destroys comparability. Use x_ and propose the addition centrally.

  9. Ninety-day MVP (earlier version) (Superseded sequence)

    • Instrument one live decision-support deployment with the P1 event schema (two weeks of engineering)
    • Add predict-then-reveal on the highest-consequence decision type only
    • Establish unaided baseline from priors captured in first month
    • Publish aggregate result to service owner and Hub — including if it shows nothing
    • Run first canary batch under ethics approval, aggregate only, agreed with unions in advance
    • Write up event schema and prior-capture component as reusable spec

  10. What departments are asked to do (README) (Programme)

    • Map existing telemetry onto the event schema
    • Add predict-then-reveal on one high-consequence decision type
    • Run run_baseline.py against real events instead of simulated ones
    • Publish the aggregate result, including if it shows nothing

  11. Immediate sequence post-MoG (Programme)

    • Establish where the AI assurance profession work landed
    • Submit the ministerial brief
    • Contact MHCLG Local AI and the LGA
    • Offer the schema and pipeline to GDS in DCMS as a candidate first delivery artefact
    • Identify one department willing to be instrumented

  12. Recommended order to publication (Programme)

    • Repository
    • Pilot
    • Exemplar
    • Accessibility conformance
    • Publication

Governance templates

Data protection impact assessment — starting positions
  • Is a DPIA required? Probably yes at tier 2 and certainly at tier 3. The processing concerns staff conduct at work, involves systematic monitoring of a workforce, and relates to the evaluation of performance — even though the design deliberately prevents individual evaluation. Argue it through rather than assuming the aggregation exempts you.
  • The question your DPO will ask: if it is genuinely non-identifying, why does it need a DPIA? Answer: because the collection point is identifying, and because the risk being assessed is function creep, not the current design.
Equality impact assessment — the questions that actually bite
  • The generic template will not surface the real issues. These will.
  • Differential effect of friction. Cognitive forcing interventions benefit people with higher need for cognition more than others. Uniform application therefore produces unequal benefit. Who is disadvantaged — staff with dyslexia, ADHD, English as an additional language, high caseloads, caring responsibilities affecting available concentration?
  • Reasonable adjustments. Does predict-then-reveal interact badly with any assistive technology in use? Has it been tested with a screen reader, with magnification, and at the time pressure a real queue applies?
  • Cohort composition. If cohorts map to teams, and teams differ systematically in composition, aggregate comparison between cohorts can become proxy discrimination. Check before publishing cohort comparisons.
  • Who is in determine-class roles? If the roles carrying the heaviest oversight burden are disproportionately held by any group, the burden is not equally distributed.
  • Effect of the junior-role finding. If entry-level roles are being reshaped, who currently holds them and who is affected by their redesign? This has a clear equality dimension and is the longest-lead item in the programme.
  • Language. Where the body has Welsh Language Standards obligations, the interface and any staff-facing materials fall within them.
  • Do not conclude "no impact". The honest finding is that the impact is real, differential and manageable — and that uniform friction is the version that fails the duty.
Trade union engagement — a note to open the conversation
  • Draft for adaptation. Send before anything is built, not before it launches.
  • We are proposing to measure whether human oversight of AI systems in this service is working. We want to design it with you, and there is one design decision we would rather you set than we did.
  • The background: every instrument governing our use of AI treats human oversight as the main safeguard. None of them checks whether that safeguard is functioning. That is a risk to the public and, more immediately, a risk to members — because a colleague placed in an approval loop without the time, information or practised skill to exercise it meaningfully is not exercising accountability. They are absorbing liability for an institutional decision they could not realistically have controlled.
  • What we are proposing to measure: how the service as a whole is performing — how quickly outputs are approved, how much they are changed, whether errors are being caught.
  • What we are not proposing to measure, in any form: individual performance. There is no user identifier in the data schema. The schema is closed, so one cannot be added. The analysis tools refuse any query resolving to fewer than ten people, and refuse outright any file containing an identifier column. This is enforced in code rather than promised in policy, because we think a promise is worth less than a system that cannot do the thing.
  • What we would like to agree with you before we build: that this operates on a just-culture basis — closer to confidential safety reporting in aviation than to appraisal; that findings are never attributed, formally or informally; that participation in any unaided practice or sampling is scheduled work rather than an addition to workload; and that we jointly review, annually, whether any request for individual-level data has been made, and record that it was refused.
  • What we would ask in return: that where the measurement shows oversight is not working, the response is to fix the workload, the interface or the deployment — not the individual.
  • We would rather have this conversation now, at design stage, than present you with something finished. If the answer is that this cannot be made acceptable, we would rather know before we build it.
Ethics application for canary injection — the content that will be asked for
  • Only needed at tier 3. Expect months, not weeks.
  • What is proposed. Injecting synthetic known-bad AI outputs, at a low randomised rate, into a live review queue, to measure whether reviewers detect them.
  • Why it cannot be done in a simulation. Detection under real time pressure, real caseload and real fatigue is the thing being measured. A laboratory version measures something else. This is the same reasoning behind live fire drills and phishing simulations, both of which have established precedent in government.
  • Harm to the public — the safety case. No canary can reach a citizen. Injected items are suppressed downstream by the platform regardless of the reviewer's disposition. State the technical mechanism, not the intention. Include the failure mode: what happens if the suppression fails, how it would be detected, and how quickly.
  • Harm to staff. Reviewers know canaries exist but not which items they are. The measure is aggregate and non-attributable; failing to catch one has no individual consequence and cannot be traced to a person. Address the stress question directly: this is a workload and design intervention if catch rates fall, not a disciplinary one.
  • Consent. Individual consent is not sought, for the same reason it is not sought for fire drills — announced tests measure announced behaviour. Collective agreement is sought instead, through the recognised unions, and staff are told the programme exists, its purpose, and that results are never individual.
  • Withdrawal. The union side can suspend injection. Say so explicitly; it is what makes the collective-agreement route legitimate.
  • Data. Canary events carry no identifier. Retention as per the DPIA.
  • Reporting. Aggregate catch rate by canary class, reported to the service owner and the SRO. Published internally including when results are poor.
  • The question the committee will ask: what happens if catch rates are very low? Answer in advance: it triggers a review of workload, interface and deployment scope — and, for a determine-class service, consideration of whether the deployment should continue in its current form. If you cannot commit to that, the case for injecting is weak.
Governance templates — preamble
  • Four artefacts a department cannot deploy this without. Skeletons, not legal advice — take them to your DPO, equality lead and Government Legal Department contact. They exist so the conversation starts from a draft rather than a blank page.
CONTRIBUTING.md
  • Run python3 -m pytest tests/ -q and python3 ../verify.py. Both must pass. CI runs them anyway.
  • Codes are additive and permanent. A code is never removed or repurposed; superseded codes are marked deprecated with a named successor. To propose an addition, give a definition, a worked example, and a statement of why an existing code does not fit.
  • Local codes must be prefixed x_. Anything unprefixed is reserved centrally so that local extension never collides with a future addition.
  • The schema is closed (additionalProperties: false) and contains no individual identifier field. Both properties are load-bearing: they are what makes the privacy commitment credible to staff and to unions rather than merely stated. A change that weakens either needs an explicit case, not a pull request.
  • Say what data the new threshold was calibrated against. Thresholds set by judgement should be labelled as such in the finding text, as the current ones are.
  • Prefer a test that would have caught a real defect. Every fix in the changelog was found by one of: a test, the verification harness, or a reader asking a sharp question. Only the first two scale.

FinOps & models

A builder's design choice sets a budget holder's cost

AI cost is a portfolio, not a licence line. You are billed per token, in and out — roughly four characters or three-quarters of a word each; an A4 page is 600–800 tokens. Micro-costs stack when an agent runs on repeat. Report by service, product, agent, owner, model and cost driver; showback before chargeback; no expenditure classification without finance-led assessment.

Licences Credits Model calls Compute Storage Connectors Monitoring Evaluation Adoption & training Remediation Security Human review Support

How the two main vendors now charge, and where they process

Published list positions at 19 October 2026
Microsoft Copilot

Cost: a per-user licence ($30 per month list) covers Chat and Copilot in the Office apps. Cowork, Code, Autopilot and frontier models consume Copilot Credits at $0.01 each on pay-as-you-go. Agent security for custom agents needs Agent 365.

Residency: follows the tenant's Microsoft 365 geography. Web grounding, subprocessor models (Claude, Grok) and Code apps on Managed Runtime need separate checks.

Anthropic Claude

Cost: a seat per user, plus usage at token rates by model (Opus 5.5 lists at $4 input / $20 output per million tokens). Model routing, effort settings and prompt caching are the main levers.

Residency: set by deployment route. Anthropic-processed with a US-only option, or in-region through Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry. Connectors carry the content they fetch to the model.

Four lenses of value — the estate case, measured and modelled

Reclaimed time
~£0.5M–£1.6M / yr at ~680 staff

A 10% findability gain on ~1.8 hrs/day spent searching. The big lever — and it can cover the licence bill 2.5–8× over ("earned allocation").

Storage cost ~£1.5k / yr Effectively £0 marginal under bundled M365. Symbolic.

Environmental
~9 TB ≈ 55–360 kg CO₂e / yr

Modest; aligns with Greening Government; curbs future growth.

Wellbeing
117 emails/day · ~23 min to refocus

Interrupted every ~2 minutes; 48% find work chaotic and fragmented. The human case.

Rules that hold: require total-cost and portability evidence before scaling any tool or agent · per-agent consumption caps and anomaly alerts · unit economics per production agent published within 12 months · value measured through the evidence chain: activity → output quality → workflow change → organisational outcome → public outcome.

Dependency, lock-in & exit

The ecosystem behind an AI-enabled public service

AI-enabled services rely on a chain of suppliers, platforms, models, data sources and infrastructure. Visibility of these dependencies is what makes risk management, resilience, portability and value possible.

Public sector consumers

Key dependency categories

Platform dependencyReliance on specific platforms and ecosystems

Model dependencyReliance on model providers and availability

Data dependencyAccess to quality, timely and trusted data

Infrastructure dependencyCompute, storage, network and region reliance

Supplier & contractual dependencyThird-party services, SLAs, pricing and contractual terms

Operational dependencySkills, support, monitoring and continuity

Key questions to ask
  • What happens if a supplier or model is unavailable?
  • Can we switch models or platforms easily?
  • Where is our data stored and processed?
  • Do we have visibility of usage, cost and performance?
  • What contractual rights do we have — audit, data portability?
  • Are we building excessive lock-in or technical debt?
  • Do we have a clear exit and migration plan?
Managing dependencies
  • Map and document all dependencies
  • Assess risk and criticality
  • Ensure contractual protections
  • Design for portability
  • Monitor usage, cost and performance
  • Plan for resilience and exit
  • Review and adapt continuously
Outcomes

Better risk management Resilience & continuity Cost optimisation Informed supplier strategy Sustainable innovation Public value protection

Design for choice today. Exit with confidence tomorrow.

Avoid unintended dependency. Preserve portability across data, models, agents, integrations and knowledge, so you can adapt, switch or exit when you need to.

PortabilityKeep your data, prompts, models and agents portable

TransparencyKnow what you use, where it is, and the terms

InteroperabilityUse open standards and avoid proprietary traps

Plan aheadDesign exit and migration paths from day one

Control costsUnderstand true switching and transition costs

ContinuityMaintain service and compliance through change

Sources of lock-in
  • Proprietary platforms and ecosystems
  • Closed data formats and schemas
  • Proprietary connectors and APIs
  • Model dependency and exclusivity
  • Managed services and operations
  • Contractual restrictions and terms
  • Data residency and jurisdiction
  • Skills and tooling
The lock-in zone — where dependencies accumulate

Technology dependencies

  • Proprietary features and roadmaps
  • Custom integrations
  • Closed standards
  • Single-tenant architectures

Data & knowledge dependencies

  • Data locked in proprietary stores
  • Non-exportable metadata
  • Knowledge bases tied to platform
  • Prompt libraries not portable

Model & AI dependencies

  • Model exclusivity clauses
  • No right to substitute
  • Fine-tuned models not exportable
  • Training data use restrictions

Operational dependencies

  • Managed service entanglement
  • Monitoring and tool lock-in
  • Infrastructure coupling
  • Support and SLAs tied to stack

Commercial dependencies

  • Long contracts with penalties
  • Limited termination rights
  • IP and data use restrictions
  • Unilateral price change rights

Organisational dependencies

  • Specialist skills tied to vendor
  • Processes built around tools
  • Change resistance
  • Limited market knowledge
Exit & transition path — reduce risk, preserve value
1
Discover & inventory
  • Map all assets, services and data
  • Identify critical dependencies
  • Assess complexity and effort
2
Define target state
  • Choose target platform / model
  • Define data, security and compliance needs
  • Agree outcomes and constraints
3
Design migration strategy
  • Prioritise workloads
  • Phased or parallel approach
  • Define data and application migration
  • Plan cutover and rollback
4
Prepare & extract
  • Extract data, metadata and documents
  • Export prompts, agents and configurations
  • Validate completeness and quality
5
Build & test
  • Rebuild integrations
  • Adapt to target platform / model
  • Test functionality, performance and security
6
Migrate & cutover
  • Migrate data and configurations
  • Switch traffic and users
  • Monitor closely post-cutover
7
Optimise & decommission
  • Optimise costs and performance
  • Retire old assets safely
  • Capture lessons and update runbooks
Exit readiness check
Not assessed

Rate how prepared you are to exit. The path above is the work; this is the readiness.

What to preserve and make portable

Data Metadata & schemas Documents & content Prompts & instructions Agents & workflows Configurations & settings Integrations & APIs Access & permissions Audit logs & evidence Knowledge & context

De-risking strategies
  • Use open standards and portable formats
  • Negotiate data and IP rights up front
  • Retain audit and telemetry access
  • Stay multi-cloud and multi-model ready
  • Modular architecture and loose coupling
  • Regular dependency reviews
Red flags — high lock-in risk
  • No export or portability options
  • Data only accessible via proprietary APIs
  • High egress or extraction charges
  • Contract penalties for early exit or data retrieval
  • Complex custom integrations with no standards
  • Single model or provider dependency
  • Lack of roadmap visibility or support
Exit cost components
  • Data extraction and transformation
  • Rebuild / re-engineering
  • Dual running (parallel operations)
  • Testing and assurance
  • Training and change
  • Contract exit and penalties
  • Downtime / disruption risk
Exit success outcomes
  • Freedom to innovate and adapt
  • Lower total cost of ownership
  • Stronger resilience and continuity
  • Better negotiation power
  • Protected public data and trust
  • Sustainable, future-proof services

Inclusive & accessible adoption

Different people. Different needs. Shared success.

AI tools should empower everyone by offering choice, clarity and support. The spectrum below runs from empowered and confident to apprehensive — and inclusion is not one size for all: listening, choice and support help everyone succeed with AI.

Enthusiastic & confident

Sees AI as a productivity booster and enjoys exploring new tools.

May typically
  • Experiment and customise
  • Share tips and best practice
  • Integrate AI into daily work
Key needs
Advanced features
Experimentation space
Recognition & influence
Ways to contribute back
Cautious but willing

Interested and willing to try, but wants reassurance and guidance.

May typically
  • Use AI for simple, low-risk tasks
  • Seek examples and best practice
  • Prefers structured learning
Key needs
Clear guidance & examples
Safe practice environments
Step-by-step learning
Trusted peer support
Needs support & clarity

Wants to benefit from AI but needs help understanding how and when.

May typically
  • Uses guided features
  • Needs help in context
  • Prefers practical, relevant training
Key needs
Plain language & relevance
Role-based training
Hand-holding & coaching
Time to learn & practise
Anxious & overwhelmed

Feels unsure or overwhelmed by change, complexity or risk.

May typically
  • Avoids or minimises use
  • Worried about errors or job impact
  • Prefers human interaction
Key needs
Reassurance & transparency
Simple, limited choices
Human support always available
Safe, low-pressure options
Resistant / disengaged

Does not see value or may distrust AI or the organisation's intent.

May typically
  • Declines to use
  • Questions fairness or reliability
  • Prefers current ways of working
Key needs
Listen & understand concerns
Involve in decisions
Address trust & fairness
Show tangible benefits
Design for inclusion

Choice & controlLet users choose how AI helps, when and in what way

Clear & simpleUse plain language, short explanations and examples

Flexible interactionSupport different workflows, speeds and preferences

Neuroinclusive designReduce cognitive load, provide structure, minimise distractions

Accessible by defaultWCAG compliant, multimodal, and assistive-tech friendly

Safe & trustedProtect data, explain limits, and make AI behaviour predictable

Human supportEasy access to help, feedback channels and champions

Enablers & supports

Leadership sponsorship Digital & AI champions Inclusive communication Role-based learning paths Protected learning time Local support networks Feedback & continuous listening Measure & adapt for all users

Remember

Inclusion is not one size fits all. Listening, choice and support help everyone succeed with AI — and inclusive adoption empowers people, strengthens trust and delivers better public services.

Operating model & programme

One operating model. Everyone aboard.

One AI capability operating model — not separate Copilot, agent, data, assurance and FinOps programmes. Cognitive load down, recognition up, DEIA by default rather than afterthought.

Every product, every build. DPIA in, not post.

DEIA by default — who this serves, and the checklist

Every product must actively serve those experiencing the greatest adversity: economic hardship, disabled and neurodivergent users, underrepresented communities, vulnerable households and carers, digital exclusion and low literacy, and everyone algorithmic unfairness would otherwise reach first.

Who is most harmed if this fails or excludes?

Does the design assume internet access or literacy?

Has it been tested with people from affected groups?

Are legal obligations (Equality Act, PSED) documented?

Is there a non-digital fallback route?

Does the data we collect reflect the full population?

Are there language and accessibility alternatives?

How will we measure equitable outcomes, not just usage?

Bias will be reproduced unless actively constrained

A model trained on historical outcomes learns the discrimination in the record, not the potential of a well-supported person. Four pre-specified bias domains to audit — and abstention ("insufficient data — human decision only") is always acceptable, and must be possible.

Allocation

Systematically fewer or lesser recommendations for protected groups with equivalent profiles.

Calibration

Predictions accurate against a biased historical record, wrong about supported potential.

Representation gap

Too few cases for a group; the model fills gaps with majority priors.

Feedback loop

Biased outputs produce worse outcomes that retrain the model — break the loop by design.

Training-data standards: exclude invalidated-treatment-era and sanctioned-employer records and proxy features; require minimum cases per group, representation audits, labelled synthetic augmentation for regularisation only, and temporal weighting toward modern practice. Lived-experience panels review real outputs; community bodies sign off the test criteria; explanations reference functional needs, never the diagnosis.

The capability programme — four phases

The sequence — three, six, twelve, twenty-four months

3 months

Establish preconditions
  • Reachability audit and permissions remediation
  • Publish agent-register schema and intake form
  • Consumption dashboards and per-agent caps
  • Agree retention and FOI position

6 months

Govern
  • Operate the register; classify every agent by tier
  • Apply assurance tiers; define the orphaned-agent process
  • Secure exit, portability and audit rights
  • Publish an evaluation method standard

12 months

Integrate
  • Fund adoption as a standing operating line
  • Publish unit economics per production agent
  • Unify information and agent governance
  • Publish one outcome measure, not an activity

24 months

Federate
  • Share registered agent patterns across bodies
  • Aggregate demand for small public bodies
  • Prove exit is real via a live substitution
  • Publish a community value evaluation

Sequence matters more than speed: permissions before scale, register before governance claims, cost instrumentation before volume. Recognition runs throughout — named people, visible work, credited contributions, minister-level visibility on citizen wins.

Accessibility and workplace adjustments

Two questions, kept separate: is the AI tool itself accessible, and can AI support someone as a workplace adjustment? Request either through your line manager or the adjustments route. Every tool needs a non-AI alternative.

Guest and cross-tenant access

Do not rely on meeting recaps for guests. Store resources where external participants can reach them, set permissions deliberately and provide an accessible copy.

Transcription dictionary

Maintain a controlled glossary of cross-government terms and acronyms so that transcription and summaries get names right.

Employment and workplace effects

Include workload, role, delegation, autonomy, training and workplace-adjustment impact in the adoption assessment, and monitor them after rollout.

Part 7 · People and adoptionChapter 7.12 · 55 of 85

People and adoption · inclusion

AI as assistive technology, designed for everyone

How AI tools help and hinder people across neurotypes at work, how to talk about them without a deficit framing, and the questions that are still open. Build one version that works for everyone, layered, rather than a separate one. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: Proposed items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

What people say helps

I like clear structure and knowing what to expect

“I want to know exactly what the tool will and won't do before I rely on it.”

Helps: Ask the tool to explain its steps before it does something complex; Build a short personal routine for how you use it, and stick to it

Watch for: Answers can vary between attempts — plan for that, it's not a fault

Busy screens and long text wear me out fast

“Too much on the page at once and I lose track of what matters.”

Helps: Ask for short answers first, then "tell me more" only if needed; Turn off extra plug-ins or add-ons you don't use

Watch for: Take a proper break between tasks — don't stack requests back to back

I want the tool to say exactly what it means

“I find it easier when nothing is left for me to guess or read between the lines.”

Helps: Ask it directly: "say this in plain, literal terms"; Ask it to list assumptions it's making, not just the answer

Watch for: General advice about people or feelings can be too generic — check it fits your actual situation

My focus and energy shift a lot, hour to hour

“Some days I fly through things, other days the same task feels impossible.”

Helps: Let AI help you start a task — a blank page is often the hardest part; On a low-energy day, it's fine to lean on it more than usual

Watch for: On a good day, try the task yourself first — it keeps your own skill sharp

I catch small details well, but time pressure throws me

“Give me time and I'll spot the error. Rush me and I'll miss it.”

Helps: Use AI for a fast first pass, then take your own unhurried time to check it; Ask it to flag its own uncertain bits so you know where to look closest

Watch for: Don't let a fast deadline push you into skipping your own check

I feel uneasy sharing work before it's ready

“I'd rather get it right privately than be seen figuring it out.”

Helps: Use the tool as a private practice space before anything goes to a colleague; It's fine to use it purely to build confidence, not just to produce a final version

Watch for: Don't share more personal detail with it than the task actually needs

Communicating about AI tools

  • Don't build two versions (one for neurodiverse staff, one for everyone else). Managers' attitudes shaped use and control-group awareness was low; a split communication badges it as a 'special accommodation', undersells it to neurotypical staff and stigmatises it for neurodiverse staff.
  • Lead with the curb-cut framing, not the deficit framing. Outcome language ('levelled the playing field'), not diagnosis language. Avoid 'crutch' language even to knock it down.
  • Layer the detail rather than write two documents: a one-page plain-language summary with the fuller evidence base undern eath.
  • Talking to your manager: frame it in terms of outcome, not diagnosis ('this helps me structure written work faster and m ore confidently'); no need to disclose a condition; if it functions as a genuine accessibility aid, say so explicitly so it is treated like any reasonable adjustment if the licence is reviewed.
  • For managers: neutral, informed encouragement - not enthusiasm or scepticism - produces the best outcomes for the whole team.
  • one layout/format alone will not meet everyone's needs (some autism sub-types are polar oppos ites); present tailored around common characteristics or a compromise that best serves all; Easy Read version is a must. This partly overrides the turn-5 'one layered document' advice: the turn-11 solution is a characteristics poster plus a separate Easy Read version.

Deployment and licensing

  • Don't blanket-licence. Target by task profile first, need second (admin-heavy/high-information roles benefited; Legal and Policy did not).
  • Fund self-led exploration over formal training sessions; budget time, not just courseware (p < 0.01 at 2+ hours self-led use).
  • Plan continuity, not just onboarding. If a licence functions as assistive technology for someone, treat withdrawal with the same seriousness as withdrawing any other reasonable adjustment, not as an IT asset reclaim.
  • Build QA expectations that vary by task, not a blanket 'always check' policy nobody follows. Drafting/summarising: light-touch spot-check. Data analysis and anything feeding a decision: mandate verification (DBT observed tasks showed Copilot users did worse on Excel analysis).
  • Track dependency alongside satisfaction in any evaluation commissioned; none of the three government evaluations measure d these jointly at individual level - a genuine gap.
  • Cost transparency matters to uptake: address ethical/environmental concerns rather than dismiss them.

Keeping research current

  • Model-dependent findings Describe a specific model's failure mode at a specific point in time (e.g. 2024 ChatGPT advising an autistic user to 'just walk up and start talking'). Testable claims, not settled facts. Re-run the equivalent prompt against current models before relying on it (five-minute check). Tag [model-dependent — re-verify before citing]; note model and test date; anything older than about six months needs a fresh spot-check.
  • Structural (human-factors and organisational) findings About people and institutions, not the model. Safe to build governance policy on now. Tag [structural — durable].
  • More fluent models are more persuasive when wrong Newer, more fluent, more agreeable models are not guaranteed to reduce dependency risk — they may increase it, because a model better at sounding authoritative and more consistently agreeable is more persuasive when wrong. 'The tooling has evolved' is a reason to scrutinise sycophancy and over-reliance harder, not to trust more.

Open questions

  • Is chatbot-based support for autistic people legitimate assistive technology, or a paternalistic fix aimed at the wrong target? For: Autistic users in the CMU study chose this themselves, unprompted by clinicians, because existing workplace support was inadequate or absent — 'it's the only thing I trust.' Respecting autonomy means respecting that choice, not gatekeeping it behind professional approval. Against: A review Begel co-authored found 90% of HRI research on autism excluded autistic perspectives — a documented history of building 'solutions' nobody with autism wanted. Chatbot advice-giving individualises a structural workplace-inclusion failure: asking an autistic employee to get better at masking via AI coaching instead of making the workplace accessible treats the symptom.
  • Does satisfaction without measured productivity gain justify public licensing spend? For: DBT frames wellbeing, confidence and inclusion as legitimate outcomes independent of output volume; a more sustainable, less anxious workforce is a defensible use of public money, especially for a protected characteristic. Against: DBT's own conclusion: no evidence time savings led to improved productivity; value for money unassessed. Licences justified by self-reported satisfaction are weak in any Treasury-facing review and risk being read as subsidised comfort.
  • Does normalising AI-mediated compensation reduce institutional pressure to provide genuine accommodation? For: (risk is real) If AI drafting becomes the default fix for a dyslexic employee, the organisation has less incentive to fund proper adjustments, job redesign or human support - AI is cheaper and needs no line-management change. Against: Assumes accommodation is zero-sum; DBT and Capita evidence shows the tool works alongside existing adjustments and often surfaces previously invisible/unfunded need - additive, not replacement.
  • Universal rollout versus targeted, disclosure-based provisioning? For: (universal) Curb-cut argument: benefits accrue to non-native English speakers, hearing- and vision-impaired staff and many neurotypical staff (80% of use cases rated satisfactory across DBT). Targeting requires disclosure, which carries stigma risk (CMU respondents worried). Against: Untargeted rollout produced DBT's finding that Legal and Policy roles got minor benefit while absorbing the same licence cost and verification burden; also removes a comparison group, making it harder to tell real accessibility benefit from placebo/novelty.
  • Is self-report evidence trustworthy? For: Confidence, cognitive load and satisfaction are inherently subjective - self-report is the correct instrument. DBT triangulated with interviews and observed tasks and found broadly consistent patterns. Against: Respondents volunteered (70% of DBT) or knew they were evaluated on a tool their employer promoted - social-desirability and novelty bias. The only non-self-report measure (observed tasks) contradicted diary data on Excel analysis and PowerPoint quality.
  • Is it responsible to act on this evidence at all, given how fast tooling changes? For: (act now) Waiting for model-current research means never acting. Structural findings (manager influence, training modality, compensatory-vs-substitutive risk) are durable - acting on those is low-risk. Against: The most policy-relevant claims (advice quality, hallucination frequency, persuasiveness/over-reliance risk) are model-dependent and most likely wrong by the time a document reaches a minister. Citing a 2024 finding as current without re-testing is a factual risk.

Part 8 · Live pilotChapter 8.1 · 56 of 85

Live pilot handbook · prototype pilot pack, 25 August 2026

Testing this guide through a real deployment

We are not reviewing a document. We are using the playbook during a live AI deployment to determine whether it improves decisions, delivery, assurance and public-service outcomes, and whether there is sufficient evidence and appetite to establish a permanent, interactive toolkit.

Evidence status. The pilot model, thresholds and templates are proposed practice. They must be agreed for the selected live deployment. No pilot outcome is claimed in advance.

Seven stages, seven decisions

Mobilise

Is the pilot worth initiating?

Mandate, sponsor, scope and evaluation plan. Proceed or stop.

Select

Is the deployment suitable and safe for a pilot?

Candidate assessment and baseline. Select, condition or reject.

Prepare

Are people, controls, evidence and fallbacks ready?

Readiness and assurance plan. Authorise controlled deployment.

Deploy

Can the playbook be used during real delivery?

Operational evidence and decision trail. Continue, restrict, pause or stop.

Challenge

Did governance and assurance improve decisions?

Independent findings and participant evidence. Accept, remediate or retest.

Evaluate

Was the playbook useful, proportionate and valuable?

Evaluation and options appraisal. Stop, retain, simplify or evolve.

Decide

Is there appetite and evidence for a permanent capability?

Investment recommendation and roadmap. Toolkit decision.

Who this is for, and their first action

Sponsor or SRO

Decision points, risk boundaries, evidence and investment gate.

First action: Confirm outcome, authority and resourcing.
Candidate team

Eligibility, readiness criteria, expected contribution and safeguards.

First action: Complete the candidate screen.

Step-by-step lifecycle, artefacts, ceremonies and feedback routes.

First action: Attend induction and baseline assessment.
Assurance reviewer

Review lenses, evidence standards and independence rules.

First action: Agree assurance plan and conflicts.
Interested party

Ways to observe, challenge and contribute without disrupting delivery.

First action: Choose an engagement route.
Toolkit product team

Evidence needed to decide whether to stop, retain a static guide or build a living toolkit.

First action: Establish evaluation repository.

Part 8 · Live pilotChapter 8.2 · 57 of 85

Live pilot · hypothesis and test dimensions

What the pilot is testing

Primary hypothesis: using the playbook during a live deployment will improve the clarity, consistency, traceability and proportionality of governance and assurance without imposing unjustified delivery burden.

Usability

People can find and apply the right guidance without the author present.

Task observation, completion, help requests and interviews.

Proportionality

Controls reflect risk, autonomy, data, decision influence and public effect.

Exceptions, duplicated work, effort diary and reviewer judgement.

Decision quality

Material decisions have clear owners, evidence, uncertainty and conditions.

Decision records and assurance sampling.

Delivery value

The playbook prevents rework or reveals issues early enough to act.

Before and after comparison, avoided rework and issue chronology.

Assurance quality Claims are tested against meaningful evidence. Findings, closure evidence and independent opinion.

Learning value Participants gain usable capability and confidence. Applied assessments, job-aid use and follow-up interviews.

Future demand

Teams and leaders prefer a maintained toolkit over no framework or a static document.

Investment survey, sponsor decision and committed use cases.

Non-objectives

Proving that every AI deployment should use identical controls.

Treating participant satisfaction as proof of safety or value.

Using a successful pilot to claim cross-government impact.

Replacing formal legal, security, privacy, commercial or service-assessment obligations.

Part 8 · Live pilotChapter 8.3 · 58 of 85

Live pilot · candidate selection

Choosing a deployment worth learning from

Seven criteria, the evidence each needs, and the condition that turns a candidate into a rejection or an escalation.

Real deployment

Named service, users, owner and intended live or limited-live use.

Reject or escalate when: There is only a hypothetical demo.

Bounded purpose

Defined tasks, prohibited uses and measurable outcomes. Reject or escalate when: Purpose is open-ended or unowned.

Safe test route

Controlled environment, data route, fallback and stop mechanism.

Reject or escalate when: Critical safeguards are unavailable.

Representative learning

The candidate exercises meaningful parts of the playbook.

Reject or escalate when: The use case is too trivial to generate evidence.

Team capacity

Product, operational, technical and governance participation.

Reject or escalate when: Delivery relies on one person or unavailable specialists.

Evidence access

Permission to examine decisions, tests, incidents and effort.

Reject or escalate when: Evaluation cannot access material evidence.

Change tolerance

Team accepts challenge and can alter or pause deployment.

Reject or escalate when: Go-live is predetermined regardless of evidence.

Recommended cohort

Use three contrasting deployments where feasible: a bounded low-risk assistant, a reusable internal knowledge or workflow agent, and a higher-impact agent influencing operational judgement. This is a suggested design, not a mandated sample.

Part 8 · Live pilotChapter 8.5 · 60 of 85

Live pilot · formal assurance model

Five assurance stages, five kinds of opinion

Each stage states what it is for, what evidence it reviews, and the opinions it can legitimately reach.

Readiness

Determine whether controlled deployment can begin.

Evidence: Scope, owners, risk, authority, data, tests, fallback, training.

Opinion: Ready; ready with conditions; not ready.
In-flight

Test whether controls operate and the playbook supports decisions.

Evidence: Logs, samples, incidents, exceptions, user evidence, decisions.

Opinion: Effective; partially effective; ineffective.
Change

Assess material changes to model, tools, data, purpose or service.

Evidence: Impact assessment, regression tests, permissions and updated record.

Opinion: Authorise; condition; retest; reject.
Close-out

Judge whether claims and conclusions are supported.

Evidence: Outcome evidence, costs, findings, limitations and participant testimony.

Opinion: Reasonable; qualified; insufficient assurance.
Investment

Assess whether permanence is justified.

Evidence: Need, repeat demand, value, maintainability, ownership and funding.

Opinion: Stop; static guide; simplify; interactive toolkit.

Independence rule

Delivery teams own controls and evidence. Independent assurance challenges claims and reports limitations. The SRO makes the accountable decision; assurance does not transfer accountability.

Live pilot · success framework and feedback

Twelve measures, no invented thresholds

Each measure names its evidence, owner and cadence. Thresholds are agreed after the baseline is captured: a pre-set percentage without context would create false precision.

Independent use

Participants navigate lifecycle and required artefacts without author dependency.

Observed task completion; help requests; navigation errors. Evaluation lead. Baseline and end.

Proportionality

Teams and reviewers agree controls match material risk and consequence.

Effort diary; duplicated controls; exceptions; reviewer judgement.

Assurance lead.

Weekly and close-out.

Decision traceability

Material decisions identify owner, evidence, uncertainty, conditions and review.

Decision-record sample. Pilot manager. Fortnightly.

Early issue detection

Material gaps are discovered while action remains possible.

Issue chronology and avoided or reduced rework evidence. Service owner. Monthly.

Assurance quality

Findings distinguish intent, design, implementation, operation and outcome.

Independent assurance quality review. Assurance lead. Mid-point and close.

Operational readiness

Support, monitoring, fallback and incident routes work in exercises and operation.

Readiness checks, exercises and operational records. Operations lead. Pre-live and live.

Learning efficacy

Participants demonstrate relevant competence in realistic tasks.

Applied assessment and coaching records. Learning lead. Before and after.

User and service value

Observed service outcomes improve or credible learning justifies continuation.

Service-specific baseline and evaluation. Product manager. Agreed cadence.

Burden and cost

Implementation effort and recurring cost are visible and acceptable relative to value.

Time, support and consumption data. Evaluation and finance. Monthly.

Demand and appetite

Leaders and teams prefer a maintained option and commit use cases, ownership or resources.

Structured option choice and commitments. Toolkit product owner. Close-out.

Evidence integrity

Claims separate verified results, internal evidence, assumptions and expected outcomes.

Evidence audit. Independent assurance. Close-out.

Inclusion

Research and controls address accessibility and affected-user differences.

Accessibility and inclusion evidence. Accessibility lead. Design and close-out.

Feedback as formal evidence

Observed use Whether participants can apply the guide in context. At key lifecycle tasks. Observe the framework, not individual performance.

Decision sampling Whether governance claims are traceable. Throughout deployment. Risk-based sample agreed in advance.

Effort diary Where burden, duplication and rework occur. Weekly. Record estimates honestly and label them.

Structured interviews What helped, hindered or remained missing. Baseline, mid-point, close. Separate experience from factual claims.

Tabletop scenarios Whether controls work under failure and uncertainty. Pre-live and mid-point. Use synthetic scenarios where appropriate.

Assassin review

Where the model could fail, be gamed or become bureaucratic.

Mid-point.

Facilitated, blameless challenge.

Independent evidence review Whether conclusions follow from evidence. Close-out. Declare conflicts and evidence limitations.

Option-preference survey Whether appetite exists for future forms. Close-out. Require rationale and commitment, not preference alone.

Community consultation Whether patterns transfer beyond the pilot. After initial evidence. Do not generalise from advocacy alone.

Feedback taxonomy

KEEP

Works and should remain.

Protect and evidence.

IMPROVE

Useful but unclear or incomplete.

Refine and retest.

REMOVE

Adds unjustified burden or duplicates controls.

Remove or explain exception.

MISSING

A necessary need or control is absent.

Add, assign owner, validate.

CONFLICT

Contradicts policy, service or assurance practice.

Escalate and resolve.

LOCALISE

Valid but needs context-specific adaptation.

Create configurable pattern.

Live pilot · decision and future state

What happens after the pilot

Four options, the conditions that select each, and what each commits the organisation to. No option is pre-selected.

Stop

Value is weak, burden is excessive, risks are unresolved or demand is absent.

Archive evidence and retain lessons; do not operationalise.

Retain static playbook

The guide is useful as reference but repeat operational demand is limited.

Assign light-touch ownership and scheduled review.

Simplify and retest
  • Value exists but usability or proportionality is inadequate.
  • Prioritise critical changes and conduct focused retest.
Build living toolkit

Evidence shows repeat need, practical value, appetite and sustainable ownership.

Fund discovery and product development for an ongoing service.

Investment evidence required for option D

Multiple committed user groups or deployments, not general interest alone.

A named product or service owner and multidisciplinary maintenance capacity.

A sustainable source of policy, standards and pattern updates.

Clear content governance, versioning, supersession and retirement rules.

Evidence that dynamic interaction adds value beyond a downloadable guide.

Security, privacy, accessibility, information-management and operating-cost assessment.

A measurable service outcome and roadmap, not only a feature list.

Future-state toolkit concept

Flagship implementation guide

Understand the end-to-end route.

Adaptive journey through lifecycle, roles, gates and evidence.

Evidence: Navigation, completion and repeat-use data.

Governance navigator

Know which controls and forums apply.

Context-led route based on purpose, risk, autonomy and public effect.

Evidence: Routing errors, exceptions and decision consistency.

Internal ATRS workspace

Create and maintain a transparency record.

Guided record, evidence links, review and publication decision.

Evidence: Field usability, maintenance burden and scope decisions.

Assurance workspace

Build and review an evidence-based assurance case. Claims, evidence, findings, conditions and closure. Evidence: Evidence quality and review efficiency.

Learning academy

Build competence by responsibility. Role pathways, scenarios, assessment and job aids. Evidence: Competence outcomes and support demand.

Pattern library

Reuse proven controls and artefacts. Versioned patterns with evidence, owner and applicability. Evidence: Verified reuse and reduced duplication.

Portfolio control tower

Oversee value, risk, cost and lifecycle. Inventory, status, evidence freshness and decision queues. Evidence: Decision usefulness and data quality.

Community feedback loop

Keep the toolkit relevant.

Structured proposals, challenge, supersession and release notes.

Evidence: Contribution quality and maintenance capacity.

Product principle: the implementation guide remains the flagship resource. Interactive functions should reduce cognitive load and help people act safely; they must not hide accountability, evidence or applicable authoritative guidance.

Participant checklist

Before deployment
  • Read assigned playbook route.
  • Complete induction and competence tasks.
  • Confirm purpose, authority and prohibited use.
  • Validate data, tools and owners.
  • Practise fallback and escalation.
During deployment
  • Use approved process and boundaries.
  • Record material decisions and uncertainty.
  • Report incidents and friction promptly.
  • Maintain evidence and effort diary.
  • Attend evidence clinics and assurance reviews.
At close-out
  • Complete interview and option survey.
  • Review evidence and factual accuracy.
  • Declare unresolved concerns.
  • Identify KEEP, IMPROVE, REMOVE or MISSING.
  • Confirm future interest and commitment.

Pilot safety stop rules

  • Immediate or plausible material harm to users or the public.
  • Loss of control over permissions, data or state-changing actions.

Critical security, privacy, legal or accessibility condition breached.

Required human oversight or operational fallback unavailable.

Evidence integrity compromised in a way that prevents accountable decision-making.

Deployment moves outside approved purpose or environment.

Part 9 · Product documentationChapter 9.1 · 65 of 85

Delivery documentation · PRD

Product requirements

What this guide is for, who it serves, what it must do and what it deliberately does not do. Derived from published guidance and community discussion; a proposal, not an adopted product mandate.

Problems worth solving

Each problem is visible in the source material rather than assumed.

Guidance is real but scattered

The AI Playbook, Service Standard, TCoP, ATRS, NCSC secure-AI guidelines, ethics frameworks and FinOps practice exist separately. Teams reassemble them from scratch, inconsistently, each time.

Experimentation outruns governance

Personal assistants become shared agents and then business-critical dependencies without registration, named ownership, assurance or funded support.

Cost is discussed as licences

Token and licence spend is visible; data remediation, workflow redesign, assurance, human review, monitoring, support and exit are not costed or owned.

Evidence is claimed, not demonstrated

The same product yields different results under different evaluation methods, so headline productivity figures travel further than the method that produced them.

Community knowledge decays

Sessions, transcripts, repositories and personal networks hold the learning; there is no shared discovery layer, taxonomy or evidence pack, so lessons are relearned.

Goals and how each is judged

One route from mandate to governed operation

A reader can go from no policy position to a registered, assured, monitored agent using only this guide.

All eight start-here stages have a chapter and a tool
Make the invisible costs visible

Every cost class in the investment line is named, owned and modelled.

Cost lab produces a per-run and monthly figure with review effort included
Proportionate assurance, not blanket control

Criticality drives the gate; low-risk work stays fast.

Five tiers with stated evidence and review frequency
Evidence before assertion

Claims carry method, publisher and date; illustrative material is labelled.

Every figure in the guide is attributed or marked illustrative
Reusable artefacts, not prose

Register schema, ATRS record, instruction block and evidence card can be copied out and used.

Four artefacts exportable or copyable
Accessible to every role

Leaders, engineers, assurance, commercial, finance and frontline staff each have a path.

Role pathways cover the twelve priority roles
In scope

Guidance synthesis and chapter navigation

Assessment tools (readiness, criticality, tiers, maturity, quality gate)

  • Register and ATRS record schemas
  • Cost and unit-economics modelling
  • Skill instruction builder
  • Evidence, use-case and international comparison libraries
  • Illustrative portfolio dashboard
  • Delivery documentation set (this part)
Out of scope
  • Holding the authoritative record of any live deployment
  • Storing personal or OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data
  • Connecting to tenant telemetry, licensing or billing systems
  • Issuing approvals or acting as the assurance authority
  • Publishing ATRS records on behalf of an organisation
  • Replacing or overriding central or departmental guidance

Non-functional requirements

Accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA: contrast, focus visibility, keyboard operation, reduced-motion, semantic headings and labels.Information handling OFFICIAL working content only. No personal data, no case data, no credentials. Assessment answers stay on the reader's device.Portability Runs as a single file in a browser with no build step, no backend and no network dependency beyond fonts and cited links.
Performance First paint before the whole document streams; interactions respond within one frame budget on a standard civil-service laptop.Provenance Crown-copyright content reused under the Open Government Licence v3.0, with publisher and date on every figure.Print and export Chapters print legibly; the register schema and instruction block copy to the clipboard as plain text.

Release phases

Now

Phase 1 — proposal

This guide, reviewed by the community, with illustrative figures clearly labelled.

Next

Phase 2 — validated

Illustrative figures replaced with measured departmental data; international benchmarking executed.

Later

Phase 3 — adopted

Referenced in departmental AI policy, with the register schema and assurance gates in operational use.

Risks to the product itself

Illustrative figures read as measured High

Label every illustrative frame; keep publisher and date on evidence; publication checkpoint before circulation.

Guide treated as authority Medium

Proposal status on the landing chapter and in the hierarchy; explicit statement that it does not override guidance.

Content drifts from source guidance High

Chapter-to-source map; review date per chapter; ticker tracks guidance in force.

Assessment answers mistaken for assurance Medium

Device-only storage, no scoring authority claimed, evidence-based maturity rather than self-scored levels.

Delivery documentation · SAD

Solution architecture

Principles, context, layers and the decisions that shaped them. The architecture is deliberately small: the guide holds interpretation, never the record of a live deployment.

Architectural principles

Guidance is referenced, not copied

Link to the governed source; hold interpretation and sequence here.

No shadow record

The guide never becomes the register of record for a live deployment.

Client-side by default

No backend means no new data controller, no new attack surface, no new service to run.

Accessible before decorative

Contrast, focus and keyboard behaviour are acceptance criteria, not polish.

Evidence carries method

Every figure states publisher, date and method, or is labelled illustrative.

Open by default

Crown-copyright content under OGL v3.0; the guide itself is reusable and adaptable.

Context — actors and their part

Reader Civil servant in one of the twelve priority roles Reads chapters, runs assessments, copies artefacts

Owning organisation Department, agency, council or health body Holds the register of record, policy and approvals

Central guidance GDS, DSIT, NCSC, CDDO successor functions Publishes the guidance this guide interprets

Community

Cross-government Copilot forum, AI Engineering Lab, ethics and data communities

Supplies patterns, failures and supplier intelligence

Suppliers Platform, model and integration providers Subject of dependency, exit and commercial chapters

govukOS shell Twin front door and sibling portals Hosts the guide as one app among several

Logical layers

Experience

Masthead, ticker, drawer, chapter rail, contents, chapter body, footer navigation

Chapter registry Parts, chapters, numbering, accents, icons, read state

Content

Source-derived data: principles, gates, domains, roles, tiers, schemas, dashboards

Assessment logic

Barometer, criticality, tiers, maturity evidence, quality gate, barrier scoring

Economics

Token maths, language multipliers, unit economics, allocation layers

Local state

In-memory interaction state plus one persisted barometer record on the device

Decisions

ADR-01

Single-file client-side document

No hosting, no data processing agreement, no service to operate; trades server-side features for portability.

ADR-02

No personal or case data anywhere

Removes the need for a DPIA on the guide itself; assessments stay on the device.

ADR-03

One artefact, many chapters

Keeps navigation, search and cross-references coherent; avoids a fragmented document set.

ADR-04

Illustrative data labelled, never silently synthetic

Protects the evidence boundary this playbook sets out.

ADR-05

Accent colour per part

Gives readers a positional cue; all accents are contrast-tested as text.
