Part 9 · Product documentationChapter 9.5 · 69 of 85

Delivery documentation · LLD

Low-level design

Module responsibilities, the arithmetic behind every score, the validation rules and the accessibility implementation. Enough for someone else to rebuild the behaviour exactly.

Modules and their state

Navigation module

groupDefs → flat chapter list → numbering, accents, prev/next, contents

section, groups, read, toc

Barometer module eight dimension scores → mean → band with colour and label scores (persisted)

Criticality module ten dimension scores → total → tier and gate mapping crit, gateTier

Barrier module impact × likelihood → 1–25 → four bands bar

Economics module

tokens = words ÷ 0.75; cost = in×priceIn + out×priceOut + tools + infra + review

lab, ue

Instruction module seven fields → composed block → clipboard blk, copied

Algorithms

Barometer banding

mean of rated dimensions; 0–0.9 Nascent, 1.0–1.9 Emerging, 2.0–2.4 Establishing, 2.5–3.0 Leading; unrated dimensions excluded from the mean and reported as unrated.

Criticality to gate

sum of ten dimensions scored 1–5; 10–20 personal, 21–30 team, 31–38 departmental, 39–44 operational service, 45–50 citizen impact.

Barrier banding

impact × likelihood on 1–5 scales; 1–3 low, 4–8 medium, 9–15 high, 16–25 critical.

Unit economics

value per interaction = (minutes saved ÷ 60 × hourly rate) × quality factor; net = value − cost; return = net ÷ cost expressed as a percentage.

Validation rules

Numeric inputs Clamp to declared minimum and maximum; reject non-numeric silently rather than throwing.

Unrated dimensions Show an em dash, never a zero, and exclude from means.

Currency Two decimal places, pound sign, thousands separated; never rounded away in totals.

Clipboard Plain text only; confirm with a transient state, no alert.

Persistence One key, versioned; parse defensively and fall back to blank on any error.

Accessibility implementation

Colour Every text and meaningful non-text pair contrast-tested; accents have separate text-safe variants where a fill carries text.

Keyboard All controls are buttons or inputs; aria-pressed and aria-current reflect state; focus ring never suppressed.

Motion The guidance ticker pauses on hover and respects prefers-reduced-motion.

Structure One h1 per chapter, sequential headings, aria-labels on sections, skip link to content.

Language British English, plain terms, expanded acronyms on first use in a chapter.

One navigable implementation guide Completed readiness and criticality assessments Registered agents with named owners Costed business cases including hidden costs Reusable evidence cards and patterns

Short-term outcomes

Teams find the applicable guidance quickly Proportionate assurance replaces blanket caution Agents have owners, tiers and review dates Cost conversations include people and exit

Medium-term outcomes

Fewer orphaned and unregistered agents Duplicated procurement and assurance effort falls Evidence is reused across organisations Oversight is continuous, not one-off

Impact

Governed AI-enabled services that create demonstrable public value
Sustained public trust in how government uses AI
Each row depends on the one above it holding. Outcomes are claimed only where evidence exists; everything below outputs is currently a proposal.

Assumptions

Guidance stays reasonably stable Chapters carry review dates so drift is visible rather than silent.

Teams have protected time Without funded time, the guide is read but not applied.

Leaders accept proportionality Blanket caution defeats the tiering model as surely as no control at all.

Community keeps sharing Reuse depends on organisations publishing failures as well as successes.

Illustrative figures get replaced Measured departmental data must supersede the labelled placeholders.

Indicators to track

Chapters opened per role pathway

Agents registered with a named owner and review date

Proportion of agents with an ATRS record

Assurance decisions made at the tier they belong to

Business cases including the full investment line

Patterns and evidence cards reused across organisations

Personas, stories, journeys and service blueprints

Drawn from the roles, frictions and lifecycle material in published guidance and community discussion. These are evidence-derived working personas, not research participants — they need validating with real users before they carry design decisions.

Six personas

Accountable leader
Director or SRO, accounting-officer line

Decide where AI is worth the risk and the money, and be able to answer for it.

Needs

  • Evidence that a claim is measured, not asserted
  • A defensible risk appetite
  • One page that survives a select-committee question

Frustrations

  • Productivity figures with no method attached
  • Being asked to approve what nobody owns
  • Cost framed as licences only
Reads: Assurance tiers, evidence chapter, investment line, control tower
Service owner
Owns an operational service with real users

Adopt agents without destabilising a service people depend on.

Needs

  • Clear promotion gates
  • Named ownership and support model
  • A rollback and exit route

Frustrations

  • Agents appearing in the service without registration
  • Unclear escalation when output is wrong
  • Support cost landing on the service unfunded
Reads: Agent journey, criticality and gates, failure and recovery, dependency and exit
AI engineer
Builds and evaluates agents

Build well-grounded agents and prove they work.

Needs

  • Evaluation and red-team patterns
  • Grounding decision tree
  • Instruction blocks that transfer between platforms

Frustrations

  • Ungoverned copies of source data made for grounding
  • No baseline to evaluate drift against
  • Prototype standards applied to production, and the reverse
Reads: Skill studio, architecture and quality, knowledge foundation, AI Engineering Lab
Assurance and ethics specialist
Reviews, challenges and signs off

Apply proportionate control and see the evidence behind it.

Needs

  • Criticality scoring that distinguishes usage from consequence
  • ATRS record completeness
  • A residual-risk statement per agent

Frustrations

  • Assurance as a gate at the end rather than a thread throughout
  • Self-scored maturity with no evidence
  • Incidents surfacing without a route to redress
Reads: Risks and mitigations, internal ATRS registry, maturity evidence, autonomy boundaries
Commercial and FinOps lead
Buys, allocates and forecasts

Fund adoption honestly and keep exit possible.

Needs

  • Unit economics per use case
  • Allocation model across six cost layers
  • Supplier requirements for telemetry, portability and exit

Frustrations

  • Token cost mistaken for total cost
  • Lock-in discovered at renewal
  • Shared costs with no agreed allocation
Reads: Cost value and investment, commercial and suppliers, FinOps, dependency and exit
Frontline practitioner
Uses agents in daily casework

Do the work faster without carrying unowned risk.

Needs

  • Plain guidance on what is allowed
  • A way to challenge an output
  • Training in the flow of work

Frustrations

  • Guidance written for architects
  • No clear escalation when the agent is wrong
  • Being blamed for a tool decision made elsewhere
Reads: Support around every colleague, inclusive adoption, roles and pathways

User stories with acceptance criteria

As a Accountable leader, I need to see the method behind any productivity claim, so that I do not repeat an unevidenced figure in public.

Accepted when: Every figure shows publisher, date and method, or is labelled illustrative

As a Accountable leader, I need to know which agents are high risk and who owns them, so that I can direct attention where consequence is highest.

Accepted when: Control tower lists risk level, owner and next review per agent

As a Service owner, I need to know the gate an agent must pass before it touches my service, so that I can plan assurance rather than discover it.

Accepted when: Criticality score returns a tier with named evidence and review frequency

As a Service owner, I need to have an exit path for a platform or model, so that a supplier change does not stop my service.

Accepted when: Seven-step exit path with the dependencies it addresses

As a AI engineer, I need to decide where grounding information should live, so that I do not create ungoverned copies.

Accepted when: Decision tree returns one of four options in priority order

As a AI engineer, I need to compose an instruction block once and reuse it, so that behaviour is consistent across platforms.

Accepted when: Seven-part block copies out as plain text

As a Assurance specialist, I need to score criticality across ten dimensions, so that control is proportionate to consequence.

Accepted when: Score maps to one of five gates with its controls

As a Assurance specialist, I need to record transparency information for every internal agent, so that oversight and audit have something to inspect.

Accepted when: Eight-section ATRS record with all fields listed

As a FinOps lead, I need to model cost per run and per month, so that a business case includes consumption, not guesses.

Accepted when: Cost lab returns per-run and monthly figures with a language multiplier

As a FinOps lead, I need to see value against cost per interaction, so that I can show whether the agent earns its keep.

Accepted when: Unit economics returns value, net and return

As a Frontline practitioner, I need to know what I may use and when to escalate, so that I can work confidently within the guardrails.

Accepted when: Support chapter states allowed use, escalation and where help comes from

As a Community manager, I need to turn a session into a reusable evidence pack, so that learning survives the meeting.

Accepted when: Evidence pack structure with owner, taxonomy and review date

Journeys

First-time reader to first decision

Arrives with a question Lands on the overview, sees proposal status “Is this authoritative?” Proposal flag and hierarchy answer it in one screen

Finds the applicable chapter Uses search or contents “Where does my case sit?” Chapter numbering and part accents orient quickly

Runs an assessment Tier finder or criticality radar “Am I over- or under-controlling?” Tier arrives with evidence and review expectations

Takes an artefact away Copies the register schema or instruction block “What do I do on Monday?” Copyable artefacts, not prose

Returns for oversight Re-opens the control tower and maturity evidence “Has anything drifted?” Read state and review cadence bring them back

Agent from idea to retirement

Idea Someone builds a helpful agent “This saves me an hour a day” Register at creation, not at scale

Share Colleagues start relying on it “It works, so why formalise it?” Promotion gate between personal and team scope

Assure Criticality scored, tier applied “How much control is proportionate?” Gate names the evidence needed

Operate Monitoring, cost and quality watched “Who notices if it degrades?” Named owner and continuous duties

Review Re-authorise, improve, restrict or retire “Is it still earning its authority?” Review date forces the decision

Retire Access revoked, records archived “What happens to the evidence?” Archive and audit stage in the lifecycle

Community session to reused pattern

Session happens Weekly call, recorded from 17 August 2026 “Will I find this again?” Automatic recording closes part of the capture gap

Capture Transcript, chat, files, commitments “Who owns the follow-up?” Session evidence pack with owner and actions

Classify Taxonomy: capability, use case, sensitivity, owner, review date “Which of these applies to me?” Shared taxonomy across communities

Connect Federated index links to governed sources “Is this the current version?” Index links rather than copies

Reuse Another organisation adopts the pattern “Has anyone tried this already?” Discovery by role, sector, maturity and supplier

Learn Outcome and corrections returned “Did it actually work?” Value reported as reuse, not attendance

Service blueprint — an agent in an operational service

Five lanes across the same five moments: what the user does, what they see, what happens behind it, what supports it, and what is recorded.

User actions

Requests help Reviews agent output Accepts or challenges Escalates an error Feeds back on value

Frontstage

Agent responds with citation Confidence and limits shown Human review point Escalation route offered Feedback captured in service

Backstage

Retrieval over authoritative sources Guardrails and permission checks Logging and audit trail Incident triage and rollback Evaluation against baseline

Supporting processes

Register and ATRS record maintained Assurance gate evidence held Cost allocated to the use case Supplier and model change managed Review or retirement decision

Evidence and records

Source provenance Approval and sign-off Monitoring and drift reports Incident records Benefit evidence

Knowledge and navigation · 10 entries

Thesaurus

Preferred term, the variants you will hear, and why the distinction matters. Cross-government acronyms and loose synonyms are the main cause of transcripts and registers that cannot be searched.

Agent

digital worker

assistant

copilot

bot

Use agent for the governed capability; digital worker only when the employment framing is deliberate.

Assurance

governance

compliance

sign-off

Assurance tests claims against evidence; governance sets the rules. Do not use them interchangeably.

Criticality

risk level

importance

priority

Criticality is dependency and consequence. Risk level is the output of scoring it.

Register

inventory

catalogue

asset register

Register for agents; catalogue for data; asset register for information assets. Three registers, integrated, not merged.

Evaluation

testing

benchmarking

evals

Evaluation covers accuracy, safety and fitness against a baseline; testing alone implies pass or fail.

Guardrail

control

policy

limit

Guardrails are technical constraints; controls include process and people; policy is the rule they enforce.

Retirement

decommissioning

offboarding

sunsetting

Retirement is the lifecycle stage; decommissioning is the technical work inside it.

Transparency record

ATRS record

algorithmic transparency

publication

ATRS record is the published artefact; the internal registry extension is proposed, not mandated.

Value

benefit

ROI

savings

State value as an outcome with a method. Reserve savings for cash-releasing benefits that finance has agreed.

Adoption

rollout

deployment

enablement

Adoption is people changing how they work; deployment is the technology going live. They are not the same date.

Deploy for real · working tool

Derive the governance set for any agent

Two bands and ten factors in. Tier, autonomy cap, oversight regime, currency window, evaluation set, threat priorities, DPIA route, contract clauses, workforce actions, register fields and kill criteria out — with the rules that produced them, so the answer can be argued with rather than accepted.

Volume

Criticality

Extended factors

No factors selected

Q1

Automate with sampling

Tier 1 · Light

The strongest agent case in government. Volume pays for the governance; a mistake is recoverable. The risk here is not harm, it is quietly losing the ability to do the work.

Effective criticality

1 / 14

Autonomy cap

L4

Act with post-hoc sampling — exceptions escalate

Challenge-rate floor

0.5%

Below this, suspect oversight, not excellence.

Sign-off

Service owner

Oversight regime

2% random sample, weekly

Data protection route

Screening assessment, recorded and dated

A screening that concludes no full DPIA is needed is still evidence. Keep it, and re-run it when scope changes.

Evaluations that must exist

Golden-set regression

A frozen set of real historical cases with agreed correct outputs, re-run on every model or prompt change.

Refusal and out-of-scope set

Cases the agent must decline, escalate or flag rather than attempt.

Cost and latency envelope

Per-transaction cost and response time, with the ceiling that triggers review.

Threat priorities

Prompt injection via ingested content High

Any document, email or record the agent reads is untrusted input. Test with adversarial content in every ingestion path.

Tool over-permission High

The agent holds broader credentials than its task needs. Scope per action, not per agent.

Contract clauses that become mandatory

Model change notification

Written notice before any model, weight or default change that affects behaviour, with a defined notice period.

Log and evidence export

All prompts, outputs, tool calls and decisions exportable in a documented open format, during and after the contract.

No training on our data

Explicit prohibition, with the right to evidence of compliance.

Exit and portability

Prompts, instruction blocks, eval sets and grounding indexes are ours, exportable, and documented well enough to rebuild elsewhere.

Workforce actions

Say where the freed capacity went

Volume automation releases hours. Publish where they were redeployed. Unnamed savings become quiet headcount reduction with no decision behind it.

Consultation before design freeze

Staff and unions see the job-redesign proposal while it can still change. After the build is a briefing, not a consultation.

Register fields beyond the baseline

Accountable officer

A named person, not a team or a role inbox.

Reversal path

How an effect is undone, tested, with the last test date.

Currency holders

Who currently holds valid approval authority, and when each window expires.

Kill criteria

Challenge rate falls below floor

Reviewers overturning less than 0.5% of outputs. Either the agent is perfect or oversight has stopped. Assume the second.

Golden-set regression unexplained

Any drop on the frozen set that cannot be explained and fixed within the rollback SLA.

An outcome nobody can explain

A single decision the accountable officer cannot account for in plain language.

Why it produced that answer

  • Low criticality sets a base of 1.
  • Effective criticality 1 of 14 places this in Tier 1 · Light.

Very high volume with low criticality places this in Q1 · Automate with sampling.

The weights are a defensible starting point, not a measured value. Change them with your assurance function and record the change — a tool whose reasoning is hidden cannot be challenged, and a governance answer nobody can challenge is not governance.

Part 11 · Deploy for realChapter 11.3 · 79 of 85

Deploy for real · four agents, one per quadrant

Correspondence triage, mandate to operation

Every artefact filled in, including the ones that are uncomfortable. Very high volume, moderate criticality — the case most departments would call easy. Named honestly it lands in Tier 3 · Enhanced, and that is the most useful thing in this chapter.

These four agents are composites, not case studies. The figures are internally consistent and illustrative, and the decisions are the ones the sources support. Your organisation will ratify and adapt every one of them.

Mandate

1 of 10

Signed by the service owner before any build. One page, and it fits.

Problem

Inbound correspondence arrives across six channels into one queue. Median time to first correct routing is four days; 11% is routed wrong at least once. Statutory deadlines are met by escalation, not by process.

In scope

Classify inbound correspondence to one of 34 work queues, extract sender, reference, subject and any stated deadline, and draft a suggested reply from the approved template set.

Explicitly out of scope

Deciding any case. Sending anything. Replying to anyone. Handling correspondence flagged as a complaint, a legal threat, a safeguarding concern or a data-subject request — those route to a human unopened by the agent.

Success measures

Time to correct routing, misroute rate, deadline breaches, and reviewer challenge rate. Not volume processed, and not staff satisfaction alone.

Decision rights

The agent proposes. A caseworker commits. Nothing leaves the organisation without a named person attached to it.

Funding and duration

Twelve months, one delivery team, with a stop point at month four and a re-authorisation decision at month twelve.

What would make us stop

Any statutory deadline missed because of the agent, or a challenge rate below 5% sustained for two months.

What changes the answer inside this quadrant

Same agent, same quadrant, one factor different. Each variant below is scored by the generator on this page, not asserted — so what moves and what does not is the tool's own arithmetic.

The agent sends the reply itself Tier moves

+ Irreversible Tier 4 · Critical Q1 · Automate with sampling L1 · Draft only — a person edits and commits every output

One word in the mandate — send rather than draft — and an effect exists that no later correction undoes. Autonomy is forced to draft-only regardless of tier, and shadow mode becomes mandatory. This is the most common scope change requested after go-live, and the cheapest one to refuse.

Correspondence routinely contains health detail Tier moves

+ Special-category data Tier 4 · Critical Q1 · Automate with sampling L1 · Draft only — a person edits and commits every output

The screening guardrail stops being a nicety and becomes the control the DPIA rests on. A leakage probe joins the evaluation set, and the grounding index has to be provably free of the material.

Internal-only queue, rule-based routing Tier moves

− Discretionary judgement
− Vulnerable users
Tier 2 · Standard
Q1 · Automate with sampling
L3 · Act within guardrails — every action logged and sampled

Remove the discretion and the vulnerable recipient and the same agent, at the same volume, drops a tier. Most of the governance in the worked example is paid for by those two factors, not by the volume.

Part 11 · Deploy for realChapter 11.4 · 80 of 85

Deploy for real · scope boundary

What this guide does not cover

A guide that does not state its boundary strands the team at the point where the interesting problems start. This chapter exists so nobody reaches gate 3 believing the architecture, the security testing or the legal advice was somewhere in the earlier parts.

Fully covered here

Principles, criticality and tiering, autonomy boundaries, registers and transparency records, oversight design including currency, cost and value modelling, roles and adoption, the pilot method.

Structured, needs your content

Instruction blocks, evaluation plans, threat profiles, DPIA routes, contract clause sets, job redesign. The shape is here; the substance is yours.

Named but not solved

Reference architecture for your estate, engineering pipeline, executed security testing, model selection, sector regulation, organisational design, safety cases.

What a team must bring

Eight things this guide names but cannot supply. Each one has a normal home in an organisation. Find the home before the build starts, not after.

A target architecture for your estate Enterprise architecture

This guide names what an architecture must satisfy. It does not know your identity provider, your network, your data platform or your existing contracts. Someone with authority over those has to draw it.

Executed security testing Security function or an appointed third party

The threat model here tells you what to test. Running the test — penetration testing, red-teaming, adversarial evaluation — is specialist work with a report at the end of it.

Legal advice on your specific case Legal and your DPO

Everything here about lawful basis, automated decision-making and liability is structure for a conversation with a lawyer. It is not the advice.

Model selection and benchmarking Technical owner

Which model, at what cost, with what evaluation on your data. This guide is deliberately model-agnostic, which means it cannot answer the question you will be asked first.

Sector regulation Your regulator and legal

Health, policing, immigration, education and financial services each carry duties this guide does not enumerate. Where it conflicts with your regulator, your regulator wins.

Organisational design Accountable leadership

Who reports to whom, which team holds the capability, and how it is funded past the pilot. The roles here are role names; you have people, budgets and politics.

Accessibility conformance Accessibility specialist

The comprehension and inclusion tests here are necessary and not sufficient. A conformance audit against WCAG is a separate, evidenced exercise.

Safety cases Clinical or safety governance

Where an agent touches physical safety or clinical outcomes, a structured safety case is required and this guide does not contain one.

Five things to be honest about

Read these before citing anything in this guide to a board, an auditor or a regulator.

Every artefact here is a proposal

Nothing in this guide has statutory force. Until your organisation ratifies it, an artefact is a well-argued suggestion. Ratify it, or expect it to be ignored at the first disagreement.

Figures marked illustrative are illustrative

Where this guide shows a threshold, a percentage or a band, it is a defensible starting point drawn from the sources, not a measured value from your service. Replace it with yours.

Volume and criticality placements are judgements

The fifty-four services in the atlas are placed on published volume bands and an assessment of consequence. They are a starting position for an argument, not a classification you can cite.

The generator does not approve anything

It derives a consistent governance set from the inputs you give it. Give it flattering inputs and it will produce a flattering answer. That is a property of every assessment tool, including the ones with logos on.

The four worked examples are composites

They are built from the sources, from published service data and from patterns that recur across deployments. They are not case studies of four real agents, and no organisation in them is identifiable. Their numbers are internally consistent and illustrative — treat them as a model answer to compare your own against, not as evidence of what happened somewhere.

Sequence is not schedule

The life cycle here is ordered. It carries no durations, because the honest answer depends on your assurance capacity, and that is the constraint nobody plans for.

Pan-UK

All four nations have strategy. One has published evaluation.

Counting strategies overstates maturity: a benchmark that measures published strategy ranks all four nations comparable. Only one has a published body of controlled evaluation of deployment. What each nation can borrow from the others is the point of comparing.

International

Benchmarking the UK's position

Five reference jurisdictions, five different bets: from the EU's binding risk tiers to Singapore's testing-led pragmatism. Genuinely transferable: Canada's public assessment and inventory approach, Australia's named AI ownership and workforce model, Singapore's central adoption flywheel, US inventory discipline, and the EU's joint procurement direction.

Where Key instrument Model For public bodies

UK

AI Playbook + sector regulators; ATRS; AI Security Institute evaluations

Principles-led, pro-innovation; non-statutory for now

Playbook principles and ATRS records; four published evaluations; frontier legislation under consideration

EU

AI Act (in force 1 Aug 2024; Digital Omnibus 2026 defers high-risk duties to Dec 2027, public authorities to Aug 2030); EuropAI joint procurement

Binding, risk-based regulation

High-risk public deployments: conformity assessment, logging, human oversight, fundamental-rights impact assessment

US

NIST AI Risk Management Framework; OMB memoranda; GAO oversight

Voluntary framework + agency rules; state laws vary

Federal AI use-case inventories and Chief AI Officers; rapid growth with persistent policy and budget challenges

Canada

Directive on Automated Decision-Making + Algorithmic Impact Assessment; agentic-AI guidance (May 2026)

Binding on federal automated decisions

Mandatory AIA before deployment; names skill atrophy as an oversight risk; bounded autonomy and recoverability

Singapore

Model AI Governance Framework · AI Verify toolkit

Voluntary, testing-led

Central funding, shared platforms, problem intake, applied learning — an adoption flywheel

The EU AI Act's four risk tiers

In force 1 August 2024. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026) moved stand-alone high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028 and high-risk systems for public authorities to 2 August 2030. Article 50 transparency duties have applied since 2 August 2026. Obligations follow the use case, not the technology. The benchmark other regimes are measured against.

Unacceptable

Banned outright: social scoring, subliminal manipulation, real-time remote biometric ID in public spaces (narrow exceptions).

High risk

Essential public services, law enforcement, employment, critical infrastructure: conformity assessment, documentation, human oversight, EU database registration.

Limited risk

Transparency duties: chatbots must say they are AI; synthetic media must be labelled.

Minimal risk

Most systems: spam filters, recommenders. No mandatory obligations; voluntary codes encouraged.

The supranational layer

OECD AI Principles + OECD.AI Observatory

The shared definition of AI used by the UK Playbook and the EU AI Act. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks national AI policies worldwide; it is the model for this app's observatory.

Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024)

The first binding international AI treaty: human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The UK is a signatory.

G7 Hiroshima AI Process (2023)

International guiding principles and a code of conduct for organisations developing advanced AI systems.

AI Safety Summit series: Bletchley, Seoul, Paris

Frontier-safety declarations and the network of national AI safety and security institutes. Started at Bletchley Park, November 2023.

UN General Assembly resolution (2024)

First UN consensus resolution on safe, secure and trustworthy AI for sustainable development.

Part 12 · ReferenceChapter 12.3 · 83 of 85

Reference · pace and parity

Named once. Controlled nowhere.

Skill atrophy appears in this guide as a single sentence in the evidence chapter, credited to Canada. Nothing sits behind it: no control, no metric, no register field, no gate criterion, no owner. That is the honest answer to the question, and it is now backlog item PACE-01. This chapter closes it, then applies the same test to everything else the world has built that we have not.

Named

Yes

One sentence, evidence chapter, attributed to Canada

Controlled

No

No control, no owner, no frequency

Measured

No

No metric in the barometer or control tower

Gated

No

No criterion in the quality gate

What Canada actually did

Six moves, and the last is the operable one. The instrument is the Guide on the Use of Agentic Artificial Intelligence, published by the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat on 22 May 2026, sitting on top of a directive that already made assessment mandatory.

Named the risk inside an instrument

Continued offloading of decisions to AI agents can lead to knowledge and skill atrophy and weakened human judgment. Employees become less practiced at core tasks and slower to notice when something is wrong.

Guide on the Use of Agentic AI, TBS, 22 May 2026

Tied it to the validity of oversight

Maintenance of relevant skill sets among agentic AI users and deployers is treated as a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight. Not a wellbeing concern — a validity condition on the control itself.

Same instrument, mitigations

Added two agent-specific principles

Bounded autonomy and recoverability, introduced alongside the existing generative-AI principles rather than replacing them.

Same instrument

Named the consequence chain

Service quality, privacy and security, legal defensibility and public trust. The risk is framed as legal and operational exposure, not a training preference.

Same instrument

Made assessment mandatory and public

Algorithmic Impact Assessment before deployment, four impact levels, external peer review at levels III and IV, questionnaire published openly including on GitHub.

Directive on Automated Decision-Making

Pointed at a concrete drill

Periodic human-only execution of agent-handled tasks for comparison; staff trained to interrogate agent outputs rather than accept them.

Commentary on the guide, May 2026

PACE-01 · proposed instrument

Oversight currency

Canada names skill maintenance as a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight. A prerequisite that nobody measures is a sentiment. Aviation, nuclear operations and clinical practice all solved this the same way: recency requirements, evidenced, with authority attached. If you supervise the work, you stay current in the work. Six components, all of them auditable.

Component What it does Who holds it Evidence

Manual-mode drill

A reviewer executes an agent-handled task unaided, then compares. Tier 1 monthly, tier 2 quarterly, tier 3 twice yearly.

Reviewer

Drill record holding both outputs

Currency window

A reviewer whose last unaided execution predates the tier window loses approval authority on that queue until re-current. Enforced, not advised.

Service owner

Authority state in the register

Divergence log

Every drill records agreement or disagreement and why. Sustained perfect agreement is itself a signal — it is what rubber-stamping looks like from outside.

Reviewer

Divergence entries with reasons

Challenge rate

Proportion of agent outputs materially amended before acceptance. A falling challenge rate against a flat error rate is drift, not improvement.

Control tower

Monthly trend per queue

Rotation

No reviewer supervises the same agent-handled queue continuously. Rotation preserves unaided practice somewhere in the role.

Line manager

Rota showing unaided work

Displaced-skill field

The register records which skills the agent displaces, who must retain them and to what standard. If nobody is named, the deployment is not approvable.

Deployment owner

Register field, tested at each gate

The uncomfortable component is the divergence log. A reviewer who agrees with the agent every time is either supervising a perfect agent or not supervising at all, and the record cannot tell the difference. Convergence has to be read as a warning rather than a result.

Eight instruments elsewhere, measured against ours

Three are outright gaps: something binding or published elsewhere with no UK counterpart. Four are partial. One is context we should track rather than copy.

EU AI Act Article 4 — the AI literacy duty Gap

Binding since 2 February 2025 and unaffected by the proposed high-risk delay. Applies to deployers of every AI system, not only high-risk ones, and covers staff and contractors regardless of seniority. The compliance test is a dated, role-mapped programme that plausibly matches actual use.

Where we stand

Training is encouraged throughout UK guidance but is nowhere a duty, and course completion is not evidence of competence.

Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI Gap

World-first agentic framework, Davos 22 January 2026; version 1.5 on 20 May 2026 after feedback from over sixty organisations, with more than ten deployment case studies. Four pillars, unique agent identities tied to a supervising agent or user, threat modelling for memory poisoning, tool misuse and privilege compromise.

Where we stand

We hold secure-AI guidance and our own patterns, but no single agentic instrument and no agent identity requirement.

Canada

Directive on Automated Decision-Making, plus the agentic guide

Gap

Assessment is mandatory before deployment, scored across four impact levels, with external peer review at the top two. The questionnaire is published openly, including on GitHub, and has become the instrument others copy.

Where we stand

ATRS is transparency after the fact, not assessment before it, and it is not a gate.

Australia AI Safety Institute inaugural report, 9 August 2026 Open to all

Found that NIST's risk framework, OWASP's Agentic Top 10, Singapore's agentic framework and ASD's agentic guidance all rest on the same hidden assumption: that one organisation owns every agent in a system. Cross-organisational agent risk is a structural gap none of them covers.

Where we stand

Our register assumes single-owner agents too. The gap is identified and unimplemented everywhere, including here — which makes it available.

Global Singapore Consensus companion report on agentic risk Partial

Ten foundational principles for managing agentic risk: least privilege, traceable identity, auditability, validated deployment, adversarial resilience, multi-agent stability, runtime assurance, interruptibility, legibility and human oversight.

Where we stand

We hold most of these as scattered controls. None is consolidated into a named principle set an approver can test a deployment against.

OECD Digital Government Outlook 2026 Partial

Thirty-two of thirty-six countries run AI training programmes; only thirteen of thirty-six train on using AI in public services or in policymaking. Broad capability is improving faster than role-specific readiness. Thirty of thirty-six have an institution governing public-sector AI; twenty-one of thirty-six offer central procurement support.

Where we stand

Our academy is role-based on paper. Depth of oversight-specific training has never been tested against this benchmark.

G7 GAIN network and the GovAI Grand Challenge Partial

A G7 AI network convened and chaired by Canada, tasked with a roadmap to scale successful public-sector AI projects and a catalogue of open-source, shareable AI solutions for members.

Where we stand

We participate. We have contributed no reusable instrument to the catalogue.

Asia-Pacific Korea AI Basic Act (2026), Taiwan AI Basic Act (2025) Tracking

Regional convergence on human oversight, data safeguards and prohibitions on harmful or deceptive use, arriving through basic law rather than sectoral guidance.

Where we stand

Context rather than gap: the UK route is guidance-led by choice. Worth tracking for interoperability, not imitation.

The backlog, MoSCoW'd

Thirteen items and three deliberate refusals. Every item has an owner and a first deliverable, because an unowned backlog item is a wish.

Must

This quarter. Each one closes a gap that leaves an existing control unsound.

PACE-01
Oversight currency

Manual-mode drills, currency windows, divergence log, rotation and the displaced-skill register field. Turns the Canada finding into something an auditor can test.

Owner: Learning lead with service owners First: Control spec and tier windows

PACE-02
Evidenced literacy duty

A dated, role-mapped competence requirement for anyone who operates or approves an agent, contractors in scope. The Article 4 test, applied voluntarily and ahead of any obligation.

Owner: Learning lead First: Role-to-competence map

PACE-03
Agent identity

Every agent carries a unique identity bound to a named human owner and, where orchestrated, to a supervising agent. Prerequisite for audit, for handover and for retirement.

Owner: Architecture First: Identity schema in the register

PACE-04
Bounded autonomy and recoverability

Adopt both as named approval principles. Every agent has a tested interrupt and a tested rollback before it goes live, with the test evidenced.

Owner: Assurance lead First: Two gate criteria and a test script

PACE-05
Drift telemetry

Challenge rate and divergence surfaced in the control tower beside assurance status, per queue, monthly.

Owner: Control tower First: Two new tiles

Should

Next two quarters. These extend reach rather than repair a fault.

PACE-06
Cross-boundary agents

Register fields for agents we interact with but do not own: supplier, other department, arm's-length body. The first implementation of the gap Australia named.

Owner: Architecture with commercial First: Field set and one worked case

PACE-07
Multi-agent systemic risk

An assessment step for orchestrated patterns, covering interaction effects that no single-agent assessment can see.

Owner: Assurance lead First: Assessment addendum

PACE-08
Oversight-specific training

Not general AI awareness. Training in interrogating outputs, recognising plausible-but-wrong, and running a manual-mode drill.

Owner: Academy First: Curriculum for three roles

PACE-09
Assessment before deployment

A scored pre-deployment assessment distinct from the transparency record, with independent peer review at the top tiers.

Owner: Governance office First: Scoring instrument

PACE-10
Extended threat model

Memory poisoning, tool misuse and privilege compromise added to the agent threat model and to the security review.

Owner: Security lead First: Threat model revision

Could

Worth doing, sequenced behind the above. This is where the leadership case is actually made.

PACE-11
Publish the instruments

Register schema, gate criteria and the currency control released openly under the Open Government Licence, versioned, as Canada did with its assessment.

Owner: Governance office First: Public repository

PACE-12
Reciprocal assurance pilot

One partner nation, one deployment class, mutual recognition of assurance evidence. Tests whether our evidence travels before we offer it widely.

Owner: Governance office First: Pilot terms with one partner

PACE-13
Atrophy measurement study

Longitudinal measurement of unaided performance in agent-supported roles, with an academic partner. Nobody holds this data, which is why everyone is asserting rather than measuring.

Owner: Evaluation lead First: Study protocol

Won't — for now

Named, so the omission reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

PACE-W1
Statutory literacy penalties

Not ours to set. We build the evidence base a policy decision would need.

Owner: — First: Revisit when policy opens

PACE-W2
A UK agentic act

The guidance route moves faster, and we do not yet hold the evidence to legislate well.

Owner: — First: Revisit after PACE-13

PACE-W3
Certifying supplier agents

Capacity we do not have. Contract terms and evidence requirements instead.

Owner: — First: Revisit at scale

Four things nobody has published yet

Parity is a floor, and reaching it puts us level with instruments already a year old. Each of these is a control we could be first to publish, and three of the four came out of our own case work rather than the international scan.

Oversight currency as a revocable authority

Canada names skill maintenance as a prerequisite for oversight. Nobody has made it measurable and revocable — an approval right you can lose by going stale. Publishing the control with tier windows and drill records would be first.

The orphaned-agent control

Machinery-of-government change moves an owner; active agent work continues unattended and is later inherited by a team that never approved it. No framework surveyed handles ownership transfer on reorganisation.

Attention budgets for review

Approval capacity treated as a finite, costed resource and rationed by risk tier, so review is real where it matters instead of uniform and hollow everywhere.

Cross-boundary agent handshake

Australia's institute named cross-organisational agent risk as a gap no framework covers. A register field plus a handshake at departmental and supplier boundaries would be the first implementation of it.

Keeping pace is a rhythm, not a document

Four of the eight instruments above were published or revised in the last eight months. A guide refreshed annually is a guide that is wrong for eleven of them.

Weekly

Horizon scan into the guidance ticker: new instrument, new version, new enforcement action.

Scan rota

Fortnightly

Instrument diff across the eight tracked jurisdictions. What changed, what it obliges, whether it touches a control we hold.

Governance office

Monthly

Re-MoSCoW the backlog. Anything sitting in Should for two cycles is promoted or killed, never carried.

Governance office

Quarterly

Publish the delta pack and contribute one reusable instrument to a shared catalogue.

Governance office

Annually

Reciprocal review with a partner nation: they read our instruments, we read theirs, both publish the findings.

SRO

Where the work goes once it exists

Five routes already open to us. None of them takes a position paper; all of them take a working instrument.

G7 GAIN

The network's remit includes a catalogue of open-source, shareable AI solutions for members. A register schema and a currency control are exactly that shape.

OECD.AI and the Digital Government Outlook

The comparative baseline every country is measured against. Contributing method, rather than only returning survey answers, changes what the baseline measures.

Council of Europe Framework Convention

The first binding international AI treaty, on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The UK is a signatory, and the validity of human oversight sits squarely inside its scope.

The AI safety institute network

The UK allocated roughly A$460m at the 2025 spending review, against about A$50m over five years in Canada and about A$11m a year in Singapore. Capacity to convene is not the constraint.

Open publication

Open Government Licence v3.0, public repository, versioned. Canada published its assessment questionnaire openly and it became the reference others adopted.

Sources: Guide on the Use of Agentic Artificial Intelligence and Directive on Automated Decision-Making, Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat; EU AI Act Article 4 and the AI Office Q&A on AI literacy; IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI v1.5 (20 May 2026); Australian AI Safety Institute inaugural report (9 August 2026); Singapore Consensus companion report on agentic risk; OECD Digital Government Outlook 2026 and Building an AI-ready public workforce (2026); G7 GovAI Grand Challenge and GAIN, Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat and Impact Canada. Figures are as published by each source and are not converted or combined.

Generative AI and Crown copyright: a brief guide for government departmentsUK-wide. Guidance, CurrentWork that civil servants create with generative AI in the course of their duties, and then review, modify and assure, may be Crown copyright. Where a provider's terms give the user ownership of outputs, those outputs belong to the Crown. If the terms assign outputs to the provider, seek legal advice. Departments must still publish attribution and licensing statements and attribute third-party material. Caveat: No exact publication date; the copyright notice is 2025.The National ArchivesGenerative AI and Crown copyright: A brief guide for government departments (opens an external website)
Open Government Licence and AI training on government contentUK-wide. TNA's view on training is guidance, not a court ruling.The National ArchivesGenerative AI and Crown copyright: A brief guide for government departments (opens an external website)
Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (DUAA ss.135-136)UK-wide. Policy, CurrentThe government no longer prefers a broad text and data mining exception with a rightsholder opt-out, and has not chosen an alternative. It will gather more evidence, explore output labelling and digital replica rights, and keep protection for computer-generated works under review. There is no change to copyright law yet, so public bodies using AI must respect third-party copyright under existing law. Caveat: No legislative timetable. A digital replicas consultation was expected in summer 2026 and its publication is unconfirmed. UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018UK-wide. Law, In forceAny AI tool that processes personal data (in prompts, uploaded files, grounding data or outputs) is subject to UK GDPR and the DPA 2018. Data protection is reserved in Scotland and Northern Ireland and is a specific reservation for Wales, so the same law applies across the UK; devolved bodies follow it but have their own records and FOI regimes. Caveat: Explanatory notes say Scotland Act Sch 5 Pt II B2 and NI Act Sch 3 para 40 make it reserved; Wales Act 2017 adds a specific reservation (para 170). Amended by DUAA 2025 from 2025-2026.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Data Protection Act 2018 Explanatory Notes (territorial extent) (opens an external website)
Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 — commencement statusUK-wide. Law, Partly commencedMost data protection reforms commenced on 5 February 2026 (Commencement No. 6, SI 2026/82), including the new transfer regime, recognised legitimate interests and the new automated decision-making Articles 22A-D. The complaints duty started on 19 June 2026 and the Information Commission replaced the ICO on 30 September 2026. Check commencement before relying on any individual provision. Caveat: Earlier commencement orders: No.1 20 Aug 2025, No.3 5 Sep/17 Nov 2025, No.4 1 Dec 2025 (per Kennedys, grade B). Whether every remaining section has now commenced is unconfirmed; the departmental owner of data protection policy after July 2026 is inferred from the DCMS-published Information Commission release.DCMS (UK data policy since the July 2026 machinery of government change); regulator: Information CommissionThe Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82) (opens an external website)
Information Commission succeeds the ICOUK-wide. Regulation, In forceFrom 30 September 2026 the Information Commission (a body corporate) replaced the Information Commissioner's Office as regulator for data protection, FOIA and EIR. The government says powers and responsibilities are unchanged and existing guidance continues, so ICO-branded guidance remains the reference. Update policy documents, privacy notices and DPIA templates that name the ICO. Caveat: Published by DCMS. Whether ico.org.uk URLs will move is not stated; URLs in this dataset still point to ico.org.uk.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Information Commission succeeds the ICO as UK's data protection regulator (GOV.UK news) (opens an external website)
Recognised legitimate interests (Article 6(1)(ea))UK-wide. Law, In forceA new lawful basis with five pre-approved public-interest purposes (responding to another body's public-task request, national security/defence, emergencies, crime, safeguarding) where no balancing test is needed. The ICO says public authorities performing their tasks should generally still rely on public task, not this basis, so it rarely justifies a department's own AI processing. Caveat: Commenced 5 Feb 2026 via DUAA s.70 and Sch 4.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Recognised legitimate interest (ICO guidance) (opens an external website)
Automated decision-making — UK GDPR Articles 22A-22DUK-wide. Law, In forceSince 5 February 2026 the old near-ban on solely automated decisions is replaced by Articles 22A-D: significant decisions based solely on automated processing are allowed with safeguards (information, a way to make representations, human intervention and the right to contest), with tighter limits where special category data is used. If an AI tool makes or effectively makes a significant decision without meaningful human involvement, these rules apply. The ICO's updated ADM guidance is still a draft. Caveat: Commenced by DUAA s.80 and Sch 6; does not apply to decisions taken before 5 Feb 2026 (SI 2026/82 reg 5). ICO consultation ran 31 Mar to 29 May 2026; final guidance not confirmed published as of 2026-10-19.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Automated decision-making, including profiling (ICO, draft guidance under consultation) (opens an external website)
Statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-makingUK-wide. Regulation, In forceRegulations in force from 12 May 2026 require the Information Commissioner to prepare a statutory code on processing personal data when developing and using AI and ADM, including children's data. The regulations do not themselves add obligations; once issued, courts and the regulator must take the code into account. Plan for it but do not assume its content yet. Caveat: The code itself is not published; secondary reporting (Arnold & Porter, Aug 2026, grade B) says it is not expected to take effect until 2027.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425) (opens an external website)
ICO Guidance on AI and data protection (including DPIAs)UK-wide. Guidance, CurrentThe main regulator guidance on fairness, lawfulness, transparency, accountability and DPIAs for AI. Deploying an AI tool that processes personal data at scale or in novel ways will normally need a DPIA before go-live. The ICO marks this guidance as under review following the DUAA, so check for updates before relying on detail. Caveat: Page states 'under review and may be subject to change'. The 'DPIA normally needed' wording is a summary of UK GDPR Art 35 practice, not a quotation from this page. The ICO also told government (27 May 2026 letter, reported by Local Government Lawyer, grade B) it will publish a procurement due-diligence resource for off-the-shelf cloud AI tools and agentic AI guidance; neither confirmed published.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Guidance on AI and data protection (opens an external website)
Using AI in public services — Digital Scotland Service ManualScotland. Guidance, CurrentScottish Government guidance for the Scottish public sector on responsible use, transparency, human oversight and accountability: people remain responsible for decisions and AI should not be used where decisions cannot be explained or reviewed. It is a first iteration and will be revised. Caveat: The guidance URL shown in the blog carried a preview token; the guidance text was not read, so its coverage of data, records and FOI is unconfirmed.Scottish Government (Public Sector AI Team, Digital Directorate)New Artificial Intelligence (AI) guidance available for Scottish public sector (Digital Scotland blog) (opens an external website)
Workforce Partnership Council guidance on AI and algorithmic management (Wales)Wales. If an AI supplier processes prompts or files outside the UK, someone must have done this assessment or the destination must be covered by UK adequacy regulations.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)UK GDPR Article 46 (as amended by DUAA 2025 Sch 7) (opens an external website)

Framework, CurrentThe industry-standard model for running technology spend as a shared business discipline: Inform, Optimize and Operate phases across four domains (understand usage and cost; quantify business value; optimise usage and cost; manage the practice). The 2026 edition treats AI as its own technology category ('Scope') alongside public cloud, SaaS, licences and data centres. It recommends bottom-up budgets revised more often than for ordinary cloud, alerts when token or GPU use jumps, and matching the model to the task instead of defaulting to the most capable (and most expensive) model. Provisioned or reserved AI capacity (for example Azure PTUs) suits only predictable workloads; unused blocks are wasted money. Practice, CurrentPutting an AI gateway in front of model endpoints lets you enforce tokens-per-minute limits and daily or monthly token quotas per team or application, emit token-usage metrics with custom dimensions for showback and chargeback, cache semantically similar answers to cut repeat calls, and route traffic to prepaid capacity first with pay-as-you-go as overflow. Azure API Management is one documented example; equivalent controls exist in other gateways. Caveat: Supplier-specific example; capability availability varies by service tier. Not a government mandate – presented as good practice.Microsoft (supplier documentation, used as an example)AI gateway in Azure API Management (opens an external website)

Financial controls and business cases (9)

ObligationWhere, kind and statusWhat it means for AI useOwnerBasis
Managing Public Money (HM Treasury)UK-wide. Guidance, In forceThe rules accounting officers must follow for regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility. A revised edition (DAO 02/25, June 2025) applies to all central government bodies, with new material on accounting officer duties and use of models; in April 2026 guidance on interpreting 'Novel, Contentious and Repercussive' (NCR) and delegated-authority guidance were added. AI spend that is novel for your organisation may need HM Treasury approval even below your delegated limit. Caveat: Applies to UK government departments and their ALBs; devolved administrations have their own equivalents. Latest page entry (13 August 2026) added an ALB template and updated delegated-authority letter template.HM TreasuryManaging public money (opens an external website)
Digital Assurance Playbook (replaces GDS digital and technology spend controls)UK-wide. Policy, CurrentFrom 1 April 2026 GDS digital and technology spend controls (v6: £100k public-facing, £1m other) were withdrawn. Departments now own their own assurance, must record digital and technology initiatives over £5m whole-life cost (any spend for cryptographic products) on a pipeline monitored by HM Treasury, and need central approval only above their Treasury-set Delegated Authority Limit or for Novel, Contentious or Repercussive work. AI initiatives should follow the AI Playbook and the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, and AI new to an organisation may be treated as Novel. Caveat: Most other Cabinet Office spend controls also ceased on 1 April 2026 (advertising, marketing and communications control retained), following HM Treasury's Office for Value for Money controls review (Budget, 26 Nov 2025). Departmental Delegated Authority Limits were not published at the time of checking. Publisher shown as DCMS and DSIT; DSIT has since been abolished (21 July 2026).Government Digital Service (DCMS) with HM TreasuryDigital Assurance Playbook (opens an external website)
The Green Book (2026 edition)UK-wide. Guidance, CurrentHM Treasury's appraisal guidance for any spending proposal, including AI. The 2026 edition is much shorter and says a single benefit-cost ratio is not enough: decision makers must weigh monetised and unmonetised costs, benefits and risks, and a BCR below one does not automatically mean poor value. AI business cases should show the full range of costs (licences, credits, compute, assurance, skills) against realistic, evidenced benefits. Caveat: No AI-specific content. Proportionality guidance on business case detail was still an outstanding commitment at 30 June 2026.HM TreasuryThe Green Book: appraisal and evaluation in central government (opens an external website)
Guidance on developing business cases (Five Case Model, consolidated 2026)UK-wide. Guidance, CurrentThe single HM Treasury guide to the Five Case Model (strategic, economic, commercial, financial, management) for projects and programmes, consolidated in June 2026. Use it for any AI investment that needs a business case; the AI Playbook notes investments approaching £10m typically need a five-case business case. Caveat: The £10m rule of thumb is from the AI Playbook (Feb 2025), which also quotes the now-withdrawn £100k spend control threshold.HM TreasuryGuidance on developing business cases (opens an external website)
Accounting for SaaS/cloud configuration costs (capital vs resource)UK-wide. Guidance, CurrentWhether money spent setting up an AI or cloud service can be capitalised depends on whether you control an intangible asset under IAS 38. The IFRS Interpretations Committee's March 2021 agenda decision on configuration and customisation costs in SaaS arrangements applies; HM Treasury's Financial Reporting Advisory Board proposed no public-sector adaptation in the FReM. Most subscription AI (licences, credits, tokens) is therefore likely to score as resource spending – agree treatment with your finance team before the business case. Caveat: The 'likely resource' conclusion is an inference, not a Treasury statement. No 2025-26 HM Treasury guidance specific to AI capitalisation was found.HM Treasury (Financial Reporting Advisory Board)FRAB 144(13): IFRS Interpretations Committee summary of announcements (opens an external website)
Scottish Public Finance Manual: Digital Portfolio in major investmentsScotland. Guidance, CurrentThe Scottish Public Finance Manual is the Scottish equivalent of Managing Public Money. Finance Guidance Note 2025/04 added a Digital Portfolio section to major investment projects, setting a mandated portfolio approach for relevant public bodies' digital investment, linked to the Digital Scotland Service Manual and a Digital Portfolio Board. Scottish bodies planning significant AI investment should check whether it falls into the Digital Portfolio. Caveat: Inclusion thresholds were not stated on the guidance note page. No AI-specific provisions.Scottish GovernmentFGN 2025/04: SPFM amendment – Digital Portfolio added to major investments (opens an external website)
Managing Welsh Public MoneyWales. Guidance, CurrentThe Welsh Government's framework for handling public funds, applying to the Welsh Government, its sponsored bodies, NHS Wales and others. Welsh bodies buying or budgeting for AI follow this rather than HM Treasury's Managing Public Money. Caveat: Dated 2018 with no visible later update; no AI-specific content.Welsh GovernmentManaging Welsh public money (opens an external website)
Managing Public Money Northern Ireland (MPMNI)Northern Ireland. Guidance, CurrentDepartment of Finance guidance on the proper handling of public money across the NI public sector – the NI equivalent of Managing Public Money. Anyone committing NI public funds to AI tools must follow it. Caveat: Page metadata shows last update 12 August 2024. No AI-specific content.Department of Finance (Northern Ireland)Managing Public Money NI (MPMNI) (opens an external website)
Better Business Cases NINorthern Ireland. Guidance, CurrentThe primary NI guidance on developing and reviewing business cases, based on the Five Case Model and HM Treasury business case guidance with NI supplements. It superseded the NI Guide to Expenditure Appraisal and Evaluation (NIGEAE) from 2 November 2020 and applies, proportionately, to every proposal that spends or saves public money – including AI. Caveat: Has not yet been checked against the June 2026 consolidated HM Treasury business case guide.Department of Finance (Northern Ireland)Better Business Cases NI (opens an external website)

Chatbots and voice systems must give an equivalent Welsh service, and AI-delivered training, recruitment and performance tools must not disadvantage Welsh speakers. Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 - WCAG 2.2 AAUK-wide. Where AI might be used to deliver a 'non-AI' service, consider requiring suppliers to declare it and set contract terms on use of data such as meeting transcripts. Freedom of Information Act 2000 — AI prompts and outputs are 'information'England, Wales, Northern Ireland. Addresses FOIA only, not EIR or private accounts specifically.Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)Freedom of information (FOI) and artificial intelligence (ICO) (opens an external website)

Its case study cautions against extrapolating early time savings to the whole civil service. Working tool

Can I use AI for this?

Five questions give a first route. Governance follows what the AI can see, create and do, not which company made it. Nothing you enter leaves your browser.

1 Would the output decide, or directly change, someone’s rights, entitlements, safety or access to a service?
2 Will you use personal data or information marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or above?
3 Can the AI take actions, run on a schedule or work through several steps without you?
4 Is there an approved tool in your organisation's catalogue that already does this?
5 Could a conventional rule, form or automation do the job reliably?

Answer the five questions

The route appears when every question has an answer. “Not sure” is a valid answer.

How the route is decided

The first rule that matches wins. A first sort, not an approval: every route other than an approved tool leads to a registered use case.

  1. Would the output decide, or directly change, someone’s rights, entitlements, safety or access to a service?
  2. Will you use personal data or information marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or above?
  3. Can the AI take actions, run on a schedule or work through several steps without you?
  4. Is there an approved tool in your organisation's catalogue that already does this?
  5. Could a conventional rule, form or automation do the job reliably?
WhenRouteWhat it means
Q1 is YesSeek advice before going furtherAI must not make or directly change this kind of decision on its own. Register a use case; it takes the specialist route with a named human decision-maker.
Q5 is YesTry conventional automation firstA rule, form or workflow is usually safer, cheaper and more consistent. Use AI only where judgement over unstructured material is the task.
Q3 is Yes or Not sureTake the agent routeAnything that acts, runs on a schedule or works through steps without you needs an agent design record, approval points and a stop control.
Q1 is Not sure, or Q2 is Yes or Not sureRegister a use casePersonal or sensitive information, or an unclear impact on people, needs data readiness and privacy screening before use.
Q4 is YesGo ahead with an approved toolUse it within its approved uses and check its catalogue entry for conditions. Review every output before you rely on it.
OtherwiseCheck for reuse, then registerNo approved tool is known to fit. Search your organisation's catalogue first; if nothing fits, request a tool through a use case.

Assurance

Human-centred controls for trustworthy AI work

Risk-based human-in-the-loop controls make sure AI never grants authority a user does not already possess, and that every material output can be defended after the fact.

The five-stage assurance workflow

  1. Classify — identify service impact, data sensitivity, equality and accessibility risk, security risk and model/agent autonomy. Use the triage tool →
  2. Select — apply the standards, source guidance, skills, agents, conformance packs and review level the classification demands.
  3. Execute — work with least privilege, mandatory source citation, deterministic checks and pair or buddy support where competence is thin.
  4. Review — 4-eyes or 6-eyes review, specialist assurance, and no self-approval for material or high-risk outputs.
  5. Learn — capture evidence, incidents, near-misses, feedback, source drift and model changes; feed them back into the corpus.

The H0–H5 human review model

Review levels, when they apply and the evidence each produces
LevelNameWhat it meansTypical examplesEvidence
H0No review neededPersonal, throwaway, non-published exploration with no personal or sensitive data.Explaining a concept to yourself; drafting private notes.None required.
H1Self-checkAuthor verifies facts, sources and accessibility before use. Low impact, easily reversible.Internal meeting notes, first-draft ideas.AI-use note in the document.
H2Peer checkA second competent person checks output before it leaves the team.Internal reports, non-public analysis, low-risk code in a sandbox.Reviewer name, date, issues found.
H3Specialist review (4-eyes)A named specialist in the relevant discipline reviews. No self-approval.Accessibility, security, legal, statistical or clinical content; production code.Specialist sign-off + test results.
H4Multi-specialist review (6-eyes)Two or more specialisms plus the accountable owner. Independent challenge required.Public-facing decisions, casework support, anything affecting entitlements.Panel record, dissent captured, residual risk stated.
H5Governance board and publicationFormal board approval, published transparency record and monitored deployment.Automated or semi-automated decisions about people; national services.ATRS record, DPIA, EQIA, monitoring plan, review date.

Reviewer checklist

Always check

  • Every citation opens, exists and says what the text claims
  • Numbers, dates, thresholds and legal references independently verified
  • Nothing asserts compliance that has not actually been tested
  • No personal or sensitive data was entered into an unapproved tool
  • Accessibility and plain-language requirements met, not assumed
  • Assumptions, gaps and residual risk stated explicitly
  • Reviewer is independent of the author at H3 and above

Common failure patterns

  • • Confident fabrication — plausible citations that do not exist
  • • Stale authority — quoting withdrawn or superseded guidance
  • • Compliance theatre — a checklist ticked without a test run
  • • Silent scope creep — an agent doing more than was authorised
  • • Automation bias — reviewers rubber-stamping fluent output
  • • Averaged users — outputs tuned to a majority that excludes minorities
  • • Evidence gaps — no record of who checked what, or when

Metadata catalogue

Treat skills, agents and code as assets in their own right

Every reusable AI capability should be discoverable, accountable, interoperable and governed like any other public asset — with an owner, a version, a risk rating and a retirement plan.

FieldWhy it matters
asset_idStable identifier so evidence, incidents and dependencies can point at it.
