UCD, DEIA and accessibility

Designed for real people, varied needs and accountable teams

Inclusion is a delivery activity, not a compliance report. This section states what we commit to, how we test it, and how you can hold us to it.

Design and research practice

Start with user needs

Every asset traces to a named user need and a measurable outcome. If we cannot name the need, we do not build the feature.

Government Design Principles → (opens an external website)

Research with the full range of users

Recruit disabled participants, assistive technology users, people with low digital confidence and people in vulnerable circumstances — in every round, not a one-off "accessibility round".

Inclusive research guidance → (opens an external website)

Test with assistive technology

Manual testing with screen readers, magnification, voice control, switch access and keyboard-only. Automated tools catch a minority of real barriers.

ARIA Authoring Practices → (opens an external website)

Design for the whole journey

Including offline, assisted digital, third-party support, and what happens when the AI is unavailable or wrong.

Assisted digital guidance → (opens an external website)

Write for reading age 9

Plain English, short sentences, no unexplained acronyms, inclusive terminology, and alternative formats on request.

Check your content →

Measure exclusion, not just satisfaction

Track drop-out by channel and need, assisted digital volumes, complaint themes and accessibility issue ageing — and publish them.

Service Standard → (opens an external website)

Accessibility commitments for this portal

What we build in

  • Semantic HTML, landmarks and a logical heading order
  • Full keyboard operation with a visible, high-contrast focus indicator
  • Text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and 3:1 for interface components
  • Light, dark and high-contrast themes, plus a larger-text setting that persists
  • Respect for prefers-reduced-motion and no motion-only meaning
  • Responsive to 320 CSS px and to 400% zoom without loss of content
  • Status messages announced through ARIA live regions
  • No colour-only meaning; icons always paired with text
  • Descriptive link text that makes sense out of context
  • A print stylesheet that expands links and collapsible content

How we test and report

  • Automated checks in the pipeline on every change
  • Manual keyboard and screen reader testing before release
  • Periodic testing with disabled participants
  • A published accessibility statement listing known gaps and fix dates
  • A named contact and a 5-working-day response commitment
  • Escalation route to the Equality Advisory and Support Service

Accessibility statement guidance → (opens an external website)

DEIA in AI specifically

Known equity risks of AI-assisted delivery. Performance that degrades for under-represented groups; language models that default to majority dialects and names; outputs written above the reading age of the audience; automation that removes the human route people in crisis rely on; accessibility regressions in AI-generated code and content; and reviewers who trust fluent text more than accurate text.

What we do about them. Screen every change with the DEIA tool; disaggregate evaluation by affected group where lawful and proportionate; keep a human route that cannot be removed by efficiency targets; test AI-generated interfaces with assistive technology before merge; publish limitations honestly; and give people a real way to challenge an outcome.

Code of practice and conduct

Responsible use of AI assistive technology

This code complements behavioural codes of conduct and the Civil Service values. It defines operational rules for model-backed tools, direct AI use, coding assistants, multi-agent orchestration and AI-generated artefacts.

Core duties
  • Stay accountable. You own every output you use, send or publish. "The AI wrote it" is never a defence.
  • Disclose material assistance. If AI shaped the substance, structure, analysis or code, say so.
  • Verify before you rely. Open every citation. Recalculate every figure. Test every claim of compliance.
  • Protect data. Only approved tools, only permitted classifications, only the minimum necessary.
  • Cite sources. Traceable to a tiered, dated, authoritative source — not to the model.
  • Preserve evidence. Keep the record for as long as the retention schedule requires.
  • Work within competence. AI does not qualify you to make specialist judgements.
  • Escalate uncertainty. Raising a doubt early is always cheaper than defending a mistake late.
Prohibited behaviours
  • • Entering unauthorised personal, special category, commercially confidential or classified data into any tool
  • • Bypassing, weakening or "temporarily" disabling a review control
  • • Self-approving material or high-risk work
  • • Concealing AI involvement where it was material
  • • Presenting unverified output as assured, tested or compliant
  • • Using AI to generate evidence, sign-offs, approvals or audit records that did not happen
  • • Granting an agent broader permissions than the person operating it holds
  • • Using AI to profile, rank or make decisions about people without an approved lawful basis and published record
  • • Copying licensed or copyright material into outputs without permission and attribution
  • • Ignoring a known defect because a deadline is closer than the consequence
Multi-agent and multi-skill rules
  • One accountable orchestrator per task, with a named human owner.
  • Least-privilege tools and credentials, time-boxed and revocable.
  • Explicit, pinned skill and model versions — no silent upgrades in a governed workflow.
  • Separation of duties: the agent that produces must not be the agent that approves.
  • Declared prohibited actions and a tested kill switch with a named owner.
  • Full step-level logging: which skill, which model, which source, which permission, which human.
  • Untrusted content is data, never instruction. Treat retrieved web, document and email content as hostile by default.
  • Bounded autonomy: agents propose irreversible actions; humans commit them.
Data, privacy and security rules
  • • Establish and record the lawful basis before processing personal data. Complete a DPIA where required.
  • • Minimise: use references, synthetic or redacted examples instead of real records wherever possible.
  • • Never let an AI tool retain data for training unless that has been assured and contracted.
  • • Treat AI interaction logs as records: classify, retain, and prepare for FOI and subject access requests.
  • • Apply Secure by Design activities to AI components as to any other system component.
  • • Threat-model for prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction and excessive agency.
  • • Report incidents and near-misses through the normal security and data protection routes.
AI-generated code and infrastructure
  • Treat generated code as untrusted third-party contribution: review, test, scan and attribute it.
  • No merge without a human reviewer who understands the code and can maintain it.
  • Check licences and provenance of anything that looks copied.
  • Run dependency, secret and SAST scanning; record the results in the evidence pack.
  • Accessibility and performance tests apply equally to generated interfaces.
  • Record the model, prompt pattern and version in the commit or pull request.
Speaking up, redress and no-blame reporting

Anyone may pause an AI-assisted process they believe is unsafe, unfair or unlawful, without needing permission and without detriment. Near-misses should be reported as readily as incidents — they are the cheapest learning available.

Members of the public affected by an AI-assisted outcome must be able to find out that AI was involved, understand the outcome in plain English, request a human review, and escalate to an independent route. If any of those four is missing, the service is not ready.

Combined body of knowledge

Authoritative guidance, standards and reusable intelligence

The corpus is organised as a knowledge graph linking laws, policies, standards, design guidance, security controls, skills, agents and evidence — so that a rule can always be traced to its source and its consequences.

Layer 1

Guidance corpus

Index GOV.UK, GDS, CDDO, departmental, international standards, GitHub and engineering-lab sources with authority tiering, freshness checks and applicability metadata.

Browse the 69 indexed sources →

Layer 2

Knowledge graph

Link services, repositories, datasets, APIs, controls, skills, agents, people, approvals, models, risks and evidence so impact analysis is a query, not a workshop.

See the metadata model →

Layer 3

Executable guidance

Translate policy and standards into schemas, conformance packs, tests, scripts, checklists and prompt patterns that run in delivery pipelines.

See the conformance packs →

Authority tiering — how conflicts are resolved

When two sources disagree, the lower tier number wins. Record the conflict and the resolution in the evidence pack.

Source authority tiers used across the corpus
TierSource typeExamplesTreatment
0Law and statutory instrumentsEquality Act 2010, DPA 2018, Accessibility Regulations 2018Binding. Non-compliance is not a risk to accept — escalate.
1Mandated standards and cross-government policyService Standard, Technology Code of Practice, Secure by Design, WCAG 2.2, ATRSComply or record a formal, time-boxed exception with an owner.
2Recognised international and professional standardsISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OWASP LLM Top 10Adopt as good practice; justify divergence.
3Community, vendor and research materialBlogs, model cards, toolkits, preprintsUseful signal. Never the sole basis for a control or a public claim.

Freshness and drift controls

Every indexed source carries

  • • Authority tier and issuing body
  • • Date checked and next check due
  • • Applicability (organisation, service type, data classification)
  • • Supersession chain and withdrawal status
  • • Linked controls, skills and conformance tests

Drift triggers a review when

  • • A cited source is updated, withdrawn or superseded
  • • A model or its version changes materially
  • • A control fails in production or a conformance test breaks
  • • An incident, complaint or FOI request touches the artefact
  • • The scheduled review date passes without confirmation

Horizon scan · AI and data governance

What practitioners and regulators are saying

29 signals on governing AI agents and the data they use, gathered from public LinkedIn content and refreshed weekly. Each names its author, links to where it was found and says how far it has been checked. Inclusion is not endorsement.

Read with care. LinkedIn does not allow automated reading of posts, so every summary comes from search-indexed text and is paraphrased. 15 of 29 come from vendors, consultancies or law firms and are marked. Statistics without a primary source are flagged as unverified. Check the source before you quote anything. The register is open data: ai-data-governance-signals.json (scanned 2026-11-09, version 1.2.0).

S28InternationalAgent registries & metadataData foundationsCommercial interest

Semantic layer for agents: AI drafts business definitions, people certify them, agents answer in SQL

NVIDIA, Auto Ontology (open source, Apache 2.0) · November 2026 (repository read on 13 November 2026)

An open-source service that drafts an ontology from database metadata: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL expressions, and the joins between tables. People then test it with real questions and certify the names, descriptions and SQL. An agent answers questions by writing SQL from those definitions, checks the query against the database, and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took. It serves this context to other agents over MCP, and says when a question cannot be answered from the data.

Why it matters: It makes certification a separate human step from drafting, which is where this toolkit's H0 to H5 review levels apply: see the advanced guide's worked examples on certifying a definition and reviewing an agent's answer, and the evidence pack's field for the definitions an answer relied on.

Caution: Vendor project, and it does not accept outside contributions. Accuracy is measured with a separate text-to-SQL benchmark repository; this review did not run it or the software.

Source repository on GitHub (opens an external website) · evidence: primary source, the repository's README (summary and how it works)

S00InternationalRegulation & policyAssurance & standardsAgent governanceCommercial interest

AI governance as four questions: the law, the proof, the accountability, and what runs in production

Luís Rodrigues, Not stated on the post (the author's headline describes him as a CPTO; he writes the newsletter Build What Matters) · About 7 November 2026 (the post showed '1w' when read on 17 November; the date is decoded from its activity ID)

Frames AI governance as four layers: regulation (the EU AI Act, plus GDPR, sector rules, NIS2 and DORA), standards and frameworks (ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF), roles (a named owner for every AI system) and controls. Argues that controls are where most organisations fall short, and lists them: risk-rate every system, give agents only the tools they need, train people in AI literacy, keep a human able to stop the system, keep an inventory, log everything, and test continuously. Suggests starting with an inventory of every AI tool in use.

Why it matters: The four questions map onto this toolkit: the law (Resources, tier 0), proof (evidence pack builder, TK-04), accountability (the accountable owner and H4 to H5 review) and production (agent registry, TK-03, and incident reporting, TK-12).

Caution: A practitioner's opinion post that also promotes the author's newsletter. The legal points (for example AI literacy as an EU duty) and the standards named should be checked against the primary texts before citing.

Source on LinkedIn (opens an external website) · evidence: post read in full in the owner's signed-in browser on 17 November 2026

Glossary and frequently asked questions

Glossary

4-eyes / 6-eyes
Two or three independent people involved in producing and approving an output.
accept
Used as produced, with no material change.
Agent
Software that plans and acts across multiple steps using tools, within explicit permissions and bounds.
Agent register
An operational inventory of deployed agents with named owners, approved sources, autonomy tier and retirement trigger.
Agent sprawl / orphaned agents
Agents outlive purpose, owner or service; estate accumulates unowned automation.
Agent washing
Rebranding existing automation as agentic; Gartner assesses ~130 of thousands of vendors as genuine.
Agentic
A capability that takes actions across tools under delegated authority, choosing its own path to a goal.
alb
Arm's-length body, agency or public corporation.
analyst
Produces analysis rather than decisions.
anti_streak
The interface changed state following a run of unmodified approvals.
Approval fatigue
Volume-driven degradation of review quality — the agentic form of clinical alert fatigue Remedy: Batching, risk-triage of what reaches a human at all.
assist
Drafts, summarises or analyses. No decision about a person is attached to the output.
Assist / recommend / determine
Deployment classes: assist = drafting/summarisation, no decision; recommend = informs a decision a person makes; determine = constitutes or directly produces the decision.
Assisted digital
Support for people who cannot use a digital service independently.
Assurance tier
The proportionate level of control an agent attracts, derived from criticality rather than popularity.
ATRS
Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard — the UK format for publishing algorithmic tool use.
Authority
What an agent is permitted to do, as distinct from what it is technically capable of doing.
Automation bias
The tendency to accept an automated output without enough scrutiny.
Automation complacency
Reduced monitoring effort — not looking rather than looking and agreeing Remedy: Canaries; anti-streak interventions.
Automation drift
The gradual shift of an automated system's behaviour or use over time so it no longer aligns with the original design intent or approved scope. (Adopted from TBS Canada.)
Automation drift vs model/data/concept drift
Automation drift is behaviour or use shifting away from approved scope — a governance question. Model, data and concept drift are statistical changes in inputs or the target relationship — an ML operations question.
Autonomy level
How far an agent may act without a human decision, from suggest-only to bounded execution.
Barometer
The eight-dimension readiness self-assessment held on the reader's own device.
bias_pattern
The output reflects a disparate pattern across a protected characteristic.
Bimodality coefficient
(skew²+1)/(excess kurtosis + 3(n−1)²/((n−2)(n−3))); >~0.555 suggests bimodality; applied to time-to-decision as rubber-stamping signature.
Bounded autonomy
TBS Canada principle: tight explicit limits on data, tools, permissions and scope; labelled activity level ('draft only','read only'); named trained owners incl. sub-agents.
Canary
Synthetic known-bad output injected at low randomised rate under ethics approval with guaranteed downstream suppression.
canary.detected
True only where the reviewer's action demonstrates detection — modify, reject or escalate citing the seeded defect. Accepting a canary is never 'detected'.
Capability class
Whether a deployment is generative, agentic or declarative — the determinant of which controls carry the weight.
caseworker
Handles individual cases within established policy.
central_department
Ministerial or non-ministerial department.
Cognitive debt
Kosmyna et al. term for reduced cognitive engagement and unaided performance after LLM assistance.
Compensatory use
AI use that offsets a stable access barrier — one that's stable regardless of effort (e.g. drafting support for dyslexia, checking tone, structuring a first draft, holding several things in working memory). Carries little skill-atrophy risk because the underlying skill was never the bottleneck. 'This is what assistive technology is.'
Comprehension debt
Loss of understanding of code created via AI generation; targeted by comprehension gates at PR.
confidence_gated
The output was withheld because model uncertainty was high.
Conformance pack
A bundle of automated checks that tests an artefact against a named standard.
Connector
An integration that lets an AI tool read from, or write to, another system.
consecutive_unmodified_count
Derived from the actual ordered sequence of dispositions within a session. Reset to zero on any disposition other than 'accept'. Never estimated or sampled.
Contestability erosion
If the decision-maker cannot explain reasoning, the citizen cannot meaningfully challenge it.
Copilot Credit
The consumption billing unit for Microsoft agent activity, replacing the previous message unit from 1 September 2025.
Counterfactual
The comparison against which a benefit is measured, typically a group not using the tool.
Criticality
Operational dependency and consequence of failure, scored across ten dimensions to set the gate.
Crypto-agility
The ability to change cryptographic algorithms without redesigning the system.
Curb-cut framing / effect
Framing an accessibility tool by benefits that accrue to everyone, rather than as a deficit fix.
Currency
Recency/proficiency regime by analogy with aviation recency and clinical revalidation; NHS DCB0129/DCB0160 Clinical Safety Officer as domestic precedent.
Data boundary
A supplier commitment about where data is stored and processed. Check which features and models sit outside it.
DBT 'cold turkey' test
Imagine the licence removed tomorrow: which tasks become mildly annoying vs genuinely destabilising.
Decay class
How quickly a claim goes out of date: structural, positional, volatile or expiring.
Declarative
A capability defined by a specification — instructions, sources, permitted actions and constraints — that the platform executes.
Declarative agent
An agent defined by configuration: purpose, instructions, knowledge and permitted actions, run on a platform’s own model and orchestration.
Degraded-mode operating standard
Every agentic deployment demonstrates periodically and for real that the service runs without the agent at acceptable quality for a defined period.
DEIA
Diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility.
Delegation competence
Skill of setting appropriate bounds, reading evidence they are wrong, and withdrawing agency without service collapse. Replaces task-audit definition of oversight competence.
Deployment route
The same model reached directly, through a cloud platform or inside another supplier’s product is a different governance object each time.
Deprecation
A supplier’s notice that a model, feature or interface will be withdrawn.
determine
The output constitutes, or directly produces, a decision about a person.
Deterministic automation
Rules-based automation that gives the same output for the same input every time.
developer
Builds or maintains the system.
Digital worker
An agent framed as a managed member of the workforce, with recruitment, probation, review and retirement.
disconfirmation_panel
Contradicting evidence was surfaced alongside the output.
DPIA
Data protection impact assessment, required for high-risk processing.
Drift
Divergence between a cited source, a model version or a control and what is actually in use.
Earned autonomy
Teams demonstrating sustained catch performance move to lighter oversight modes and higher agent autonomy.
Easy Read
Accessible format: short sentences, one idea per chunk, large type, simple icon per point, plain words, explicit permission to ignore what doesn't fit; normally reviewed by Easy Read readers before publication.
edit_distance_normalised
Normalised difference between the output as presented and the output as finalised, in [0,1]. Report the algorithm used alongside the data; values are not comparable across different distance measures.
EQIA
Equality impact assessment evidencing the public sector equality duty.
equality_concern
The output raised a potential discriminatory or disparate-impact issue.
escalate
Referred to another person or process rather than decided.
Evidence card
The standard record of a claim: what was done, method, result, publisher, date and known limitations.
Evidence log
A record of how a piece of AI-assisted work was produced, retained with the work.
Evidence pack
The bundle of records proving how an AI-assisted output was produced, checked and approved.
Exit path
The seven-step route out of a platform, model or supplier dependency: discover, target, design, extract, test, cutover, decommission.
Expiring
Carries an explicit date. Auto-flags for review on that date.
extension
Local codes must be namespaced with a 'x_' prefix (e.g. 'x_local_triage_override'). Anything unprefixed is reserved for the central vocabulary so that local extension never collides with a future addition.
FACT / INTERPRETATION convention
Evidence-discipline convention used in turn-5 paragraph.
factual_correction
A fact in the output was wrong.
factual_error
A verifiably incorrect fact.
FASTER principles
Canada: Fair, Accountable, Secure, Transparent, Educated, Relevant.
FinOps
The practice of joining consumption, cost, quality and value so spend is forecast, allocated and optimised.
Friction budget
f(consequence of error × model uncertainty × recency of demonstrated catch performance × novelty of the case).
Generative
A capability that produces content, analysis or options; nothing changes until a person acts on the output.
Grounding
Supplying authoritative source material so outputs can be traced, cited and checked.
Guardrail
A constraint that holds regardless of instruction: prohibited actions, data limits, escalation triggers.
Harvest now, decrypt later
Capturing encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computers are capable.
high
Statutory or rights-bearing; detriment is material and correction requires appeal or is not possible.
Human in the loop
A person who must act before an output takes effect.
Human on the loop
A person who monitors and can intervene in an otherwise automated process.
Human-agent system
The agent, the people who instruct and review it, and the controls between them, tested as one.
Information asset owner
The named person accountable for an information asset, its use, sharing and risks.
injected_instruction
Content in the case record attempts to redirect the agent.
Instruction block
The seven-part specification of an agent's behaviour: goal, context, sources, task, format, guardrails, output.
insufficient_confidence
The reviewer could not satisfy themselves either way and did not proceed.
Investment line
The full cost of adoption: visible, foundational, people and change, operational, and transition and exit.
Ironies of automation
Automation takes the easy, routine parts and leaves humans the hard residue while removing the routine practice through which people became competent at the hard parts. Structural root of the programme.
Kill switch
A control that stops an agent immediately and blocks further actions.
Lapsed
Had a stated end date which has now passed. Status after that date is unknown.
Least privilege
Granting only the minimum permissions needed for the shortest necessary time.
local_authority
Principal council or combined authority.
Lock-in
Dependency on a platform, model, connector or supplier that raises the cost or risk of leaving.
low
Recoverable before effect; no material detriment.
manager
Supervises a team performing any of the above.
Material AI assistance
AI involvement that a reasonable reader would want disclosed because it shaped the output.
Meaningful human involvement
Under the UK GDPR, a significant decision with no meaningful human involvement counts as solely automated and needs safeguards, including the right to contest it (Articles 22A to 22C, from 5 February 2026). The ICO's draft guidance says the person must have the authority, training and information to change the outcome, and actually consider it.
medium
Correctable through normal review; some detriment or delay.
missing_context
The output was reasonable on what it saw but omitted material the reviewer held.
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
An open standard that lets an AI client call tools and read resources on an outside system through one interface.
Model version churn
Silent model upgrade resets the error profile human trust calibration was built against.
Model-dependent finding
Finding about a specific model's output quality at a point in time; short half-life; re-verify before citing.
modify
Used after alteration.
Monoculture / correlated error
A few frontier models underpin most deployment so errors correlate across services.
Moral crumple zone
A human positioned as the responsible party for a system they could not realistically have controlled; liability absorption rather than accountability.
Neurodiverse (preferred) vs neurodivergent
The preferred term in this portal is "neurodiverse", used throughout the Inclusive use section.
nhs
NHS body or integrated care system.
none
Standard presentation.
Not located
The cited item could not be found to exist at all.
Novice pipeline
The supply of experienced people to do oversight, threatened by removal of entry-level roles whose routine work functioned as practice.
Orphaned agent
An agent still in use whose owner has moved on — the most common governance failure in a growing estate.
other_public_body
Any other public sector organisation.
Out-of-the-loop performance
Inability to re-acquire situational awareness fast enough when the system hands back Remedy: Handback design; keeping the human's mental model warm.
out_of_scope
The output addressed something outside the agent's approved scope. Also a drift signal.
Oversharing
Content reachable by more people than intended, usually through accumulated permission drift.
Oversight Assurance Layer
Shared platform component: schema, SDK, prior-capture widget, canary service, baseline scheduler, privacy-enforcing aggregation, currency ledger, conformance suite.
plausible_fabrication
A confident, well-formed output with no basis in the source material.
Plugin
A packaged custom action, such as an MCP or API plugin, that lets an agent read or change data in another system.
policy_misapplication
The output applied the wrong rule, threshold or guidance.
Positional
Who holds a role, what is in force, what has been published. Review quarterly.
PQC
Post-quantum cryptography — algorithms resistant to quantum attack.
Predict-then-reveal
User records provisional judgement (decision, confidence, one-line rationale) before agent output is displayed. Keystone pattern.
predict_then_reveal
The reviewer's provisional judgement was captured before the output was shown.
Preview
A feature released before general availability. Terms, controls and data handling may differ.
Process ossification
Agents encode current process; changing it means re-engineering agents, so process stops evolving.
Prohibited fields
Never present in an oversight event: user_id, staff_id, employee_id, staff_number, person_id, username, email, name, line_manager, ip_address, device_id. These must never appear in an oversight event, at any tier. The privacy contract is what makes the regime credible to staff and to unions; it is enforced in the schema, in the aggregator and in the analyser, not merely stated here.
Promotion gate
The checkpoint between personal, team, departmental, operational and cross-government scope.
Prompt injection
Untrusted content that manipulates a model into unintended actions.
Proportionality
Control matched to risk, autonomy, data sensitivity, decision influence and public effect.
Provenance
The verifiable record of where content, data or code came from and how it changed.
Provenance rot
Case records increasingly contain agent-generated text that future agents retrieve as evidence; record ceases to be an independent source.
reason_required
Approval required a structured reason.
Reasoned-disagreement sampling
Sample cases for independent human reasoning; grade quality of reasoning on both sides; never treat divergence as error. Replaces unaided-baseline sampling.
recommend
The output informs a decision that a person then makes about someone.
Recoverability
TBS Canada principle: pause/stop/return-to-safe-state by design; actions logged in a system the agent cannot alter; fail safely.
Register
The eighteen-field record every agent needs, held by the owning organisation, not by this guide.
reject
Not used; the reviewer produced their own outcome.
Residual risk
What remains after controls are applied — stated, owned and accepted rather than assumed away.
Responsibility diffusion
Accountability becomes hard across sub-agents, tool calls and cross-departmental service composition.
review
Proposed additions go to the vocabulary owner with a definition, a worked example, and a statement of why an existing code does not fit.
reviewer
Second-line check on another person's or system's output.
Scheme of delegation
Government's existing model of delegated authority with limits, thresholds, named accountable officers and withdrawal; agents should sit inside it.
Scissor (volume vs capability)
Volume requiring oversight rises with adoption while capability to oversee falls with the same adoption; reinforcing loop overload→skimming→atrophy.
scope_overstep
The agent proposes an action outside its permitted scope.
senior_caseworker
Handles complex or escalated cases.
Seniority-biased technological change
Harvard working-paper term for entry-level hiring falling at generative-AI-adopting firms.
Shadow AI
Unregistered tools in operational use: unknown ownership, cost and risk. Maturity level zero.
Skill
A packaged, versioned capability an assistant or agent can invoke, with defined inputs and limits.
Skill atrophy
Degradation of the knowledge and practised judgement that oversight roles depend on, caused by sustained offloading of the underlying task. (Adopted from TBS Canada.)
Sophistication index
The prototype quality score across grounding, evaluation, guardrails, observability and support.
Source tiering
Ranking sources by authority so conflicts resolve predictably.
stability
Codes are additive. A code is never removed or repurposed; superseded codes are marked deprecated with a successor.
stale_data
The output relies on superseded information.
Structural
An argument, framework or finding about how things work. Review annually.
Structural finding
Human-factors/organisational finding about people and institutions; durable across model versions.
Subprocessor
A third party that processes data on behalf of the supplier, such as a model provider.
Substitutive use
AI use that replaces a judgement the practitioner would otherwise exercise (e.g. assessing whether an argument holds, deciding a course of action, interpreting data, summarising a policy paper one would otherwise have read). Carries the same oversight risk regardless of neurotype.
Superseded
Was correct when recorded; a later event has changed the position.
Supervisory control
Human-automation interaction concept; agency is a variable set per task and context on a levels-of-automation scale.
time_to_decision_ms
From presentation of the output to recording of the disposition. Excludes time before the item was opened.
tone_or_style
Presentation only; substance unchanged.
Unit economics
Cost and value per interaction: the figure that decides whether an agent earns its keep.
Unverified
No accessible primary or strong institutional source located across two independent passes. Not relied upon.
Verification state
Whether a claim is verified, verified in substance, unverified, superseded, lapsed or not located.
Verified
Source located; organisation, date and substance all confirmed.
Verified in substance
Claim is correct but the originally cited link, reference or date did not resolve.
Vigilance decrement
Sustained-attention performance falls sharply within the first half hour of monitoring Remedy: Queue design, shift length, task interleaving.
Volatile
Supplier rate cards, product availability, live counts. Verify at point of use; never cache.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to declare every use of AI?

No. Declare material assistance — where AI shaped the substance, structure, analysis or code of an output. Trivial uses such as spell-checking do not need a declaration, but your local policy may set a lower threshold.

Can AI approve my work?

No. AI can suggest, draft, check and explain. Approval is a human act by someone with the authority to make that decision. AI never grants authority a user does not already hold.

What if the AI cites a source that does not exist?

Treat it as an incident. Do not publish. Verify every citation against the original, log the failure in the drift and incident register, and check whether the same prompt pattern has been used elsewhere.

Is this a substitute for a DPIA, EQIA or security assurance?

No. This toolkit helps you prepare and evidence those assessments; it does not replace them or the professionals accountable for them.

Can I paste official-sensitive information into a general assistant?

Not unless the tool is explicitly approved for that classification and the data-handling terms have been assured. When in doubt, do not paste — ask your information asset owner.

How do I handle AI-generated code?

Treat it as untrusted third-party code: review it, test it, scan dependencies, record provenance and never merge without a human reviewer who understands it.

What accessibility duties apply to AI-generated content?

The same ones that apply to everything else. WCAG 2.2 AA, plain language, alternative formats and the accessibility statement duty all apply regardless of who or what drafted the content.

Who do I contact if something goes wrong?

Your service owner and the named AI assurance contact for your organisation. Report near-misses too — they are the cheapest form of learning.

Trust and transparency

How to check, challenge and contribute

A guidance utility that cannot be questioned is not trustworthy. Here is how this one is governed, and how you hold it to account.

Provenance of this content

Every substantive claim links to a tiered source. Where this portal expresses an opinion or a house rule rather than a legal requirement, it says so.

Licence and reuse

CC BY 4.0 (content) / MIT (code); Crown copyright material quoted here stays under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Fork it, adapt it for your organisation, and tell us what you changed so others benefit.

Data and privacy

This site is static and client-side. It sets no tracking cookies, runs no analytics that identify you, and sends nothing you type in the tools to any server. Preferences are stored locally in your browser and you can clear them at any time.

Known limitations

This is a concept portal, not a statutory instrument. It does not replace your organisation's policies, your DPO, your security team or your legal advice. Some linked standards sit behind paywalls.

Report a problem

Tell us about a broken link, an out-of-date claim, an accessibility barrier or a gap. Accessibility issues get a response within five working days.

Gaps and roadmap

What is missing, prioritised with MoSCoW

An honest backlog is a trust signal. These are the gaps identified in this portal and in most public sector AI guidance, ordered by whether they are essential, valuable, desirable or deliberately out of scope.

Must have

Named accountable owner and published contact route

Nothing on this page is credible without a person who owns it and answers questions.

Must have

Accessibility statement, testing evidence and feedback route

Legally required for UK public sector sites; also the fastest trust signal.

Must have

Version, last-reviewed and next-review dates on every artefact

Freshness is the main failure mode of guidance portals.

Must have

Machine-readable metadata schema published openly

Without a schema, registries cannot federate and evidence cannot be automated.

Must have

Risk-based human review model with no self-approval

The core control that keeps accountability with people.

Must have

Source citation and provenance for every claim

Prevents hallucination becoming policy.

Must have

DEIA screening built into the default workflow

Equality duty is a due-regard duty — it must happen before decisions, not after.

Should have

Search across the whole corpus with filters and permalinks

Findability is the top usability complaint for guidance sites.

Should have

Role-based entry points and task-first navigation

Users arrive with a task, not an interest in your information architecture.

Should have

Downloadable, offline and printable formats

Supports assisted digital, low bandwidth and audit contexts.

Should have

Worked examples and anti-patterns for each control

Abstract principles do not change behaviour; examples do.

Should have

Change log and subscribe-to-updates

Lets teams re-check work when guidance changes.

Should have

Multilingual and alternative-format provision (Welsh, Easy Read, BSL)

Statutory in some contexts and essential for inclusion in all.

Should have

Automated link-health and freshness checking

Broken authority links silently destroy trust.

Could have

API and JSON export of the registry and corpus

Enables reuse by other departments and tooling.

Could have

Maturity self-assessment with benchmarking

Helps organisations see where they are without a consultant.

Could have

Community contribution workflow with moderation

Scales the corpus beyond a single team.

Could have

Interactive decision tree for tool selection

Reduces the "which tool may I use?" support burden.

Could have

Carbon and cost telemetry per model call

Makes proportionality measurable rather than rhetorical.

Won't have (this time)

Automated approval of any high-risk output

Out of scope by design — approval stays human.

Won't have (this time)

Storing personal or official-sensitive data in this portal

The portal is public and stateless; sensitive records belong in assured systems.

Won't have (this time)

Vendor-specific lock-in to a single model provider

Conflicts with interoperability and exit obligations.

Won't have (this time)

Replacing professional assurance roles

The toolkit supports specialists; it does not substitute for them.

Contact, feedback and support

Tell us what is wrong, missing or unclear

Every route below goes through GitHub, so it is public and auditable. There is no email route. Choose the one that fits — if you are not sure, raise an issue and we will redirect it.

Bug

Something is broken

Broken links, tools that do not work, layout failures, incorrect calculations or console errors.

Report a bug on GitHub

Accessibility

An accessibility barrier

Anything that stops you using this site with a screen reader, keyboard, magnification, voice control or any other assistive technology. These are treated as priority defects.

Report a barrier

Target first response: 5 working days.

Feature

A feature or resource request

A tool you need, a section that is missing, or an authoritative source that should be in the library.

Request a feature

Correction

Content is wrong or out of date

Superseded guidance, a withdrawn standard, a mis-stated legal duty or a dead authority link. Include the source that proves it.

Submit a correction

Security

A security vulnerability

Do not open a public issue. Use private disclosure so we can fix it before it is known. See our security policy for scope and timescales.

Report privately

Discussion

A question or an idea

Not sure it is a defect? Want to talk about approach, reuse this in your organisation, or contribute? Start there.

Use the contact form

Write it here first

This form helps you write a clear report, then opens the GitHub contact form with it filled in. Issues are public: do not include personal data, case details or anything above OFFICIAL. For a security problem, use private reporting instead.

Do not include personal data about anyone else, case details, credentials or anything above OFFICIAL.

A preview of your message will appear here before anything is sent.

What happens to your message

How it is handled

  • • Nothing is transmitted from this page. The form builds a report and opens GitHub with it, so you stay in control of what is posted.
  • • GitHub issues are public. Do not put personal or sensitive information in them.
  • • Accessibility reports are logged as defects with a target first response of five working days.
  • • Security reports follow coordinated disclosure and are never opened as public issues.

If we cannot resolve it

  • • Ask for the decision to be reviewed by the accountable owner named in the transparency section.
  • • For accessibility complaints in the UK, you can escalate to the Equality Advisory and Support Service.
  • • For data protection concerns, contact the host organisation's data protection officer, then the Information Commissioner's Office.
  • • All correspondence about this repository is capable of being disclosed under freedom of information law.

Make guidance usable, testable and accountable.

Start with the corpus, encode the metadata, publish the skills, bound the agents, enforce the review — and keep improving it in the open.
